args.research_brief:
I want to understand how Netflix managed to successfully adapt Gabriel García Márquez's *One Hundred Years of Solitude* for the screen, given that the novel is widely considered "unfilmable" due to its dense narrative, magical realism, nonlinear timeline, and large cast of characters. Specifically, I want to know:

1. What creative and production strategies did Netflix employ (e.g., screenwriting approach, narrative structure, visual style for magical realism, casting decisions, use of language/dialogue, music/sound design)?
2. How did Netflix secure the rights to the novel, and what role did the García Márquez estate or family play in the adaptation process?
3. Was the production filmed in Colombia, and to what extent did Netflix collaborate with local talent (directors, writers, actors, crew) to ensure authenticity?
4. How did the adaptation handle the novel's magical realism — what specific visual effects, cinematography, or directorial choices were made to bring this element to life?
5. What was the critical and audience reception, and how does it compare to previous failed attempts to adapt the novel?
6. What was the budget, timeline, and scale of the production?

I am open to any reputable sources, but I would prefer to prioritize official Netflix press releases, interviews with the showrunners/directors/writers, articles from major entertainment publications (Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, The New York Times), and academic or critical analyses of the adaptation. Since the novel is originally in Spanish, sources in Spanish are also welcome.

args.research_topic: Netflix adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel García Márquez — Rights acquisition, García Márquez family/estate involvement, budget, production timeline, and overall scale of the series. This includes: how Netflix obtained the rights to the novel (which was long considered unadaptable and whose rights were fiercely guarded by the García Márquez family), what role the García Márquez estate (including his sons Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha) played in the adaptation process, the reported budget for the series, the production timeline from announcement to release, and the scale of the production (number of episodes, runtime, etc.). Look for official Netflix press releases, interviews with Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha, and reports from Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, and The New York Times.

Netflix adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude — Creative and production strategies used to adapt the novel. This includes: the screenwriting approach (who wrote the screenplay, how they adapted the dense narrative and nonlinear timeline), the narrative structure chosen for the series, the visual style and cinematography choices used to depict magical realism, casting decisions (who was cast and how they were selected), the use of language (Spanish vs. indigenous languages, dialogue style), and music/sound design. Also research specific visual effects and directorial choices made to bring the novel's magical realism elements to life. Look for interviews with the showrunners, directors, screenwriters, cinematographers, and production designers. Sources should include interviews with directors like Alex García López or Laura Mora, production notes from Netflix, and articles from major entertainment publications.

Netflix adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude — Filming in Colombia, collaboration with local talent, and critical reception. This includes: was the production filmed entirely in Colombia and what specific locations were used; to what extent did Netflix collaborate with Colombian directors, writers, actors, and crew to ensure authenticity; what was the critical and audience reception of the series (including reviews, ratings, and audience response); and how does this adaptation compare to previous failed attempts to adapt the novel (such as the attempts by Emir Kusturica, Anthony Quinn, or others). Look for information about Colombian talent involved, including directors like Laura Mora (Colombian) and Alex García López (Argentine-Colombian), and reports from Colombian media outlets as well as international reviews. Spanish-language sources are welcome.

The streaming company announced on Wednesday that the book will be adapted into a Spanish-language series and filmed largely in the author’s home country of Colombia. Márquez’s sons, Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha, will serve as executive producers.

Acquiring rights to adapt *One Hundred Years of Solitude* wasn't easy. García said that his father was sceptical of the novel fitting within a traditional film structure, and wanted the story to be told in Spanish.

“For decades our father was reluctant to sell the film rights to One Hundred Years of Solitude because he believed that it could not be made under the time constraints of a feature film, or that producing it in a language other than Spanish would not do it justice," García said.

“But in the current golden age of series, with the level of talented writing and directing, the cinematic quality of content, and the acceptance by worldwide audiences of programs in foreign languages, the time could not be better to bring an adaptation to the extraordinary global viewership that Netflix provides. We are excited to support Netflix and the filmmakers in this venture, and eager to see the final product," he added.

“We are incredibly honoured to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world," said Francisco Ramos, Vice President, Spanish Language Originals for Netflix. “We know our members around the world love watching Spanish-language films and series and we feel this will be a perfect match of project and our platform."

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* follows the Buendía dynasty, founders of the rural and isolated town of Macondo, and fuses fantastical and allegorical elements such as rains of yellow flowers, alchemy and religious apparitions, with realism and history. It became a defining work of magical realism and one of the most celebrated Latin American novels of the 20th century, having sold an estimated 47 million copies and been translated into 46 languages.

Netflix's *Narcos*, which is also based on the concept of magic realism in parts, was a successful venture.

Another seminal work by Márquez, *Love In The Time of Cholera*, was adapted into a film by Mike Newell in 2007, starring Javier Bardem and Benjamin Bratt. His *Chronicle of a Death Foretold* was adapted for both film and Broadway.

# Netflix buys the rights to make first ever adaptation of 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'

Gabriel García Márquez's iconic novel will become a Spanish language series.

By

[Laura Byager](/author/laura-byager)

 on

[Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Farticle%2Fgabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix "(opens in a new window)")   [Share on Twitter](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Farticle%2Fgabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix&text=Netflix+buys+the+rights+to+make+first+ever+adaptation+of+%27One+Hundred+Years+of+Solitude%27 "(opens in a new window)")   [Share on Flipboard](https://share.flipboard.com/bookmarklet/popout?v=2&url=https%3A%2F%2Fmashable.com%2Farticle%2Fgabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix&title=Netflix+buys+the+rights+to+make+first+ever+adaptation+of+%27One+Hundred+Years+of+Solitude%27 "(opens in a new window)")

![Netflix buys the rights to make first ever adaptation of 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'](https://helios-i.mashable.com/imagery/articles/04mKxkKgOzMtKPzOmWnT667/hero-image.fill.size_1248x702.v1623383965.jpg)

The family of Gabriel Garcia Marquez, who passed away in 2014, sold the rights to 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' to Netflix Credit: Ulf Andersen/Getty Images

---

The first ever screen adaptation of Nobel Prize winning author Gabriel García Márquez's classic novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude* is coming to Netflix.

The streaming service will be turning the 1967 magical realist masterwork into a Spanish language original series, the company [said in a press release.](https://media.netflix.com/en/press-releases/netflix-acquires-the-rights-to-develop-gabriel-garc%C3%ADa-m%C3%A1rquezs-masterpiece-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-as-a-new-netflix-series "(opens in a new window)") The series will be shot mainly in Márquez's home country of Colombia, and will have the author's two sons as executive producers.

SEE ALSO:  [Netflix's 'Paddleton' shows how desperately we need the words to describe our more-than-friendships](/article/paddleton-review)

Rodrigo García, Márquez's eldest son, said that while their father, who passed away in 2014, was reluctant to sell the rights to his novel, the family trusts that the Netflix production will do his work justice.

"For decades our father was reluctant to sell the film rights to *Cien Años de Soledad* because he believed that it could not be made under the time constraints of a feature film, or that producing it in a language other than Spanish would not do it justice,” Rodrigo García said in the press release, adding that given that we live in "golden age of series," the time for an adaptation could "not be better."

Rodrigo García [elaborated in an interview with The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/06/books/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-is-coming-to-netflix.html?smid=tw-nytimes&smtyp=cur "(opens in a new window)"), saying that his father's main concern about adapting *One Hundred Years of Solitude* into a movie had been that the story is too big and complicated to tell in one or even two feature films.

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* tells the story of the Buendía family through seven generations in a fictional town in Colombia.

Some fans of the novel expressed scepticism on social media at the idea of a screen adaption of the novel. Given the vastness of the story, and the fact that it belongs in the magical realist genre, it's not going to translate well onto the screen, writer [Kara Brown](https://twitter.com/KaraRBrown "(opens in a new window)") said in a thread of tweets that received over 1,7 K likes.

"Anyone who has read it and actually understands it knows this book cannot and should not be a made into a movie," Kara Brown wrote.

> [This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed.](https://twitter.com/KaraRBrown/status/1103313700784504832 "(Opens in a new tab) (opens in a new window)")

Vice President of Spanish Language Originals for Netflix, Francisco Ramos, said in Netflix's press release that the company is "thrilled" to be trusted with the work of adapting the iconic novel.

"We are incredibly honoured to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world,” Ramos said.

Netflix has had great success with Spanish language content in the past, such as hit series *Narcos* and the Oscar nominated movie *Roma.*

args.summary: Netflix has acquired the rights to produce the first-ever screen adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's iconic 1967 novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (Cien Años de Soledad). The novel will be adapted as a Spanish-language original series, shot primarily in Colombia, with García Márquez's two sons serving as executive producers. The author's eldest son, Rodrigo García, explained that their father was previously reluctant to sell the film rights because he believed the story was too vast and complex to be told in a feature film format, but the family now believes that the "golden age of series" makes this the right time for adaptation. The novel tells the multi-generational story of the Buendía family across seven generations in a fictional Colombian town. Some fans expressed skepticism about adapting the magical realist novel to screen, with writer Kara Brown stating the book "cannot and should not be made into a movie." Netflix's Vice President of Spanish Language Originals, Francisco Ramos, expressed the company's excitement and honor at being entrusted with the adaptation. Netflix has previously found success with Spanish-language content including "Narcos" and "Roma."

# Netflix to Adapt Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ for TV

Nobel Prize winner Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s signature novel 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' is headed to Netflix. The video streaming giant has acquired the rights to develop the literary classic, first published in 1967, as a Spanish language TV series.

By
[Etan Vlessing](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/author/etan-vlessing/)

### [Etan Vlessing](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/author/etan-vlessing/)

Canada Bureau Chief

### More Stories by Etan

![Gabriel Garcia Marquez '100 Years of Solitude' to Be Netflix TV](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/gabriel_garcia_marquez.jpg?w=2000&h=1126&crop=1)

Nobel Prize winner Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s signature novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude* is headed to [Netflix](https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/t/netflix/).

The video streaming giant has acquired the rights to develop the literary classic, first published in 1967, as a Spanish-language TV series. Garcia Marquez’s sons Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo Garcia Barcha will executive produce the series, to be shot in Colombia.

“For decades our father was reluctant to sell the film rights to *Cien Anos de Soledad* because he believed that it could not be made under the time constraints of a feature film, or that producing it in a language other than Spanish would not do it justice,” said Garcia in a statement.

The Colombian writer’s other novels like *Chronicles of a Death Foretold* and *Love in a Time of Cholera* were adapted as movies or TV series, but Marquez never allowed the rights to *One Hundred Years of Solitude* to be optioned as he couldn’t see how a novel about the Buendia family told over many generations could be adapted for the big or small screen.

Alvaro Santana-Acuna, assistant professor of sociology at Whitman College in Washington State, who is writing a book on *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, told *THR* that major Hollywood studios early on came knocking for the adaptation rights to the classic novel, especially after the Colombian writer won the Nobel Prize in 1982.

But Marquez resisted, on creative grounds, while welcoming adaptations of his other novels. “García Marquez was concerned that an adaptation for the screen would reduce the reader’s creativity, as they would imagine characters, events, and places in a more personal way (reading the novel) than when presented on the screen,” Santana-Acuna explained.

Garcia insisted the talent in writing and direction required to turn his father’s novel into a TV series was now at hand. “We are excited to support Netflix and the filmmakers in this venture, and eager to see the final product,” Garcia added.

Francisco Ramos, vp of Spanish language originals for Netflix, added in his own statement: “We are incredibly honored to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world.”

Just over a half century since Garcia Marquez’s novel was published, it has sold an estimated 47 million copies, been translated into 46 languages and become a classic of Latin American literature.

On the Spanish language front, Netflix is also producing a school-set drama, *El Desorden que Dejas*, by the co-creator of hit Netflix series *Elite*, the movie thriller *Hogar* and an animated Christmas family comedy *Klaus*, from director Sergio Pablos.

Netflix has also launched a production hub in Madrid, Spain, which is set to be unveiled April 4.

Attorney Shelley Surpin and the Agencia Literaria Carmen Balcells represented Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s estate in the deal.

args.summary: Netflix has acquired the rights to develop Gabriel García Márquez's iconic novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (Cien Años de Soledad) as a Spanish-language television series. First published in 1967, the literary classic has sold approximately 47 million copies and been translated into 46 languages. The series will be shot in Colombia, with García Márquez's sons Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo Garcia Barcha serving as executive producers. The author had long resisted adapting this novel, believing it couldn't be done justice within the constraints of a feature film or in any language other than Spanish. Francisco Ramos, Netflix's VP of Spanish Language Originals, expressed the company's honor in being entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of this iconic Latin American story. The deal was negotiated through attorney Shelley Surpin and the Agencia Literaria Carmen Balcells.

# Netflix Acquires Rights to ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ by Gabriel Garcia Marquez

[![Sayak Basu of Netflix Acquires Rights to ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ by Gabriel Garcia Marquez](https://thecinemaholic.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/sayak-49.jpg?w=26&h=26&crop=1) Sayak Basu](https://thecinemaholic.com/author/sayak/)

March 6, 2019

[Facebook](#)[Twitter](#)[Pinterest](#)[Reddit](#)[Email](mailto:?subject=Netflix%20Acquires%20Rights%20to%20%E2%80%98One%20Hundred%20Years%20of%20Solitude%E2%80%99%20by%20Gabriel%20Garcia%20Marquez&body=https%3A%2F%2Fthecinemaholic.com%2Fnetflix-acquires-rights-to-one-hundred-years-of-solitutude-by-gabriel-garcia-marquez%2F)

![](https://thecinemaholic.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/onehundredyears.jpg)

[Netflix](https://thecinemaholic.com/upcoming-shows-movies-netflix/) has announced that they have managed to acquire the rights of Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s novel ‘[A Hundred Years of Solitude](https://www.amazon.com/Hundred-Solitude-Harper-Perennial-Classics/dp/0060883286/ref=sr_1_1?crid=3DCBJCADOU44J&keywords=one+hundred+years+of+solitude&qid=1551910683&s=gateway&sprefix=one+hundred+%2Caps%2C411&sr=8-1)‘ which they will be releasing on their platform as a series. Marquez had written his seminal work ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ way back in 1967. The book, along with others like ‘Love in The Time of Cholera’, ‘Chronicle of A Death Foretold’ shot him to literary stardom during the literary movement now known as the ‘Latin American Boom’. Despite having received numerous offers earlier for the novel to be adapted for the screen, the Nobel laureate had refused to sell the rights as he believed it would not be possible to tell the story in one, or even two movies. Moreover, he was also adamant that the series had to be in Spanish.

[Marquez](https://edition.cnn.com/2019/03/06/entertainment/100-years-of-solitude-netflix-trnd/index.html)‘s son, Rodrigo Garcia, who himself is a screenwriter and filmmaker, will be acting as the executive producer along with his brother Gonzalo. Convinced that Netflix will be making the series in Spanish, the family decided to sell them the rights. Garcia said, ” Netflix was among the first to prove that people are more willing than ever to see series that are produced in foreign languages with subtitles. All that seems to be a problem that is no longer a problem.” This is not the first time that Netflix had approached Marquez’s family to obtain the rights of the book as revealed by their Spanish language originals’ vice-president Francisco Ramos. With the success of movies like ‘[Roma](https://thecinemaholic.com/roma-explained/)‘ (2019) and series like ‘[Narcos](https://thecinemaholic.com/shows-like-narcos/)‘ (2015-2017), Netflix was convinced that users were ready to watch good foreign content if the material is strong.

The novel is a poignant tale of a town established by the Buendia family where they live through seven generations and the story follows the rise and fall of this town from the perspective of the family. It is an important novel documenting Colombian history and we see many important historical incidents of Colombia finding their way into the novel and shaping its ending. A TV series is the perfect way to adapt this epic saga for the screen. Marquez had popularized the literary style magic realism through his works, and it will be fascinating to see how it manages to adapt to the screen. “We know it’s going to be very magical and very important for Colombians and Latin America, but the novel is universal”, says Marquez’s son Rodrigo.

Marquez is probably the most famous and respected Colombian in the world. When he passed away in 2014, Colombia declared a three-day national mourning. ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ is his most commercially successful novel, and one of the most popular fictional works of the twentieth century. The fact that it has never before been adapted for the screen makes this a historic moment. Ramos said, “We are incredibly honored to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of One Hundred Years of Solitude, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world”. Rodrigo, Garcia’s son, said, “In the current golden age of series, with the level of talented writing and directing, the cinematic quality of content, and the acceptance by worldwide audiences of programs in foreign languages, the time could not be better to bring an adaptation to the extraordinary global viewership that Netflix provides. We are excited to support Netflix and the filmmakers in this venture, and eager to see the final product.”

Netflix has been doing a great job of presenting viewers with stories from different parts of the world on their platform. This further shortens cultural and social borders in today’s world and helps audiences all across the world to enjoy great stories which would not have been possible earlier.

***One Hundred Years of Solitude*** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): *Cien años de soledad*, Latin American Spanish: [[sjen ˈaɲos ðe soleˈðað]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a [Colombian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") television series based on [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s 1967 novel [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude "One Hundred Years of Solitude"). The series will run for 16 episodes on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), with the first eight released on 11 December 2024. The first part of the second season was released on 5 August 2026, while the series finale is slated to be released on 26 August 2026.

## Production

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Development")]

[Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") acquired the rights to *[One Hundred Years of Solitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude "One Hundred Years of Solitude")* in March 2019.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Before his death in 2014, author [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez") had refused to sell the rights to the novel as he did not believe the time constraints of a feature film were sufficient for a proper adaptation.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The producers scouted several locations for filming, including [Cali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cali "Cali"), [Villavicencio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villavicencio "Villavicencio"), [Girardot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girardot,_Cundinamarca "Girardot, Cundinamarca"), [Palomino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palomino,_Colombia "Palomino, Colombia"), [Santa Marta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Marta "Santa Marta"), and [Barranquilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barranquilla "Barranquilla").[[6]](#cite_note-Guzmán-2024-6)

> As a filmmaker, as a Colombian, it has been an honor and an enormous challenge to work on a project of the complexity and responsibility of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, always trying to understand the difference between literary and audiovisual language, to be able to construct images that contain something of the beauty, poetry and depth of a work that has impacted the entire world. We have done it with love and respect for the novel, with the help of an exceptional technical and human team.

— Director [Laura Mora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Mora "Laura Mora")[[7]](#cite_note-7)

### Casting

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Casting")]

The cast was chosen through an open casting call in 2022.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The casting team saw more than 10,000 candidates for the 25 main roles.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) Only 30% of the cast were professional actors.[[10]](#cite_note-10) In addition to the main cast, 20,000 extras were selected.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The cast was partially leaked on 26 April 2023.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

### Filming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Filming")]

Principal photography on the first part of the series took place from May to December 2023.[[13]](#cite_note-Kay-2024-13) The series was filmed entirely in Colombia,[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) specifically in [La Guajira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guajira_Department "La Guajira Department"), [Magdalena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_Department "Magdalena Department"), [Cesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Department "Cesar Department"), [Cundinamarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cundinamarca_Department "Cundinamarca Department"), and [Tolima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolima_Department "Tolima Department").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The fictional town of [Macondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macondo "Macondo") was built near [Alvarado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvarado,_Tolima "Alvarado, Tolima") by 1,100 workers.[[6]](#cite_note-Guzmán-2024-6) Four versions of the town were built to depict the passage of time.[[13]](#cite_note-Kay-2024-13) The producers purchased furniture from local antique stores and had fabrics and artifacts made by local artisans for the sets.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) Filming required a crew of nearly 600 people, all from Colombia.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Netflix reported that series' production generated 225 billion [COP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_peso "Colombian peso") ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Production on the second part of the series began in February 2025.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

A teaser trailer for the first season was released on 17 April 2024.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) Promotional stills were released on 18 October.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) The first two episodes premiered at the [Círculo de Bellas Artes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Círculo_de_Bellas_Artes "Círculo de Bellas Artes") in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") on 22 November 2024.[[22]](#cite_note-22) The series' first episode screened at the [Biblioteca Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioteca_Vasconcelos "Biblioteca Vasconcelos") in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") on 28 November 2024.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Its first two episodes were screened at the [Havana Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Film_Festival "Havana Film Festival") on 6 December 2024.[[24]](#cite_note-24) The first season, comprising eight episodes, was released in its entirety on Netflix on 11 December 2024.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

A trailer for the second season was released on 17 July 2026.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The second season is scheduled to be released in two parts;[[27]](#cite_note-27) the first seven episodes were released on 5 August 2026 and the series finale will be released on 26 August 2026.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) To promote the second season, Netflix held special screenings in select cities in Colombia.[[1]](#cite_note-De_la_Fuente-2026-1)

## Reception

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Reception")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 83% of 30 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.9/10. The website's consensus reads: "*One Hundred Years of Solitude* faithfully realizes [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s seminal novel with sumptuous polish, making for an adaptation that is nothing short of magical."[[30]](#cite_note-30) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), it has a weighted average score of 80 out of 100, based on 16 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Keith Watson of *[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Telegraph_(London) "The Telegraph (London)")* rated the series five stars out of five, calling it a "faithful but not overly reverent take on Márquez". He commended the cast's performances, specifically those of [Marleyda Soto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marleyda_Soto "Marleyda Soto") and [Claudio Cataño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Cataño "Claudio Cataño").[[32]](#cite_note-32) Helen Coffey of *[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent")* called the series "pretty much perfect" and "nothing short of miraculous". She commended the series' creators for staying faithful to the source material while creating "a piece of visually gorgeous storytelling". She also commended the casting, script, cinematography, and music.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Julio Ricardo Varela of [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC") wrote that the series provides "countless moments of brilliance that prove creating art from other works of art is still possible." He commended the performances of the entire cast, especially Soto, Cataño, and Marco Antonio González, and noted the care that seemed to have gone into the series' production.[[34]](#cite_note-34) Judy Berman of *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* wrote, "Considering the difficulty of the assignment, it's remarkable how close Netflix's splendid *One Hundred Years of Solitude* . . . comes to recreating not just the substance, but also the kinetic spirit of the book." She wrote that the series successfully conveyed the story of the novel without oversimplifying its major themes, including the "ugly but symbolically meaningful aspects of the story, from self-harm to incest". She commended the series' production value, direction, and cinematography.[[35]](#cite_note-35)

Daniel Fienberg of *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* called the series a "gorgeous, ambitious adaptation" of the novel that is "honorable and beautiful, if not without flaws." He noted that much of the series' content was taken verbatim from the novel, which "doesn't always work" on screen, and that "everything plays better when the show is at its most figurative and least literal." He commended García López and Mora's direction, calling the series "breathlessly beautiful at times, lyrical and alive and brimming with visual and intellectual ideas." He concluded, "*One Hundred Years of Solitude* may not be as good as *[Underground Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Underground_Railroad_(miniseries) "The Underground Railroad (miniseries)")* or even *[Station Eleven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station_Eleven_(miniseries) "Station Eleven (miniseries)")*, but it's a worthy and admirable capper for a year of often exceptional prestige adaptations."[[36]](#cite_note-36) Aramide Tinubu of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")* called the series "exquisitely detailed and layered in intricate symbolism" and "one of the most faithful page-to-screen adaptations in recent years." She called the performances "exceptional", but said that certain sequences felt dense. Although she found the pacing "too lackadaisical at times", she wrote, "the beauty of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* allows the viewer to absorb every intricately curated frame and moment."[[37]](#cite_note-37) Carly Lane of *[Collider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collider_(website) "Collider (website)")* called the series "a masterpiece in its own right" and wrote, "Not only does the Spanish-language series breathe new life into Márquez's supposedly unfilmable novel, but it also succeeds as a triumph of filmmaking thanks to stunning cinematography and an epic story that spans across multiple generations of the ill-fated Buendía family." She commended the visuals of Paulo Pérez and María Sarasvati, the production design of [Eugenio Caballero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Caballero "Eugenio Caballero") and [Bárbara Enríquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bárbara_Enríquez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bárbara Enríquez (page does not exist)") [[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bárbara%20Enríquez "pt:Bárbara Enríquez")], and the ensemble's performance.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Jack Seale of *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* rated the series three stars out of five, writing that it "might struggle with the novel's problematic sexual politics, but it's a big, gorgeous adaptation".[[39]](#cite_note-39) Ed Potton of *[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")* rated the series two stars out of five, calling it "gorgeous but lethargic" and writing that it "lacks the vibrancy and energy of the novel". He commended the production design of Caballero and Enríquez, but said the series struggled to translate magic realism to the screen.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

args.summary:
One Hundred Years of Solitude is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel, produced by Netflix and filmed entirely in Colombia in Spanish and Wayuu languages. The series consists of 16 episodes across two seasons. Season 1 (8 episodes) was released on December 11, 2024, and Season 2 (8 episodes) began release on August 5, 2026, with the series finale scheduled for August 26, 2026.

The series follows the multi-generational story of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo. The cast includes Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, Diego Vásquez as José Arcadio Buendía, Marleyda Soto as Úrsula Iguarán, and others. The cast was chosen through an open casting call that saw over 10,000 candidates, with only 30% being professional actors.

Netflix acquired the rights in March 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing a feature film couldn't do justice to the novel. The series was produced with the support of his family, who requested it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors. Principal photography took place from May to December 2023, with a crew of nearly 600 Colombians. The fictional town of Macondo was built near Alvarado, Tolima, by 1,100 workers, with four versions built to depict the passage of time.

The series received positive reviews, with an 83% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes and a Metacritic score of 80/100. Critics praised its faithfulness to the source material, performances, and visual production. It won multiple awards including Best Ibero-American Miniseries at the Platino Awards and numerous India Catalina Awards.

# Colombia’s Cien Años de Soledad Finale Hits Netflix August 2026

By [Mateo Cruz](https://www.riotimesonline.com/author/mateo-cruz/) · July 19, 2026 · 5 min read

Colombia · Life & Culture

Key Facts

—**Release dates.** Seven episodes of Part 2 arrive on 5 August 2026, followed by a standalone grand finale on 26 August 2026.

—**Production base.** The series is a Colombian production by Dynamo, authorised by the estate of Nobel laureate Gabriel García Márquez.

—**Directors.** Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno direct the final eight episodes, with Mora helming the feature-length finale.

—**Cultural showcase.** Special theatrical screenings of the finale will be held in Colombian cities in partnership with Proimágenes Colombia.

—**Narrative scope.** Part 2 covers the final fifty years of the Buendía family saga, including the arrival of the banana company and Macondo’s downfall.

Netflix has confirmed that the Cien Años de Soledad finale will roll out across two dates in August 2026, closing the first-ever screen adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s masterpiece and marking a watershed moment for Colombia’s audiovisual industry on the global stage.

## A Two-Part Farewell to Macondo

The streaming giant announced on 20 May 2026 that the second and final part of \*One Hundred Years of Solitude\* will premiere on 5 August with seven episodes. A standalone grand finale episode, described by trade publication \*Variety\* as a cinematic, nearly two-hour event, will follow on 26 August.

This staggered release strategy is unusual for Netflix and signals the weight the platform places on the property. The finale will also receive special theatrical screenings in select Colombian cities, organised in partnership with Proimágenes Colombia, the country’s film-promotion agency.

## The Stakes for Colombia’s Screen Industry

The adaptation is produced by Dynamo, the Bogotá-based production house behind \*Narcos\* and \*The Hijacking of Flight 601\*, and represents one of the largest international investments in Colombian storytelling to date. While Netflix has not disclosed the production budget, industry observers have consistently framed the series as the platform’s most ambitious Latin American original.

For Colombia, the series functions as a high-profile calling card for local crews, locations, and directorial talent. Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno, both established names in Colombian cinema, direct all eight episodes of Part 2, with Mora taking sole charge of the grand finale.

## What Part 2 Covers: The Unravelling of a Dynasty

The final instalment picks up where Part 1 left off and covers the last fifty years of the Buendía family’s century-long arc. Netflix’s official synopsis promises the arrival of the banana company, Macondo’s deeper connection to the outside world, and the town’s eventual downfall through war, repression, and catastrophe.

Episode titles confirmed for the 5 August release include “The Armistice,” “The Queen of Madagascar,” and “Fernanda del Carpio,” signalling a direct engagement with the novel’s darkest political and supernatural chapters. The title of the 26 August finale remains undisclosed, adding a layer of anticipation for devoted readers and new audiences alike.

## Netflix’s Latin American Prestige Play

The \*Cien Años de Soledad\* adaptation sits at the centre of Netflix’s strategy to anchor its Latin American content slate with prestige literary properties that can travel globally. Part 1, released on 11 December 2024, earned strong critical reviews and performed well on the platform’s global charts, validating the thesis that Spanish-language heritage IP can command worldwide attention.

The series is authorised and executive-produced by García Márquez’s sons, Rodrigo and Gonzalo García Barcha, lending the project a seal of familial legitimacy that matters in a region protective of its literary giants. That authorisation, combined with Netflix’s distribution muscle, creates a model for future adaptations of Latin American classics that have long been considered unfilmable.

## What the Cien Años de Soledad Finale Means for Investors and Expats

For investors tracking Colombia’s creative economy, the finale represents a measurable milestone. The partnership with Proimágenes Colombia for theatrical screenings underscores how streaming productions can generate ancillary economic activity in tourism, hospitality, and local services, particularly in the towns and regions associated with the fictional Macondo.

Our reporting has shown this effect is already underway: since Part 1 premiered, Aracataca—the Caribbean birthplace of Gabriel García Márquez that inspired Macondo—has seen a surge in visitors walking its museum house, old train station, and the streets that shaped the Nobel laureate’s imagination, a trend Colombia has leveraged under its “Colombia: The Country of Beauty” branding.

Expats and professionals living in Colombia will find the August dates a cultural calendar highlight, with the special screenings offering a rare communal viewing experience for a streaming title. The series has already deepened international interest in Colombian literature and locations, a trend likely to accelerate as the finale approaches.

## What to Watch Next

The key unknown remains the exact runtime and title of the 26 August finale, which Netflix is expected to reveal closer to the date. Audience figures for Part 2 will also be closely watched as a barometer of sustained global appetite for Latin American literary adaptations.

Beyond the finale, attention will turn to whether the García Márquez estate and Netflix pursue further collaborations, and whether other streaming platforms accelerate their own investments in the region’s deep literary catalogue. For now, the countdown to Macondo’s last chapter has officially begun.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When does the final part of Cien Años de Soledad premiere on Netflix?

The first seven episodes of Part 2 premiere on 5 August 2026. A standalone grand finale episode follows on 26 August 2026, bringing the adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez’s novel to a close.

### Who directs the final episodes of the series?

Colombian directors Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno share directing duties across the eight episodes of Part 2. Laura Mora directs the grand finale episode on 26 August, which is described as a cinematic, nearly two-hour event.

### Is the Netflix adaptation authorised by Gabriel García Márquez’s family?

Yes. The series is executive-produced by García Márquez’s sons, Rodrigo García Barcha and Gonzalo García Barcha, and is the first authorised screen adaptation of the 1967 novel.

The production is Colombian, made by Dynamo in partnership with Netflix.

Part 2 (seven episodes) premieres on August 5, 2026, followed by a standalone feature-length grand finale on August 26, 2026. The Colombian production by Dynamo, authorized by García Márquez's estate, is directed by Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno. Part 2 covers the final fifty years of the Buendía family saga, including the arrival of the banana company and Macondo's downfall. The series is Netflix's most ambitious Latin American original and a milestone for Colombia's audiovisual industry. Special theatrical screenings will be held in Colombian cities in partnership with Proimágenes Colombia. Since Part 1 premiered in December 2024, Aracataca (García Márquez's birthplace) has seen a surge in tourism. The adaptation is executive-produced by the author's sons, Rodrigo and Gonzalo García Barcha.

# 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' Contributed Over 225 Billion Colombian Pesos to the Colombian Economy

![CADS-EP06-SCN24-10088 1 R V3](//downloads.ctfassets.net/4cd45et68cgf/tTkjGU9K24A27hVaY4QuU/8bfadf47299bbfbcc3b04d33e500ee3d/CADS-EP06-SCN24-10088_1_R_V3.jpg?w=2000)

Entertainment

![Share on Facebook](/images/icons/share-facebook.svg)
![Share on X](/images/icons/share-x.svg)

![Copy link to clipboard](/images/icons/share-link.svg)
![Share with email](/images/icons/share-email.svg)
![](/images/checkmark.svg)

The release of One Hundred Years of Solitude, already on everyone’s lips, marks a milestone for the Colombian audiovisual industry. Its impact goes far beyond the cultural sphere, as this ambitious production has also established itself as an economic driver for the country. According to Netflix data, the production has contributed over 225 billion Colombian pesos to the country's economy. This figure is a measure of the impact to GDP and includes both the impact of our direct spending on the production and of the spending that happens downstream in the supply chain.

The project reaffirmed Colombia as a competitive destination for international productions due to its diverse landscapes, talent, and high quality services, which have been strengthened by an attractive framework of production incentives that allowed one of the most ambitious projects in Latin America to take place in Colombia.

Colombian hands

The commitment made with the Garcia Marquez family established that when it was time to take Macondo out of the imagination and into a physical place, the town had to be located in Colombia and built by Colombian hands. Filmed entirely in Colombia and produced by Dynamo, the series left its mark across the country, with a production team comprising more than 900 people, most of them Colombian.

In Alvarado, Tolima, Netflix's Macondo was constructed on a plot of over 540,000 square meters, chosen not only for its natural landscapes but also for its logistical advantages. The locations team had to not only find the site but also handle tasks such as road improvements, access enhancements, drainage systems, tent installations, land preparation, and topographical studies. 

This project brought together around 150 artisans from all over the country, who collaborated with over 850 local suppliers to engineer the constructions that would make this mythical town tangible. Additionally, to meet the demands of a creative team of this magnitude, the first part of One Hundred Years of Solitude accounted for over 100,000 hotel nights booked in Ibagué throughout the filming process.

The [music](https://open.spotify.com/playlist/5yL8zA7T9YTrPCIErcePrQ?si=21bba7bd2f5e4806) produced for the series also provides this distinct Colombian seal with sounds from Los Gaiteros de San Jacinto, Toto La Momposina's drummer, Carmelo Torres, and Víctor Navarro contributed to the series' soundtrack. In costume design, approximately 40,000 garments were created, 97% of which were made with textiles of Colombian origin.

Where to see 

The series is available on Netflix as of December 11 and has already sparked the acclaim of international critics. 

In addition, locals in Bogota will have the opportunity to visit an exhibition that captures some of the most memorable moments in the production of the series, as well as some of the original costumes designed by Catherine Rodriguez. This exhibition will be available to the public at the Museo El Chicó until December 18. 

One Hundred Years of Solitude Part 1 
Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
Parts: 2
Episodes: 8 episodes (P1) 8 episodes (P2)
Directors Part 1: Alex García López (E. 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8) and Laura Mora (E. 4, 5, and 6)
Executive Producers: Diego Ramírez Schrempp, Juliana Flórez Luna, Andrés Calderón, Josep Amorós, Carolina Caicedo, Alex García López, Laura Mora, José Rivera, Rodrigo García, Gonzalo García Barcha
Production Company: Dynamo
Writers: José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, and Albatros González
Script Consultant: Maria Camila Arias
Directors of Photography: Paulo Pérez and María Sarasvati
Production Designers: Bárbara Enríquez and Eugenio Caballero
Costume Designer: Catherine Rodríguez
Casting Directors: Yolanda Serrano and Eva Leira
Music: Camilo Sanabria and Juancho Valencia
Editors: Irene Blecua and Miguel Schverdfinger
Makeup and Hair Styling: Helmuth Karpf
Visual Effects Supervision: Jose Luis Orozco
Assistant Directors: Jeiver Pinto Vargas and Nataly Valdivieso Gómez
Filming Locations: Departments of La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, and Tolima in Colombia

About One Hundred Years of Solitude:

Married against their parents' wishes, cousins José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán leave their village behind and embark on a long journey in search of a new home. Accompanied by friends and adventurers, their journey culminates with the founding of a utopian town on the banks of a river of prehistoric stones that they baptize Macondo. Several generations of the Buendía lineage will mark the future of this mythical town, tormented by madness, impossible loves, a bloody and absurd war, and the fear of a terrible curse that condemns them, without hope, to one hundred years of solitude.

Published in 1967, One Hundred Years of Solitude is one of the emblematic works of Gabriel García Márquez, winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1982. Considered a masterpiece of Spanish-American and universal literature and receiving enormous popular acclaim, it has sold more than 50 million copies and has been translated into more than 40 languages.

About Netflix:

Netflix is one of the world's leading entertainment services, with 283 million paid memberships in over 190 countries enjoying TV series, films and games across a wide variety of genres and languages. Members can play, pause and resume watching as much as they want, anytime, anywhere, and can change their plans at any time.

About Dynamo:

Founded in 2006, Dynamo is an independent Colombian entertainment company based in Bogota with offices in Mexico City, Madrid and New York. It is one of the most important audiovisual production companies in Ibero-America. To date, Dynamo has produced more than 47 feature films and 25 television series. Dynamo has supported talent including the team behind series like Wild District (Netflix), Crime Diaries (Netflix), Green Frontier (Netflix), The Head of Joaquin Murrieta (Prime Video), Mala Fortuna (Prime Video) and films such as The Hidden Face, Monos and recently Tarumama (HBO Max). Beyond developing original content, Dynamo also offers top- notch production services to foreign producers that wish to shoot in Colombia. It has provided local production services to many ambitious projects, including television shows like Narcos (Netflix), El Chapo (Netflix/Univision), Medellin (Prime Video), Falco (Prime Video) and films like Los 33 with Antonio Banderas, American Made with Tom Cruise, Mile 22 with Mark Wahlberg, and Gemini Man with Will Smith, among others.

**EXCLUSIVE:** Filming the adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* in [Colombia](https://deadline.com/tag/colombia/) delivered a 225BN Peso ($51.8M) economic boost to the country, the streamer said.

Sharing the headline figure with Deadline, [Netflix](https://deadline.com/tag/netflix/) Lat-Am said it is a measure of the impact to Colombian GDP and includes both the impact of its direct spending on the production and of the spending in the downstream supply chain. The number excludes the budget for the series, which has never been broken out.

The [adaptation](https://deadline.com/2024/12/alex-lopez-garcia-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-gabriel-garcia-marquez-netflix-1236200422/) of Gabriel García Márquez’s seminal novel is the biggest TV project ever out of Colombia. In securing the rights to the magical realist tome, Netflix agreed the mythical town of Macondo would be recreated in Colombia and built by Colombians.

args.summary: Netflix's adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude* (also known as *Cien Años de Soledad*) delivered a 225 billion Colombian peso ($51.8 million) boost to Colombia's economy, according to Netflix Lat-Am. The figure measures the impact on Colombian GDP and includes the streamer's direct spending on the production plus downstream supply chain spending, but excludes the series' budget, which has never been disclosed. The adaptation is the largest TV project ever from Colombia, produced by Dynamo and filmed entirely in Colombia with a 900-person production team. The fictional town of Macondo was recreated on a 540,000 sq. meter plot. Netflix agreed to build Macondo in Colombia and employ Colombians as part of securing the rights to the novel. The series has just launched and will be released in two eight-episode installments. Netflix has also curated an exhibition of memorable moments and costumes from the series at Museo El Chicó, running until December 18. Netflix VP of Content for Latin America, Francisco 'Paco' Ramos, noted that this is one of several major programming investments in the region, alongside series like *Senna* and *El Eternaut*.

# The Second and Final Part of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* Arrives in August

Get ready to return to the mythical town of Macondo in *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

After the critically acclaimed launch of Part 1 last year, the breathtaking adaptation of Nobel Prize–winning author Gabriel García Márquez’s bestselling magical realist novel will return for its second and final part in August 2026. The concluding eight episodes will reveal the fate of Macondo and the Buendía family. Check out the brand-new teaser trailer above.

Keep reading to learn what you can expect from Part 2.

![N/A](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/2DuQlx0fM4wd1nzqm5BFBi6ILa8/AAAAQdL21gUxtImllcSkdh7obsRpxkHQ__x0XblPHSKwSAT4uqpDLpqRdVMQ8bjfdW-gYDtLwxpVdoMr-59ZggCYSOMp6ditaU1GU8eD43YN7xZ0ExM79LA2nCg924vwomWnLsj-jFu8Ud49ipN_8q-tI3WE.jpg?r=b9c)

### What is *One Hundred Years of Solitude* about?

The story follows cousins José Arcadio Buendía (Marco González) and Úrsula Iguarán (Susana Morales), who get married against their parents’ wishes and leave their village to embark on a long journey in search of a new home. Accompanied by friends and adventurers, their voyage culminates with the founding of a utopian town on the banks of a river of prehistoric stones that they baptize Macondo. Several generations of the Buendía lineage will shape the future of this mythical town, tormented by madness, impossible loves, a bloody and absurd war, and a terrible curse that condemns them, without hope, to 100 years of solitude.

Claudio Cataño, who felt an “enormous responsibility” in playing Colonel Aureliano Buendía, tells Tudum it was “an honor and a risk” to take on the role. He adds, “Macondo and its host of characters, who I truly feel as my own blood, are universal, but at the same time so unique — so from Colombia, so beautifully tragic that it is impossible not to be trapped in this world.”

Bringing the mythical town’s magical elements to life was a “huge challenge for everyone involved,” Cataño says. “I think the scripts and the direction combine both aspects of magic and humanity, of exuberance and realism. From the performing side, it was an arduous and exquisite pleasure.”

García Márquez’s novel, published in 1967, has sold more than 50 million copies and been translated into more than 40 languages. This adaptation is one of the most ambitious productions in Latin American history, filmed in Spanish and shot in García Márquez’s native Colombia with the support of the author’s family.

“Directing this project has been both a challenge and an adventure. After all, in life, taking risks is necessary to give meaning to what we do,” Alex García López (*The Witcher*), who directed Episodes 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8, tells Netflix. “When diving into the adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, my intention was to create something authentic that carries the stature of an international production, because the story deserves it.”

Laura Mora (*The Kings of the World*, *Frontera Verde*), who helmed Episodes 4, 5, and 6, adds: “As a filmmaker, and as a Colombian, it has been an honor and a huge challenge to work on a project as complex and that carries as much responsibility as *One Hundred Years of Solitude.* I always strived to understand the difference between the literary and audiovisual languages and to be able to construct images that contain the beauty, poetry, and depth of a work that has impacted the entire world. We’ve done it with love and respect for the novel, with the support of an exceptional technical and human team.”

### What is Part 2 of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* about?

After the armistice and signing of the Treaty of Neerlandia, peace still does not reach Macondo. The Conservatives, fearful of Colonel Aureliano Buendía’s threats, plot an attack that — by a twist of fate — brings Fernanda del Carpio from Bogotá to the town. She marries Aureliano Segundo, one of the bastard Arcadio’s untamable twin sons, and gives Úrsula Iguarán her first legitimate heirs.

Meanwhile, the other twin, José Arcadio Segundo, absorbed in José Arcadio Buendía’s manuscripts, accomplishes the patriarch’s wild dreams of connecting Macondo with the world. The railroad’s arrival opens the doors to the banana company, which leads to the town’s downfall and ultimately fulfills Úrsula Iguarán’s curse: The races condemned to 100 years of solitude were not granted a second opportunity on earth.

### How many episodes are there in *One Hundred Years of Solitude*?

The series consists of 16 episodes total, released in two parts containing eight episodes each. The eights episodes of Part 1 are streaming now. On Aug. 5, the first seven episodes of Part 2 will come to Netflix. Those episodes are:

Then, on Aug. 26, the grand finale of the series will premiere. Directed by Laura Mora, this final installment brings the Colombian Nobel laureate’s masterpiece to its close.

![Group of women in historical clothing walking down a cobblestone street in a colonial town, looking forward with serious expressions, holding white cloths, surrounded by colorful old buildings and lanterns.](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/2DuQlx0fM4wd1nzqm5BFBi6ILa8/AAAAQVnYPh9oQlkGhNXSW21Ld7FVwOiE1ftZ1863P0Xma6Y_YCSKRwrX1ZlAYEj_X29we1ikYAwfTr0I7soE2VUIKk4EUe94y2mQ8BjcWZ2cNk0ppK5XJ_Fi5nuXnb6Pm2JKo0-nZevNoxp3jnYfHJSCFMkD.jpg?r=0a7)

### What else can we expect from Part 2 of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*?

Mora will continue to direct, along with Carlos Moreno, a Colombian director known for his work on films like [*Dogwashers*](/title/81089261?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum) and *Perro come perro* and the series [*The Final Score*](/title/81261043?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum) and [*Wild District*](/title/80230435?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum).

Marleyda Soto will be reprising her role as the adult Úrsula Iguarán, and Cataño will return as Colonel Aureliano Buendía. They’ll be joined by Ángela Cano, Emmanuel Restrepo, Estefanía Piñeres, María Adelaida Puerta, Emiliano Pernía, Juanita Molina, Laura Taylor, Obeida Benavides, Julián Román, and Carla Baratta, who all bring García Márquez’s unforgettable characters to life.

“Following the reception from our members and specialized press from all around the world, we are deeply proud to announce that the production of the second part has begun. With this series, we pay tribute to the legacy of Gabriel García Márquez and to Colombia and its extraordinary talent,” says Francisco Ramos, Netflix’s Vice President of Latin America Content. “I express my appreciation for the work of Laura Mora, whose rigor and passion have been fundamental in this journey, and who is now joined by Carlos Moreno, a remarkable Colombian filmmaker and Netflix partner. We are in the best hands to carry the Buendías’ story to a successful conclusion.”

![Behind the scenes of ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude Part 2.’](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/2DuQlx0fM4wd1nzqm5BFBi6ILa8/AAAAQZRFitvT8QoyZlrKh1eAGFTtI_8qmOdBTmZCSoODTAe3ou_8P9kmVsXLkTleW21epyYRNXg7JBLl3jWC1oyfe4mpzaPKpZy6MZ6buSJzMLOx1fClkPnBRRfTmFqGEr-eRCbwqMlc90p3B8pNWiKn2WYu.jpg?r=c53)

### What is *One Hundred Years of Solitude*’srelease date?

Part 2’s first seven episodes arrive on Aug. 5, with the grand finale coming on Aug. 26. You can watch [Part 1 now on Netflix](/title/81087583?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum).

The webpage is a Netflix Tudum article announcing that Part 2 (the final season) of the adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude" will arrive in August 2026. The series consists of 16 total episodes (8 per part). Part 1 is streaming now. Part 2's first seven episodes premiere on August 5, 2026, with the grand finale on August 26, 2026.

The story follows the Buendía family across seven generations in the mythical town of Macondo, dealing with love, war, madness, impossible loves, and a curse of 100 years of solitude. Part 2 picks up after the Treaty of Neerlandia, with political tensions, the arrival of Fernanda del Carpio, the railroad connecting Macondo to the world, and the banana company's arrival leading to the town's downfall.

The adaptation is filmed in Spanish in Colombia, with support from García Márquez's family. Directors include Alex García López (The Witcher) and Laura Mora (The Kings of the World). Returning cast includes Marleyda Soto as adult Úrsula Iguarán, Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, along with many others. New director Carlos Moreno joins for Part 2.

<webpage_content>

# Explore Colombia, the Filming Location of Netflix's 'One Hundred Years of Solitude'

[Teejay Small](/author/Teejay%20Small "Teejay Small")•Dec 15, 2024

![Santa Marta in Colombia](https://cms.travelnoire.com/cdn-cgi/image/format=auto,slow-connection-quality=30,onerror=redirect/https://cms.travelnoire.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/Santa-Marta-in-Colombia.jpg)Photo Credit: (Luis Quintero/Pexels)

If you’re [a Netflix subscriber](https://travelnoire.com/where-was-beauty-in-black-filmed), you may already be familiar with the streamer’s latest [foreign language outing](https://travelnoire.com/where-was-pedro-paramo-filmed), *One Hundred Years of Solitude*. The series, which premiered all 16 episodes of its first season on Dec. 11, has already drawn many viewers thanks to its inventive storytelling, gripping characters and gorgeous setting. It adapts the narrative of famed Colombian author Gabriel García Márquez’s 1967 novel of the same name, which sees seven generations of a close-knit family navigating the tender grasp of fate from the fictional town of Macondo. Though the setting doesn’t exist off-screen, the locale certainly offers a real frame of mind, which you too can embody during your next luxurious [trip through Colombia](https://travelnoire.com/is-colombia-safe).

Luckily, we’ve got the inside scoop on *One Hundred Years Of Solitude*‘s multiple filming locations, each offering a wide variety of beautiful views, day trips and excitement. Whether you’re a super fan of the newly-released Netflix series, or simply looking to broaden your horizons with an international vacation, you can read ahead and get the best tips for crafting your perfect Colombian itinerary. We’ll run through all the finest local restaurants, hotel stays and activities, giving you all the tools you need for a successful adventure.

## La Guajira, Colombia

**Key Scenes:** Most scenes in Macondo show the small settlement situated along a vibrant riverbank; these were mostly shot in the La Guajira department right near Colombia’s stunning northern coastline. The nearby Magdalena area also subs in for a handful of exterior wide shots, meaning both coastal neighborhoods are well worth visiting during your trip to the gorgeous nation.

**Best Time To Visit:** Though Colombia offers plenty of beautiful sights and exciting activities year-round, locals say the best time to visit the nation is during the dry season of December through March. If you love being part of a crowd, and don’t mind paying a premium for your hotel stay, consider booking in mid-February when [Carnival season](https://travelnoire.com/caribbean-carnival-calendar-2025) is in full swing!

**Transportation Options:** Though buses run through the La Guajira area, the department is known to be a little off the beaten path. Major Colombian cities like Cartagena and Santa Marta offer multiple modes of transportation, such as taxis, boats and rideshares. Those looking to explore *One Hundred Years of Solitude*‘s primary shooting locations should consider renting a 4×4 vehicle for the most reliable traversal.

Like many of Latin America’s greatest literary tales, *One Hundred Years of Solitude* offers a sense of magical realism which truly makes Macondo pop on the screen. Whether you’re biting your nails at the plight of the Buendía family, or taking in the sights as droves of newcomers flock to the fictional town, the series instills a deep sense of home, family values, and the inescapable reality of fate. As stated, there is no actual settlement of Macondo in real life, though [the Caribbean shores](https://travelnoire.com/sink-your-toes-into-these-5-famous-caribbean-beaches) of La Guajira and Magdalena serve as a perfect stand-in. Those visiting these exceptional regions should be sure to explore the lush sand dunes, indigenous fishing villages and waterfront food and beverage vendors, to get the most authentic North Colombian experience during your stay.

When booking your trip, you may find it easier to stay in a larger city like Magdalena’s Santa Marta and reserve the actual La Guajira area for a day trip or one-off excursion. Either way, you’ll certainly have enough excitement to round out your trip. Magdalena is home to a vibrant nightlife, tons of upscale restaurants and a wide array of trendy photo opportunities and tourist adventures. On the other hand, La Guajira is more rural, giving way to expert nature hikes, plenty of [wildlife interaction](https://travelnoire.com/web-stories/what-is-the-goal-of-wildlife-conservation) and some of the most beautiful beaches you’ll ever see.

**Things To Do**: Beyond serving as the primary shooting location for *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, La Guajira, Colombia is also home to some of the nation’s most scenic [horseback riding](https://travelnoire.com/play/horseback-riding-expedition) and motorcycle tours. Nature lovers are encouraged to check out the [Seviaka Indigenous People Tubing Tour](https://www.tripadvisor.com/AttractionProductReview-g3754359-d25128918-Seviaka_Indigenous_People_and_Tubing_Tour_in_Palomino-Palomino_La_Guajira_Departm.html) which runs through the very rivers and waterfalls that graced the Buendía family within the show. Others should make it a point to embark upon the [Sanctuary Los Flamingos Tour](https://www.tripadvisor.com/AttractionProductReview-g3754359-d24079284-Sanctuary_Los_Flamingos_Tour-Palomino_La_Guajira_Department.html), or pick up some souvenirs at [El Mercado Nuevo](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g676527-d9851942-Reviews-El_Mercado_Nuevo-Riohacha_La_Guajira_Department.html).

**Where To Eat**: In stark contrast to many vacation spots, the high-class eateries in La Guajira, Colombia offer excellent local flavors at exceedingly affordable prices. A few top-rated spots include [Casa Cocotte Restaurante](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g3754359-d17378052-Reviews-Casa_Cocotte_Restaurante_Palomino-Palomino_La_Guajira_Department.html), [Maria Mulata](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g3754359-d14159306-Reviews-Maria_Mulata-Palomino_La_Guajira_Department.html) and [Restaurante Finca Escondida](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g3754359-d10174317-Reviews-Restaurante_Finca_Escondida-Palomino_La_Guajira_Department.html). Those looking to be a little more adventurous can enjoy fresh seafood at [Restaurante Yotojoro](https://www.tripadvisor.in/Restaurant_Review-g676527-d7771269-Reviews-Restaurante_Yotojoro-Riohacha_La_Guajira_Department.html), or a Caribbean take on Mediterranean flavors from [Pasaporte Caribe](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g3754359-d19997252-Reviews-Pasaporte_Caribe-Palomino_La_Guajira_Department.html).

**Where To Stay**: As stated above, there are a few hotels in La Guajira, though you’re better off looking for a more centrally-located stay in Magdalena. See if you can score an ocean-view room from [Casa Verano Hotel Boutique](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g297484-d15076020-Reviews-Casa_Verano_Hotel_Boutique-Santa_Marta_Santa_Marta_Municipality_Magdalena_Department.html), [Hotel Irotama Lago](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g20326255-d616578-Reviews-Hotel_Irotama_Lago-El_Manantial_Santa_Marta_Municipality_Magdalena_Department.html) or the [Hilton Garden Inn Santa Marta](https://www.tripadvisor.ca/Hotel_Review-g297484-d13393376-Reviews-Hilton_Garden_Inn_Santa_Marta-Santa_Marta_Santa_Marta_Municipality_Magdalena_Departme.html). If you really want to stay a little further inland, you can always check out [Viajero Hostel Tayrona & Ecohabs](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g2627106-d2097622-Reviews-Viajero_Hostel_Tayrona_Ecohabs-Buritaca_Santa_Marta_Municipality_Magdalena_Department.html), which offers a lot of bang for your buck, but will definitely require you to secure your own transportation during your stay.

## Cundinamarca, Colombia

!['One Hundred Years of Solitude' Filming Location pictured: Cundinamarca, Colombia](https://cms.travelnoire.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/GettyImages-2147868640-970x546.jpg)

(Jhojan Hilarion/AFP via Getty Images)

**Key Scenes:** Though *One Hundred Years of Solitude* was shot primarily in the northern regions, the show also contains a number of scenes that took the Buendía clan further south. Much of the show was shot in departments including Cundinamarca and Tolima, located in the central west of the picturesque nation.

**Best Time To Visit:** Much like La Guajira, Cundinamarca is at its driest and most pleasant from the late winter through the spring, with December through February serving as peak months for tourism.

**Transportation Options:** Unlike the more rural areas of Colombia, Cundinamarca has a very robust public transit system, so visitors looking to remain in this general area can rely on buses, taxis, and Ubers during their stay. Of course, you’re always welcome to rent a car or motorcycle as well, especially if you’re looking to make [the 30-hour drive](https://travelnoire.com/best-time-destinations-fall-road-trip) through each of the four key shooting areas of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

Just in case lush beaches and crashing turquoise waves really aren’t your thing, there are other regions of Colombia where fans of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* can visit. The show shot some scenes in the forests and grasslands of Cundinamarca, located over 600 miles inland from the northern coast. Though Cundinamarca and neighboring departments like Tolima don’t offer as many adventures over the open water, these inland areas still contain plenty of exciting activities, perfect for solo travelers, groups or even entire families. [Rock climbing](https://travelnoire.com/memphis-crew-changing-face-of-outdoor-climbing) is a major attraction of these regions, giving way to many adrenaline-fueled activities like cliff-jumping, spelunking and cave exploration.

**Things To Do**: Visitors of Cundinamarca will surely find that the region has some of the most fascinating geology of any vacation spot, as showcased by attractions like [Piedras del Tunjo Archaeological Park](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g1222953-d6840198-Reviews-Piedras_del_Tunjo_Archaeological_Park-Facatativa_Cundinamarca_Department.html). The park, perfect for a leisurely stroll or bike ride, is home to [fossil records](https://travelnoire.com/listicle/100-million-year-old-fossil-found-in-australia-is-rosetta-stone-of-paleontology), ancient cave art and rock formations that date back more than 65 million years. Those looking for a more modern excursion can feel free to venture through the cities of Cundinamarca and Tolima for a look at their gorgeous and unique architecture, as well as their vibrant night markets. [Capilla Valvanera](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g815502-d4217393-Reviews-Capilla_Valvanera-Chia_Cundinamarca_Department.html) and [Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de Fátima](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Attraction_Review-g1488736-d10023700-Reviews-Iglesia_de_Nuestra_Senora_de_Fatima-Tocancipa_Cundinamarca_Department.html) serve as two of the most beautiful manmade structures in the region, drawing crowds of thousands each year.

**Where To Eat**: Though the restaurants in Cundinamarca can run a bit pricier than those in Colombia’s rural areas, these eateries still offer a lot of bang for your buck. Steakhouses like [Faunaticos Parque Tematico](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g1725991-d12216624-Reviews-Faunaticos_Parque_Tematico-Tenjo_Cundinamarca_Department.html), Solomillo Restaurante and [Cafe La Huerta](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g1850878-d3685878-Reviews-Cafe_La_Huerta-Guasca_Cundinamarca_Department.html) serve as local favorites, while trendy spots like [Restaurante El Transportador](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Restaurant_Review-g1019204-d11744058-Reviews-Restaurante_El_Transportador-Cota_Cundinamarca_Department.html) let you dine in style with exciting gimmicks. With blends of Southern barbecue, fresh seafood, Caribbean blends and more, you’d be hard-pressed to find a restaurant in Colombia that won’t leave you begging for more.

**Where To Stay**: Cundinamarca and Tolima are loaded with potential in terms of their luxury hotel options, leaving visitors with an embarrassment of riches. Some of the most luxurious stays include GHL Relax Hotel Club El Puente, [Hotel Tocarema](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g677790-d1652077-Reviews-Hotel_Tocarema-Girardot_Cundinamarca_Department.html) and [Anapoima Natura](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g1641484-d12838738-Reviews-Anapoima_Natura-Anapoima_Cundinamarca_Department.html). Though none of these high-end resorts offer the same rugged, homey vibe as the fictional town of Macondo, that feeling can be replicated with a bungalow booking in the [Hotel Boutique Casa La Bisbal](https://www.tripadvisor.com/Hotel_Review-g6495628-d23143353-Reviews-Hotel_Boutique_Casa_La_Bisbal-Cucunuba_Cundinamarca_Department.html).

args.summary:
This article from Travel Noire (Dec 15, 2024) serves as a travel guide for fans of Netflix's *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, which premiered all 16 episodes of its first season on Dec 11, 2024. The series adapts Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel and was filmed in Colombia. The article details two primary filming locations:

**La Guajira, Colombia** – The primary filming location for the fictional town of Macondo, situated along the northern coastline. Best visited during the dry season (December–March). Transportation is limited; renting a 4×4 vehicle is recommended. Key activities include horseback riding, motorcycle tours, the Seviaka Indigenous People Tubing Tour, and the Sanctuary Los Flamingos Tour. Recommended lodging is in nearby Santa Marta (Magdalena department) at hotels like Casa Verano Hotel Boutique, Hotel Irotama Lago, or Hilton Garden Inn Santa Marta.

**Cundinamarca, Colombia** – Located over 600 miles inland, this department (along with Tolima) was used for forest and grassland scenes. Best visited December–February. Has a robust public transit system. Key attractions include Piedras del Tunjo Archaeological Park (fossil records, ancient cave art, 65+ million-year-old rock formations), Capilla Valvanera, and Iglesia de Nuestra Señora de Fátima. Offers rock climbing, cliff-jumping, spelunking, and cave exploration. Recommended hotels include GHL Relax Hotel Club El Puente, Hotel Tocarema, and Anapoima Natura.

***One Hundred Years of Solitude*** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): *Cien años de soledad*, Latin American Spanish: [[sjen ˈaɲos ðe soleˈðað]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a [Colombian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") television series based on [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s 1967 novel [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude "One Hundred Years of Solitude"). The series will run for 16 episodes on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), with the first eight released on 11 December 2024. The first part of the second season was released on 5 August 2026, while the series finale is slated to be released on 26 August 2026.
