You are tasked with summarizing the raw content of a webpage retrieved from a web search. Your goal is to create a summary that preserves the most important information from the original web page. This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
[Buscar](/search)

# El día que fui a Macondo: Estuve en el set de Cien años de soledad y así fue como se dio vida al universo de Gabriel García Márquez

Con Cien años de soledad, Netflix se embarcó en la producción más grande que jamás había hecho en Colombia. ¿Cómo se logra algo así? Estuve en uno de los sets de filmación para averiguarlo.

Por [Fernanda Pérez Sánchez](/personaje/fernanda-perez-sanchez)

Mauro González / Netflix

La primera vez que escuché el término “valores de producción” fue en una clase de cine, en la universidad. La profesora –una de las mejores que tuve en la carrera– hablaba de cómo algunas películas pueden gustarte o no, pero sus “valores de producción” son innegables. Me gustó cómo sonaba y me gustó empezar a ver cine desde ese punto de vista. Para no ponerme muy escolar, lo voy a resumir en que los valores de producción son todo aquello que no tiene que ver con el guión, con la historia, ni las interpretaciones en una película o serie de televisión: el vestuario, escenografía, fotografía, iluminación, música, ahí encontrarás los famosísimos valores de producción.

Si en esa clase de la universidad alguien me hubiera dicho que unos cuantos años después estaría preparándome para viajar a **Colombia** a conocer **las [locaciones donde estaban grabando Cien años de soledad](https://www.vogue.mx/estilo-de-vida/articulo/macondo-netflix-cien-anos-de-soledad)**, sinceramente, no lo hubiera creído.

Curiosamente, en el aeropuerto, a pocos minutos de salir rumbo a Bogotá, no pienso en cuáles serán los valores de producción de la serie de Netflix. En ese sentido, voy sin expectativas, muy preocupada de absorber todo lo que pueda en una nueva lectura de **la novela más famosa de Gabriel García Márquez**, preguntándome qué nos dirán los valientes que se arriesgaron a dirigirla **(Alex García López y Laura Mora)** y cómo hicieron esos otros valientes, los guionistas (José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, María Camila Arias y Albatrós González), para adaptar una historia tan compleja en temporalidad y personajes.

Para esas preguntas tendré respuestas más adelante, pero lo que no imagino es lo gratamente sorprendida que volveré a México al conocer los valores de producción de una serie hecha de forma tan contundente por manos latinoamericanas y, sobre todo, colombianas, una de las condiciones que **la familia de Gabriel García Márquez** indicó al gigante del streaming para ceder los derechos de la obra.

Es septiembre de 2023 y la promesa de la adaptación de **Cien años de soledad**, ahora sí, se siente real. Pasó tanto tiempo desde que **Netflix** confirmó que tenía luz verde para comenzar la producción (cinco años, para ser exactos), que en las preguntas relacionadas de Google hay una sobre **“qué pasó con la serie de Cien años de soledad”**. ¿Y qué pasó? Para empezar, una investigación que tomó de cinco a seis años “sin prisa, el tiempo no era un factor crítico, considerando que la novela tiene más de 50 años”, dice Francisco Ramos, Vicepresidente de contenidos para Latinoamérica de Netflix. Ramos está en Ibagué, mi primera parada, junto a García López, en una cena donde compartirán un previo de lo que veré mañana junto a otros periodistas.

**El paso del tiempo [es un](https://www.vogue.mx/articulo/cien-anos-de-soledad-libro)** [**personaje en Cien años de soledad**](https://www.vogue.mx/articulo/cien-anos-de-soledad-libro), pero también en la historia de cómo se logró consolidar esta ambiciosa adaptación. En todo hubo tiempo para encontrar las piezas que permitieran armarla, pero lo más importante hubo *suficiente* tiempo y nada de premura de llegar al set de filmación. El proceso de preparación de la historia, la búsqueda de los actores, de las locaciones y de construir los sets fue meticuloso. “La filmación comienza como un ejercicio creativo, con nosotros reunidos en una habitación discutiendo con los guionistas. Sin embargo, eventualmente se convierte en un desafío logístico en el que se deben ejecutar las tareas con precisión, aprendiendo principalmente de los errores cometidos”, explica el director.

Hay una notable dualidad en la selección de quienes lideraron este proyecto. **Alex García López** es argentino y su experiencia en producciones complejas y de gran escala como The Witcher y El mundo oculto de Sabrina le permitieron adentrarse a **Cien años de soledad** con una visión de escala global, mientras que la perspectiva colombiana corrió a cargo de Laura Mora, quien ha dirigido proyectos como Pablo Escobar: El patrón del mal y Los reyes del mundo, una cinta sobre jóvenes desplazados al campo como consecuencia de la violencia en Medellín.

La vista desde el lugar donde cenamos da para las conocidas **montañas de Ibagué, capital del departamento de Tolima**. Es un lugar verde, húmedo (y más húmedo se pondrá mientras más nos adentremos a las locaciones) sus cordilleras atraen a turistas para practicar senderismo. En 1955, **Gabriel García Márquez** estuvo aquí para la filmación de la película Edipo Alcalde, de la cual escribió el guión, siete años antes de la publicación de **Cien años de soledad**. ¿Le habría gustado ver que aquí se grabaría la adaptación de una obra que él consideraba inadaptable? Nunca lo sabré, ni yo, ni ninguno de los involucrados en este proyecto, lo que sí me puedo arriesgar a adivinar es que apreciaría el valor que este equipo de producción le dio al tiempo para encontrar y construir su **Macondo** perfecto. Y es que el autor colombiano también se tomó sus años para crear este pueblo ficticio que, para muchos, nació con Cien años de soledad, pero su rumor se venía escribiendo desde varios relatos atrás. Como nombre propio, apareció por primera vez en el cuento de 1954 Un día después de sábado, donde se le refiere como un hotel llamado “Hotel Macondo”; concebido como un pueblo, aparece en el cuento El invierno (1952), que posteriormente sería conocido como Monólogo de Isabel viendo llover en Macondo gracias a su publicación en la revista Mito en 1955; sería en **La hojarasca**, ese mismo año, cuando los lectores sabrían más de este mítico lugar con unas características más alineadas a lo que leerían en Cien años de soledad.

El Departamento / Netflix ©2024

Antes de la siguiente parada en el municipio de Alvarado, a una media hora de Ibagué, me tomo unos momentos para hacer este breve rastreo de Macondo. Y la razón es que hay un paralelismo casi poético en la forma en la que los creadores de la adaptación y García Márquez encontraron este pueblo inexistente, los primeros entre viajes por todo **Colombia** y el segundo entre un montón de cuentos, relatos y apuntes. “García Márquez sostuvo en diversas oportunidades que para escribir cada libro primero había que aprender a escribirlo, y solo entonces enfrentarse a la máquina de escribir. A él le tomó casi veinte años «vivir» en Macondo para aprender a escribir su novela Cien años de soledad”, escribió Conrado Zuluaga, autor y editor colombiano, en la introducción de la antología Camino a Macondo.

Para la **producción de Netflix** no fueron 20 años, pero sí varios viajes hasta encontrar este lugar rodeado de sierras donde se encuentra parte del **pueblo de Macondo y la casa Buendía**, el resto de **las locaciones están repartidas en los departamentos colombianos de La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca**. Al día de mi visita, se está rodando el fragmento de la historia situado en 1855, la época de plena bonanza para Macondo y la familia Buendía. Junto al grupo con el que viajo, estamos rodeados de naturaleza, poca o nada de señal en los celulares, desde lejos, en la camioneta en la que llegamos, es imposible saber que aquí se está desarrollando una historia que es legado cultural de Colombia.

Lo primero que hay que saber para dimensionar la complejidad de esta producción es que **se crearon cuatro diferentes versiones de Macondo desde cero** para mantener verosimilitud en el transcurso del tiempo. “En esta producción el mayor desafío ha sido el paso del tiempo, ya que transcurren cien años y afecta a la construcción, vestuario, el elenco y todos los aspectos. Todo se adapta a las distintas épocas de la historia”, asegura Diego Ramírez Schrempp, productor ejecutivo de la serie.

Así como hay paralelismo entre el quehacer de la producción y la creación de **Macondo** en el imaginario de García Márquez, también lo hay con la forma en la que **José Arcadio Buendía** edificó ese pueblo que se le presentó en una visión onírica. “José Arcadio Buendía, que era el hombre más emprendedor que se vería jamás en la aldea, había dispuesto de tal modo la posición de las casas, que desde todas podía llegarse al río y abastecerse de agua, con igual esfuerzo, y trazó las calles con tan buen sentido que ninguna casa recibía más sol que otra a la hora del calor. En pocos años, Macondo fue una aldea más ordenada y laboriosa que cualquiera de las conocidas hasta entonces por sus 300 habitantes. Era en verdad una aldea feliz, donde nadie era mayor de treinta años y donde nadie había muerto”, escribió **el autor de Aracataca** en un fragmento de la novela que introduce a los mejores tiempos de Macondo.

Aquí hay hombres y mujeres que igualan en energía al patriarca del pueblo. **Bárbara Enríquez, diseñadora de producción y Carolina Caicedo, productora**, son un buen ejemplo de ello. Ambas hablan con pasión sobre el exhaustivo trabajo que se ha hecho hasta este momento. “La construcción principal [de Macondo y la casa Buendía] está en un terreno llamado Finca Arizona. Hicimos varias construcciones adicionales que reflejan la evolución y construcción del pueblo. Construimos una ranchería en La Guajira y para poder tener el paso del tiempo dentro de Macondo **construimos tres pueblos que se desarrollaron en etapas diferentes**”, explica Caicedo.

En esta llanura de 520,000 metros cuadrados se alzan las calles con esencia caribeña del pueblo y una carpa de aproximadamente 800 metros cuadrados donde se resguarda la casa en la que la familia Buendía vive, sufre, llora y ríe. Es una operación de 1,100 personas en su pico más alto de trabajo. [¿Queríamos **realismo mágico**?](https://www.vogue.mx/articulo/que-es-el-realismo-magico) Pues sí, como Melquiades, quienes trabajan en este lugar tienen conocimientos profundos que dejan boquiabiertos a quienes se expongan a él. No estoy exagerando, solo hay que entrar a la casa –que es otro personaje de la novela– para confirmarlo…

## Dentro de la casa Buendía

Con cuidado, en grupo y con la humedad alzándose un poco más, seguimos a Bárbara, quien ya conoce cada sendero como la palma de su mano. **La casa Buendía** se esconde como un truco de magia, en una carpa color gris que comenzó a construirse en abril de 2023 y poco tiene de mágico para el observador de paso. Entonces, Bárbara la revela como quien sabe que está a punto de mostrar algo realmente interesante. “Todo lo que ven de los jardines está vivo”, dice mientras guía el recorrido. La casa está en su momento más verde, las plantas de los jardines frontales y traseros son funcionales, hay maíz, café, plátano, begonias, todas son mencionadas en la novela. Para lograr la veracidad de un elemento tan importante y que habla tanto de la naturaleza de Colombia que destaca en las páginas de García Márquez, el trabajo del paisajismo corrió a cargo de la colombiana Marta Duque, quien a su vez, se basó en el libro Flora de Macondo de Santiago Madriñan, una publicación de 2014 que analiza meticulosamente las especies de la historia.

El castaño donde José Arcadio Buendía perderá la razón.

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Aunque pareciera que la carpa está sellada, la luz natural se filtra hacia su interior y es porque está diseñada para que así ocurra. “La iluminación natural es otro elemento destacado, gracias a la parte abierta de la carpa que permite que entre la luz caribeña a través de las ventanas”, dice Enriquez. Esto es verdaderamente mágico porque la imagen que regala es fascinante: al centro de la casa se ilumina un castaño, el árbol al que **José Arcadio Buendía** terminará atado, sin rastro de cordura (que, sinceramente, rara vez tuvo), pero este no es real, es una obra arquitectónica y escultural, hecha en cemento y refuerzo de alambrón para resistir la caótica escena.

Después de la carpa, **la casa se completó en tres meses** y luego se sumó un más piso en 19 días. Bárbara Enríquez lo define como “una pieza de ingeniería considerable”, pero también hay mucho arte en su interior. Los pasillos van revelando las habitaciones de los personajes, el comedor, salas de estar y claro, ese laboratorio de alquimia que tantas penas le trajo a Úrsula Iguarán. “**La decoración de la casa se inspira en citas textuales del libro**, como, por ejemplo, el comedor de 12 personas y la obra de arte con doncellas y flores. Aunque seguimos muchas citas literales para la decoración y los espacios, también realizamos adaptaciones para incluir todas las habitaciones mencionadas en la historia”, señala la diseñadora.

**La dirección de arte es obra de Óscar Tello y Catalina Ángulo**, hubo una enorme investigación de su parte para lograr que este set se viera como un hogar habitable: **el mobiliario se recaudó de anticuarios y museos colombianos**, el laboratorio de José Arcadio y el taller de platería de Aureliano se hicieron lo más funcionales posibles, de manera que se investigaron instrumentos que existieron en la época que están repartidos de forma desordenada por todo el espacio.

Las habitaciones de la casa Buendía.

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

El que la serie fuera grabada en Colombia no era el único deseo de la familia García Márquez, para **Rodrigo García Barcha, su hijo,** la producción *debía* ser colombiana. “Rodrigo tenía interés en que la serie no solo fuera colombiana, sino que también contribuyera al desarrollo de la industria cultural del país, dejando un legado industrial y profesional significativo. Consideramos que las industrias culturales son cruciales, ya que no solo crean empleo, sino que también promueven una mayor sofisticación en nuestras formas de comunicarnos como seres humanos”, explicaba Francisco Ramos un día antes. En esta casa y más adelante, en el pueblo de Macondo, es evidente. Insumos como las baldosas y las tejas de palma fueron adquiridos con proveedores de la región, mientras otros elementos como la ropa de cama de las habitaciones y las cerámicas se trabajaron con artesanos locales (en suma, hay manos de más de 150 artesanos de diversas comunidades en la producción).

Antes de partir rumbo a la siguiente etapa de mi trayecto, Bárbara Enríquez comparte el valor emocional de la casa Buendia. Quien haya leído **Cien años de soledad**, sabe que este hogar es más que cuatro paredes, es un espacio con valor simbólico porque se desarrolla y perece a la par de la familia. Siguiendo con los paralelismos, también hay uno muy poderoso entre la diseñadora de producción y **Úrsula Iguarán**, esa mujer que levantó levantó su casa con su propio esfuerzo y conocimiento. “Para mí, Úrsula personifica la casa; su estado de ánimo se refleja en ella. A medida que Úrsula envejece, la casa también cambia. Esta conexión hace que mantener la cohesión no sea tan difícil, ya que todo se refleja en la casa”, explica.

Este peso emocional, también se traduce en que la edificación dentro de esta carpa tiene su propia alma. “Hicimos una investigación tan larga sobre la época y la historia de García Márquez, que [la casa] está llena de detalles. **Cada flor amarilla que vemos es porque él decía que estas eran de buena suerte**. El libro está lleno de cosas que tienen que ver con su biografía, recuerdos y su infancia, todo está metido aquí”.

## En las calles de Macondo

Calle Papalelo. “Papalelo” era el nombre con el que Gabriel García Márquez se refería a su abuelo cuando era niño.

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

**Gabriel Eligio Torres García** es uno de los sobrinos que sobrevive a Gabo. En su libro, La casa de los García Márquez, lleno de anécdotas de la familia, escribió que Margarita, hermana de García Márquez, a quien sus más cercanos solían decirle “Margot”, era una niña que comía tierra y la “saboreaba como un manjar de los dioses”, como Rebeca, esa misteriosa niña que llega a la casa Buendía con un costal de huesos. Hoy, le da nombre a una de las calles del **pueblo construido para la adaptación de Netflix**, es uno de los muchos nombres en las paredes de las edificaciones, todos son tributo a familiares del escritor. Para dar una idea del nivel de detalle, las placas con los nombres de las calles fueron pintadas con manos artesanas y algunas de las imágenes junto a los títulos se obtuvieron directamente del archivo fotográfico de la familia

Estoy es el **Macondo** de los tiempos dorados, hay comercios por doquier, una tienda de cigarros, otra de abarrotes, una ebanistería, el Hotel Jacob donde se hospedaron los turcos en su llegada al pueblo… en suma, este lugar, que es plenamente una escenografía y que no tiene ni un solo habitante, de alguna forma, está vivo, porque las memorias de **Gabriel García Márquez**, que vivían en sus ficciones, no eran otra cosa sino su amor por una infancia en **Aracataca**, el lugar caribeño que lo vio crecer.

Esto le da un valor muy especial a estar aquí caminando, viendo la fachada de la casa Buendía (que se construyó aparte de la carpa), la tienda de Úrsula Iguarán donde están colocados sus animalitos cristalizados en un mostrador, la tienda de Pietro Crespi con un montón de juguetitos y figuras de lo más curiosas (todos provenientes de anticuarios, restaurados por artistas colombianos, o hechos en madera por artesanos).

Las calles de Macondo.

Juan Cristobal Cobo / Netflix

Al día de hoy, es una paradoja decir que **Macondo no existe,** porque está en el imaginario de un sinfín de lectores y, finalmente, aquí esta (por ahora), alzado con una obra de ingeniería que comenzó en noviembre de 2022, en una construcción de 40,000 metros cuadrados. Nada de lo que veo estaba antes de que se comenzara el proyecto, se trasladaron 16,000 plantas autóctonas del Caribe para darle un sentido costero a los jardines de las casas, se tuvieron que crear canales para evitar inundaciones (esta es una zona geográfica donde llueve bastante), y un sistema de electricidad por debajo de la construcción.

También están los almendros y la iglesia en la plaza del pueblo. Las oficinas de Apolinar Moscote son un buen indicador del momento que se está filmando, porque hablan del escenario político de **Cien años de soledad**, cuando los conservadores empiezan a ganar poder y lo destacan tiñendo sus casas de azul. Luego está la farmacia, donde vuelve a notarse el esfuerzo en replicar cada pequeño detalle con fidelidad histórica, en la fachada hay una leyenda que dice “Doctor Septimus”. Era el seudónimo que García Márquez usaba durante sus tiempos en El Heraldo.

Los juguetes en la tienda de Pietro Crespi.

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Los almendros del pueblo.

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

El recorrido termina en la escuela, un recinto sorprendentemente fresco gracias a su alta construcción, por dentro, sus largos pupitres se colocaron como se hacía en el modelo educativo lancasteriano del siglo XIX, son casi tan extensos como la mesa donde hay una comida muy especial preparada para nuestro grupo, decorada con vibrantes flores. En el lugar de cada uno hay una caja que resguarda un pescadito dorado con ojo color turquesa, no lo hizo Aureliano Buendía, pero sí es de filigrana y, como muchas cosas en la historia, representa el paso del tiempo y la soledad.

¿Qué hará el tiempo con todo lo que he visto hoy? Los sets fueron hechos pensando en el factor evolutivo, para desmontarse y modificarse según transcurra el paso de la historia; el **Macondo y la casa Buendía que vi hoy, inevitablemente terminarán arrasados.** El pescadito dorado que terminará atesorado en mi joyero es un buen recuerdo de que pude ver cómo se hizo la fase más luminosa de **Cien años de soledad.**

Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Varios meses después de mi visita a **Colombia**, tengo la oportunidad de ver los primeros episodios de la serie, poco antes de su estreno oficial. Basta con el primero para entender a qué se refería Francisco Ramos cuando dijo que ​​deseaban mantener la integridad de la historia. “Hemos sido muy meticulosos y detallistas en la deconstrucción del texto”, contaba en aquella cena frente a las montañas de Ibagué. Alex García López explicó que los guionistas tuvieron que “equilibrar la edición y darle más énfasis a la cronología para facilitar la comprensión”, mientras cuidaba la esencia de la historia y los personajes.

Lo cierto es que el gusto o disgusto por el resultado final del trabajo de adaptación queda en la mirada de cada espectador; sus creadores, de hecho, están conscientes de que no pueden satisfacer a todo el mundo. No obstante, sí hay algo en lo que me gustaría que muchos pensaran al ver la serie después de leer este viaje: **los centenares de manos con los que se construyó**, con el mismo ahínco con el que José Arcadio Buendía llevó a Úrsula y todo su pueblo a encontrar el mar. Valores de producción, les llaman y esta serie, probablemente de las más ambiciosas y grandes que se han producido jamás en Latinoamérica, los tiene.

args.summary: This article is a first-person account by journalist Fernanda Pérez Sánchez, who visited the set of Netflix's adaptation of *Cien años de soledad* (One Hundred Years of Solitude) in Colombia. The production, filmed across multiple Colombian departments (Tolima, La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca), is the largest Netflix has ever undertaken in the country. The adaptation took years to develop, with the García Márquez family insisting the production be Colombian-led. Four different versions of Macondo were built from scratch to depict the passage of time across the novel's century-long span. The Buendía house set was constructed inside a specially designed tent that allows natural Caribbean light to filter through, featuring a functional garden with plants mentioned in the novel. The house was built in three months, with an additional floor added in 19 days. Over 150 local artisans contributed to the production, and furniture was sourced from Colombian antique shops and museums. The article highlights the parallel between the production team's meticulous search for Macondo and García Márquez's own decades-long process of imagining the fictional town. The set includes 40,000 square meters of construction, 16,000 transplanted native plants, and streets named after García Márquez's family members. The series was co-directed by Alex García López (Argentina) and Laura Mora (Colombia), with a writing team including José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, María Camila Arias, and Albatrós González.

# From Colombia to the World: How 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' Was Brought to the Screen

Entertainment

Laura Mora and Alex García López, directors of the first part of the series, reveal the creative process and challenges of directing One Hundred Years of Solitude, the series based on Gabriel García Márquez’s masterpiece, premiering December 11th on Netflix.

“It's about living up to something that will always be bigger than all of us. We worked hard to build that particularity that has a distinct quality that embodies the Caribbean and encompasses the tropics,” says Laura Mora. 

“We accomplished something I believe has never been done in Latin America, something that isn’t just for Colombia or Latin America but for the whole world,” says Alex García Lopez.

In addition to its directors, cast members Marleyda Soto (Úrsula Iguarán), Claudio Cataño (Aureliano Buendía), and Diego Vásquez (José Arcadio Buendía) share how the dream of bringing one of Latin America’s most ambitious productions to the screen became a reality, honoring the legacy of Gabriel García Márquez’s masterpiece.

One Hundred Years of Solitude Part 1 
Title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
Parts: 2
Episodes: 8 episodes (P1) 8 episodes (P2)
Directors Part 1: Alex García López (E. 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8) and Laura Mora (E. 4, 5, and 6)
Executive Producers: Diego Ramírez Schrempp, Juliana Flórez Luna, Andrés Calderón, Josep Amorós, Carolina Caicedo, Alex García López, Laura Mora, José Rivera, Rodrigo García, Gonzalo García Barcha
Production Company: Dynamo

Editors: Irene Blecua and Miguel Schverdfinger
Makeup and Hair Styling: Helmuth Karpf
Visual Effects Supervision: Jose Luis Orozco
Assistant Directors: Jeiver Pinto Vargas and Nataly Valdivieso Gómez
Filming Locations: Departments of La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, and Tolima in Colombia

About One Hundred Years of Solitude:
Married against their parents' wishes, cousins José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán leave their village behind and embark on a long journey in search of a new home. Accompanied by friends and adventurers, their journey culminates with the founding of a utopian town on the banks of a river of prehistoric stones that they baptize Macondo. Several generations of the Buendía lineage will mark the future of this mythical town, tormented by madness, impossible loves, a bloody and absurd war, and the fear of a terrible curse that condemns them, without hope, to one hundred years of solitude.

Published in 1967, One Hundred Years of Solitude is one of the emblematic works of Gabriel García Márquez, winner of the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1982. Considered a masterpiece of Spanish-American and universal literature and receiving enormous popular acclaim, it has sold more than 50 million copies and has been translated into more than 40 languages.

**EXCLUSIVE:** Cast members including iconic Colombian star Margarita Rosa de Francisco came on board Part Two of [Netflix](https://deadline.com/tag/netflix/)’s *[100 Years Of Solitude](https://deadline.com/tag/100-years-of-solitude/)*, and with the finale of the epic adaptation about to launch, several of the stars who appear in the series-closing episode spoke exclusively to Deadline. We are also first with the trailer for the finale.

De Francisco, famous in Latin America for her role in long running series *Café Con Aroma de Mujer*, appears in Part Two, as do Estefanía Piñeres, Emmanuel Restrepo and Sebastián Osorio.

The Netflix adaptation of the classic novel by Gabriel García Márquez has been split into two parts. The eight-episode Part Two is streaming now, with a special final instalment dropping separately, [as we revealed](https://deadline.com/2026/05/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-part-2-finale-netflix-1236916528/) earlier in the year.

“It’s very intimidating to play a character in such a relevant and important work, and one that so many critics have said outright was impossible to film,” said de Francisco, who plays Fernanda del Carpio. “What we had to do is find ourselves in the work so that we can be faithful to it, and we had to trust the [series] writers.”

### Watch on Deadline

### Watch on Deadline

Season 2 scribes are: José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés and María Camila Arias.

Osorio has been in shows including the telenovela *Pasión de Gavilanes* and stars as Aureliano Babilonia. He agreed it was both exciting and intimidating to land a role in an adaptation of such a seminal novel.

Piñeres, whose credits include the movie *Malta* and the Netflix miniseries *Delirium*, plays Amaranta Úrsula in the series. “These characters take on a quality that is almost mythological,” she said. “They’re in this kind of demigod space where you have to meet them as a character. It was really important that I trusted the writers.”

She told Deadline about a pinch-me moment when she stepped onto the set for *100 Years Of Solitude*.

“I walked in and saw all of the actors that had been playing the Buendías, who were there as they were going to appear as ghosts… it was just such a surreal moment. I was like, ‘I’m walking into the Buendía house, and I’m seeing all of the Buendías together.’”

The production has given the Colombian TV industry a creative and financial boost, employing a massive cast and crew as well as local artisans who worked to recreate the mythical town of Macondo.

“So many things had to align for this particular production to be able to get off the ground… we had 1500 people working,” said Colombian actor Restrepo, who starred in Netflix’s romantic drama *Eva Lasting* and plays José Arcadio in *100 Years Of Solitude*. “I’ve never seen anything like it, and I hope I will again.”

Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno directed seven of the eight episodes in Part Two, with Alex García López (*The Witcher*) helming the final episode. Bogotá -based Dynamo is the production company. The closing episode starts streaming on August 26. Check out the trailer.

args.summary: Deadline reports exclusively on the cast of Netflix's "One Hundred Years of Solitude" Part Two, the adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's classic novel. The eight-episode second part is streaming now, with a special finale episode dropping separately on August 26, 2026. Cast members interviewed include Margarita Rosa de Francisco (Fernanda del Carpio), Estefanía Piñeres (Amaranta Úrsula), Emmanuel Restrepo (José Arcadio), and Sebastián Osorio (Aureliano Babilonia). De Francisco described the adaptation as "impossible" to film, while Piñeres noted the characters have a "mythological" quality. The production employed 1,500 people and gave a significant boost to Colombia's TV industry. Laura Mora, Carlos Moreno, and Alex García López directed episodes. Dynamo is the production company. The series writers for Season 2 are José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, and María Camila Arias.

[GET THE APP](https://vogue.smart.link/84hdiudhc)

[TV & Movies](/culture/tv-and-movies)

# What I Learned Visiting the Set of Netflix’s *One Hundred Years of Solitude*

By [Fernanda Pérez Sánchez](/contributor/fernanda-perez-sanchez)

Photo: Mauro González / Netflix

The first time I heard the term “production values” was in a film class in college: My brilliant professor was talking about how, whether you liked a film or not, its production value was undeniable. I liked the sound of it, and I liked starting to see films from that point of view. (I’ll sum it up by saying that you can identify production value in a movie or television series’s costumes, scenery, photography, lighting, music—in other words, everything that has nothing to do with the script, the story, or the performances.)

If someone had told me in that college class that a few years later, I would be preparing to travel to Colombia to see where a small-screen adaptation of [*One Hundred Years of Solitude*](https://www.netflix.com/title/81087583) was being filmed, I honestly would not have believed it.

Moments before departing for Bogotá, I have no real expectations, focused instead on absorbing as much as I can during a fresh reading of Gabriel García Márquez’s most famous novel. I find myself wondering what insights the brave directors of the series (Alex García López and Laura Mora) will share about their approach, and how the equally bold screenwriters (José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, María Camila Arias, and Albatrós González) managed to adapt such a complex story, with its intricate timelines and multifaceted characters.

It’s September 2023, a good five years after Netflix first confirmed the project had been greenlit. Why the delay? For starters, there was an extensive research phase—“without rushing, as time wasn’t a critical factor, considering the novel is more than 50 years old,” says Francisco Ramos, Netflix’s vice president of content for Latin America. Ramos is in Ibagué, my first stop, along with García López, at a dinner where they’ll share a preview of what I’ll see tomorrow with other journalists.

The passage of time is a character itself in *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, but it’s also a key element in the story of how this ambitious adaptation came to fruition. The process of preparing the story, casting the actors, scouting locations, and building the sets was meticulous. “Filming begins as a creative exercise, with us gathered in a room discussing ideas with the screenwriters. However, it eventually becomes a logistical challenge where tasks must be executed with precision, learning primarily from the mistakes made,” the director explains.

García López, an Argentine, brought his experience with complex, large-scale productions like *The Witcher* and *Chilling Adventures of Sabrina* to *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, giving it a global perspective. On the other hand, the specifically Colombian perspective was entrusted to Laura Mora, known for directing projects such as *Pablo Escobar: El patrón del mal* and *The Kings of the World*, a film about young people displaced to the countryside as a result of violence in Medellín.

The view from where we’re dining opens up to the well-known mountains of Ibagué, the capital of Tolima. It’s a green, humid place (and it will only grow more humid as we venture deeper into the filming locations). In 1955, García Márquez spent time here during the filming of *Edipo Alcalde*, for which he wrote the screenplay, seven years before the publication of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

Would he have liked to see that the adaptation of a work he considered unadaptable would be filmed here? Neither I nor anyone involved in this project can ever truly know. What I can venture to guess, however, is that he might have appreciated the care and time this production team invested in finding and constructing their perfect Macondo. After all, the Colombian author himself took years to craft this fictional town, which for many was born in *One Hundred Years of Solitude* but had been whispered into existence through earlier stories.

As a proper name, Macondo first appeared in the 1954 short story “One Day After Saturday” throufh a hotel called “Hotel Macondo.” It debuted as a town in the 1952 story “The Winter,” later republished in *Mito* magazine in 1955 as “Monologue of Isabel Watching It Rain in Macondo.” Yet it was in *Leaf Storm* (*La hojarasca*) that same year that readers were given a more detailed glimpse of this mythical place, with characteristics more closely aligned to the Macondo they would come to know in *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

Photo: El Departamento / Netflix ©2024

Before heading to the next stop in the municipality of Alvarado, about half an hour from Ibagué, I take a moment to trace the origins of Macondo. There’s an almost poetic parallel between how the creators of the adaptation and García Márquez discovered this nonexistent town—the former through journeys across Colombia, the latter through a collection of stories, tales, and notes.

“García Márquez often asserted that to write each book, one first had to learn how to write it, and only then confront the typewriter. It took him nearly 20 years of ‘living’ in Macondo to learn how to write his novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude,*” Conrado Zuluaga, Colombian author and editor, wrote in the introduction to the anthology *Camino a Macondo.*

For the Netflix production, it was not 20 years but several trips to find this place, surrounded by mountains, where part of the town of Macondo and the Buendía house are located. (The rest of the locations are spread across the Colombian departments of La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, and Cundinamarca.) On the day of my visit, the fragment of the story set in 1855, the time of full prosperity for Macondo and the Buendía family, is being filmed.

The first thing to understand in order to grasp the complexity of this production is that four different versions of Macondo were created from scratch to maintain authenticity over the course of time. “In this production, the greatest challenge has been the passage of time, as the story spans one hundred years, affecting the sets, costumes, cast, and every aspect. Everything had to be adapted to the different eras of the narrative,” explains Diego Ramírez Schrempp, the series’s executive producer.

Just as there is a parallel between the production’s work and the creation of Macondo in García Márquez’s imagination, there is also one with how José Arcadio Buendía builds the town in the book.

“José Arcadio Buendía, who was the most enterprising man ever to be seen in the village, had set up the placement of the houses in such a way that from all of them one could reach the river and draw water with the same effort, and he had lined up the streets with such good sense that no house got more sun than another during the hot time of day. Within a few years Macondo was a village that was more orderly and hard working than any known until then by its three hundred inhabitants. It was a truly happy village where no one was over thirty years of age and where no one had died,” García Márquez wrote in a passage of the novel that introduces Macondo’s golden era.

On the set of the Netflix series, there are men and women whose energy rivals that of the town’s patriarch. Bárbara Enríquez, the production designer, and Carolina Caicedo, the producer, are prime examples; both speak passionately about the exhaustive work done so far.

“The main construction [of Macondo and the Buendía house] is located on a site called Finca Arizona. We built several additional structures that reflect the evolution and development of the town. We constructed a ranchería in La Guajira, and to show the passage of time within Macondo, we built three separate towns, each representing different stages of its growth,” explains Caicedo.

The town’s streets lie on a 520,000-square-meter plain (roughly 130 acres), along with a tent of approximately 800 square meters (more than 8,600 square feet) that houses the Buendía family's home, where they live, suffer, cry, and laugh. It’s an operation involving 1,100 people at its peak.

## Inside the Buendía house

Carefully, we follow Bárbara Enríquez, who knows every path like the back of her hand. The Buendía house hides like a magic trick in a gray tent that began being built in April 2023.

“Everything you see in the gardens is alive,” she says as she guides the tour. The house is at its greenest, with the plants in the front and back gardens—corn, coffee, bananas, begonias—all taken from the novel. To guarantee its authenticity, the landscaping was overseen by a Colombian, Marta Duque, who, in turn, relied on the book *Flora de Macondo* by Santiago Madriñan. This 2014 publication meticulously analyzes the species in García Márque’s story.

The chestnut tree where José Arcadio Buendía will lose his mind.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Though the tent may appear sealed, natural light filters in, to captivating effect: in the center of the house, a chestnut tree is illuminated—the very tree to which José Arcadio Buendía will eventually be bound. But this tree isn’t real; it’s an architectural and sculptural creation, made of cement and reinforced with wire mesh.

After the tent, the house was completed in three months, with an additional floor added in 19 days—“a significant engineering feat,” per Bárbara Enríquez. The hallways reveal the characters’ rooms, the dining area, living rooms, and, of course, that alchemy lab that caused so much trouble for Úrsula Iguarán. “The decoration of the house is inspired by direct quotes from the book, like the 12-person dining table and the artwork featuring maidens and flowers. While we followed many literal references for the decor and spaces, we also made adaptations to include all the rooms mentioned in the story,” says the designer. Additionally, “every yellow flower we see is because he said these were good luck. The book is full of things that have to do with his biography, memories and his childhood, everything is tucked in here.”

Art directors Óscar Tello and Catalina Ángulo expended an extraordinary amount of effort to make the set look like a livable home: the furniture was collected from Colombian antique dealers and museums, and José Arcadio’s laboratory and Aureliano’s silver workshop were scattered with instruments that existed at the time.

The rooms of the Buendía house.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

It was an explicit wish of the García Márquez family that the series be filmed in Colombia; but more than that, for Rodrigo García Barcha, his son, it was important that the production give back to the local community. “Rodrigo was keen that the series not only be Colombian but also contribute to the development of the country’s cultural industry, leaving a significant industrial and professional legacy. We believe cultural industries are crucial, as they not only create jobs but also promote greater sophistication in how we communicate as human beings,” Francisco Ramos explained to me the day before. This is evident in the house and, later, in the greater town of Macondo. Materials like tiles and palm thatch were sourced from local suppliers, while other elements such as bed linens and ceramics were crafted by local artisans. In total, over 150 artisans from various communities contributed to the production.

## In the streets of Macondo

Papalelo Street. “Papalelo” was the name Gabriel García Márquez used to refer to his grandfather when he was a child.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Gabriel Eligio Torres García, one of García Márquez’s nephews, wrote in his book *La casa de los García Márquez* that Margarita, García Márquez’s sister, whom her loved ones affectionately called “Margot,” was a child who ate dirt and “savored it like a dish fit for the gods”—much like Rebeca, the mysterious girl who arrives at the Buendía house carrying a sack of bones. Today, her name adorns one of the streets in the town built for the Netflix adaptation. It is one of many tributes to the writer’s family. (It’s worth noting that not only were the street signs hand-painted by artisans, but some of the images alongside the titles were directly sourced from the family’s photographic archive.) This is the Macondo of the golden days, with a cigar store, a grocery store, a cabinet shop, the Hotel Jacob, and Pietro Crespi’s shop—crammed with toys and figures sourced from antique dealers, restored by Colombian artists, or made in wood by artisans.

The streets of Macondo.

Photo: Juan Cristobal Cobo / Netflix

Construction on the town began in November 2022, covering about 10 acres. Nothing I see was here before the project started; 16,000 native Caribbean plants were transplanted to give the houses’ gardens a coastal feel, channels had to be created to prevent flooding (since this is a geographically rainy area), and an electrical system was installed beneath the construction

Apolinar Moscote’s offices are a good indicator of the novel’s political backdrop: as conservatives began to gain power, they painted their houses blue. Then there’s the pharmacy, where once again, the effort to replicate every detail with historical accuracy is evident. On the facade is a sign that reads “Doctor Septimus”; this was the pseudonym García Márquez used during his time as a columnist for the paper *El Heraldo*.

The toys in Pietro Crespi's store.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

The almond trees in the village.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

The tour ends at the school, with long desks arranged according to the Lancastrian educational model of the 19th century. Of course, the sets were made to be disassembled and modified as time goes by; Macondo and the Buendía house I saw today will inevitably be razed. But at a special meal prepared for our group, each of us is gifted a little golden fish with a turquoise eye—a memento that will end up in my jewelry box.

Photo: Mauro Gonzalez / Netflix

Several months after my visit to Colombia, I have the opportunity to see the first episodes of the series, shortly before its official premiere. I quickly understand what Netflix’s Francisco Ramos meant when he talked about wanting to maintain the integrity of the story. “We have been very meticulous and detailed in the deconstruction of the text,” he said at that dinner in front of the mountains of Ibagué. Alex García López explained that the scriptwriters had to “balance the editing and give more emphasis to the chronology to make it easier to understand,” wwhile preserving the essence of the story and its characters.

The show’s creators are aware that they cannot please everyone. But production value? That, Netflix’s *One Hundred Years of Solitude*—one of the most ambitious and grandest works ever produced in Latin America—has in spades.

When Colombian director Laura Mora was first approached about joining the team tasked with adapting Gabriel García Márquez’s novel “One Hundred Years of Solitude” into a TV series, she was more than skeptical.

“I first heard of the project back in 2018, and I remember saying, ‘What is this madness?’ ” Mora said in Spanish in a Zoom interview. “How could they possibly want to do this? I was terrified. I really thought it was an act of folly. Irresponsible, even.”

[![Pedro Paramo. (L to R) Tenoch Huerta as Juan Preciado, Noe Hernandez as Abundio in Pedro Paramo. Cr. Carlos Somonte / Netflix ©2024](https://ca-times.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d516d33/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7517x5011+0+96/resize/840x560!/quality/75/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcalifornia-times-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fe8%2F9e%2F6cd21ac94c75a15cb25e994bf213%2Fpedro-paramo-netflix-handouts07.JPG)](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-11-25/pedro-paramo-director-netflix-rodrigo-pietro-manuel-garcia-rulfo)

### [To retell ‘Pedro Páramo,’ director Rodrigo Prieto went on his own journey to the past](https://www.latimes.com/delos/story/2024-11-25/pedro-paramo-director-netflix-rodrigo-pietro-manuel-garcia-rulfo)

In his debut feature film, Oscar-nominated cinematographer Rodrigo Prieto directs the newest movie adaptation of Juan Rulfo’s 1955 novel ‘Pedro Páramo.’

José Rivera, who would eventually pen the scripts that changed Mora’s mind, was initially just as wary.

Advertisement

“I’m not going to go watch that,” he recalled thinking when he heard about what Netflix was trying to do. “It’s going to suck. They’re going to blow it. It’s not going to be good.”

But as was the case with everyone who eventually signed on for what’s an ambitious and assured adaptation (Part 1, consisting of eight episodes, is now available to stream), Rivera, Mora, fellow series director Alex García López and the entire creative team realized that the best way to guarantee the series would have made García Márquez proud was to take the plunge and make it their own. To honor it but to let go of the idea of being wholly faithful to it.

Published in 1967, “One Hundred Years of Solitude” earned the Colombian novelist known affectionately as “Gabo” a Nobel prize in Literature in 1982. More than 50 years since its publication, the story of the Buendía family and the tragicomic events that ravage their small town of Macondo remains one of the most beloved novels of the 20th century.

In García Márquez’s prose, Macondo is Colombia and Colombia is Macondo. An entire sense of history was contained within its melodramatic stories. The town founded by José Arcadio Buendía (played by Marco González as a young man and Diego Vásquez as his older version in the series) with his wife, Úrsula Iguarán (played by Susana Morales and later by Marleyda Soto), slowly tracks the arrival of mysticism, then science, later still politics and the Church. Macondo soon finds itself at the heart of a political civil war wherein Buendía’s grown son, Col. Aureliano Buendía (Claudio Cataño), becomes a revolutionary leader destined for glory and infamy.

The novel covers so much ground that adapting it had long seemed impossible. Rumblings about Hollywood taking a stab at it followed the book ever since it had been published, with people as varied as Anthony Quinn and William Friedkin expressing interest at some point over the last few decades. But García Márquez, who died in 2014, always resisted such offers.

With the arrival of streaming giants like Netflix and their commitment to bolstering local talent and productions, García Márquez’s family — which includes his son, filmmaker Rodrigo García — saw a chance to give “One Hundred Years of Solitude” the adaptation it deserved, one that would be shot in Spanish and in Colombia with mostly Colombian talent in front and behind the camera. (The series uses English subtitles.)

![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/LuUUCeR8Wqw/hqdefault.jpg) 

[×](#)

García serves as an executive producer on the show but said he tried to not be too involved. He knew his mere presence might have distracted the creative team.

“I did say that I thought a lot of the adaptations that have been done with my dad’s work suffered from too much respect for the book,” he said over Zoom. “And too much awe for the writer. I told them they should feel free to truly adapt it.”

García Márquez’s poetic language and his iconic imagery were always going to be hard to translate into the language of episodic television, especially since the book didn’t follow a neat timeline.

Rivera, who was nominated for an Oscar for his screenplay for “The Motorcycle Diaries” (2004), knew that to tell the Buendías’ story he’d have to wrangle the novel’s circular sense of time. In the drafts for the show’s 16 episodes — which then were fleshed out and co-written by a coterie of Colombian writers, including Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, Albatrós González and María Camila Arias — Rivera tidied up the chronology of the show’s titular century, which begins roughly in 1850 and ends in the middle of the 20th century.

That alone unlocked a way to structure into 16 hours of what is otherwise a 400-page novel that features little dialogue and covers six generations of the Buendía family — not to mention civil wars, bloody massacres, illicit love affairs, family betrayals, ill-fated marriages, cold-blooded executions and everything in between.

[![Colombian Nobel literature laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez meets with fans and reporters outside his Mexico City home on March 6, his 87th birthday.](https://ca-times.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0ede6cd/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2048x1365+0+27/resize/840x560!/quality/75/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fcalifornia-times-brightspot.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fb5%2Fb8%2F9c40fb9a652cc8199b1ccdc03134%2Fla-et-jc-gabriel-garcia-marquez-through-the-ye-001)](https://www.latimes.com/books/jacketcopy/la-et-jc-gabriel-garcia-marquez-five-essential-reads-20140417-story.html)

[Books](https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/books)

### [Gabriel Garcia Marquez: Five essential reads](https://www.latimes.com/books/jacketcopy/la-et-jc-gabriel-garcia-marquez-five-essential-reads-20140417-story.html)

Gabriel García Márquez, who died Thursday at 87, was a prolific writer, dating back to his work as a journalist in the 1950s.

Another signficant obstacle was how to import García Márquez’s signature sensibility onto the small screen. Mora and García López worked to ground the world of the series in a believable, tangible reality. Shot on location in Colombia with sets that allow characters to move freely in long wandering shots, “One Hundred Years of Solitude” has a handcrafted, theatrical sensibility.

Advertisement

“One of the great gambles of the language of the series was precisely the chance to distance ourselves from that magical realism that has often been interpreted as a fantastic place, and embrace it instead as a poetic place,” Mora said. “A place where our reality, sometimes because of its beauty and harshness, surpasses any fiction. To do so not in an artificial way but in a very artisanal way, instead.”

“The book is well known to be a book with magical flourishes,” García adds. “But it is also a very grounded, realistic, psychological story of relationships. Of desires and frustrations. I think that’s what keeps the book alive. It’s about life.”

The currency of “One Hundred Years of Solitude” hasn’t diminished precisely because Gabo’s stories have long served as both a chronicle and a warning. As history and template.

“One of the things that marks a great work is precisely that it doesn’t lose its relevance,” Mora said. “That it always gives us insight into the world we live in. It doesn’t matter when it was written. The author becomes a prophet of his times.”

For its cast, the series’ themes — on political violence and a divided people, on the cost of peace and the price of corruption, on families torn apart and traumas passed from generation to generation — remain as topical as ever. And not nearly as local as they may at first appear.

Even as the show is clearly rooted in Colombia, “One Hundred Years of Solitude” is a text that transcends borders.

Advertisement

“The contradictions at the heart of the human experience will forever resonate across time,” said Cataño, who plays the famed Aureliano Buendía. “It is a theme with which all races on Earth can identify. All of humankind’s dualities and ambiguities are the dualities and ambiguities that exist in these characters. It is impossible not to identify with them.”

“I think its significance and relevance comes from the fact that we have gradually lost our memory,” Vásquez adds. “The cycle just keeps repeating itself.”

It’s a bleak message. But one that by its very nature, and as the Buendías themselves learn, will never get old. And it will continue to resonate not just in Colombia but elsewhere. Particularly in countries that face challenges with the very issues of power-hungry figures Gabo sketched out close to half a century ago.

“The book touches on many universals, one of which is the ever-present problem of tyranny,” Rivera says. “The idea of revolution and revolutionary fervor is universal. And it’s apropos to today, if you understand that Trump is a tyrant, or a would-be tyrant. Then we’ll have to ask ourselves, Where is our revolutionary spirit? Who is our Aureliano?”

This is why Mora is most excited, if apprehensive, about exporting this most Colombian of stories to a global audience once more.

“I do wonder how this may resonate in a place like the United States, in a country that is so divided at the moment,” Mora says. “But then I think that the whole world is very polarized. And ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ gives us insight into how difficult and dangerous such a divided world can be, and about how poetry and beauty are also what can save us.”

# The Second and Final Part of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* Arrives in August

Get ready to return to the mythical town of Macondo in *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

After the critically acclaimed launch of Part 1 last year, the breathtaking adaptation of Nobel Prize–winning author Gabriel García Márquez’s bestselling magical realist novel will return for its second and final part in August 2026. ### What is *One Hundred Years of Solitude* about?

The story follows cousins José Arcadio Buendía (Marco González) and Úrsula Iguarán (Susana Morales), who get married against their parents’ wishes and leave their village to embark on a long journey in search of a new home. Accompanied by friends and adventurers, their voyage culminates with the founding of a utopian town on the banks of a river of prehistoric stones that they baptize Macondo. Several generations of the Buendía lineage will shape the future of this mythical town, tormented by madness, impossible loves, a bloody and absurd war, and a terrible curse that condemns them, without hope, to 100 years of solitude.

Claudio Cataño, who felt an “enormous responsibility” in playing Colonel Aureliano Buendía, tells Tudum it was “an honor and a risk” to take on the role. He adds, “Macondo and its host of characters, who I truly feel as my own blood, are universal, but at the same time so unique — so from Colombia, so beautifully tragic that it is impossible not to be trapped in this world.”

Bringing the mythical town’s magical elements to life was a “huge challenge for everyone involved,” Cataño says. “I think the scripts and the direction combine both aspects of magic and humanity, of exuberance and realism. From the performing side, it was an arduous and exquisite pleasure.”

García Márquez’s novel, published in 1967, has sold more than 50 million copies and been translated into more than 40 languages. This adaptation is one of the most ambitious productions in Latin American history, filmed in Spanish and shot in García Márquez’s native Colombia with the support of the author’s family.

“Directing this project has been both a challenge and an adventure. After all, in life, taking risks is necessary to give meaning to what we do,” Alex García López (*The Witcher*), who directed Episodes 1, 2, 3, 7, and 8, tells Netflix. “When diving into the adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, my intention was to create something authentic that carries the stature of an international production, because the story deserves it.”

Laura Mora (*The Kings of the World*, *Frontera Verde*), who helmed Episodes 4, 5, and 6, adds: “As a filmmaker, and as a Colombian, it has been an honor and a huge challenge to work on a project as complex and that carries as much responsibility as *One Hundred Years of Solitude.* I always strived to understand the difference between the literary and audiovisual languages and to be able to construct images that contain the beauty, poetry, and depth of a work that has impacted the entire world. We’ve done it with love and respect for the novel, with the support of an exceptional technical and human team.”

### What is Part 2 of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* about?

After the armistice and signing of the Treaty of Neerlandia, peace still does not reach Macondo. The Conservatives, fearful of Colonel Aureliano Buendía’s threats, plot an attack that — by a twist of fate — brings Fernanda del Carpio from Bogotá to the town. She marries Aureliano Segundo, one of the bastard Arcadio’s untamable twin sons, and gives Úrsula Iguarán her first legitimate heirs.

Meanwhile, the other twin, José Arcadio Segundo, absorbed in José Arcadio Buendía’s manuscripts, accomplishes the patriarch’s wild dreams of connecting Macondo with the world. The railroad’s arrival opens the doors to the banana company, which leads to the town’s downfall and ultimately fulfills Úrsula Iguarán’s curse: The races condemned to 100 years of solitude were not granted a second opportunity on earth.

### What else can we expect from Part 2 of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*?

Mora will continue to direct, along with Carlos Moreno, a Colombian director known for his work on films like [*Dogwashers*](/title/81089261?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum) and *Perro come perro* and the series [*The Final Score*](/title/81261043?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum) and [*Wild District*](/title/80230435?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum).

Marleyda Soto will be reprising her role as the adult Úrsula Iguarán, and Cataño will return as Colonel Aureliano Buendía. They’ll be joined by Ángela Cano, Emmanuel Restrepo, Estefanía Piñeres, María Adelaida Puerta, Emiliano Pernía, Juanita Molina, Laura Taylor, Obeida Benavides, Julián Román, and Carla Baratta, who all bring García Márquez’s unforgettable characters to life.

“Following the reception from our members and specialized press from all around the world, we are deeply proud to announce that the production of the second part has begun. With this series, we pay tribute to the legacy of Gabriel García Márquez and to Colombia and its extraordinary talent,” says Francisco Ramos, Netflix’s Vice President of Latin America Content. “I express my appreciation for the work of Laura Mora, whose rigor and passion have been fundamental in this journey, and who is now joined by Carlos Moreno, a remarkable Colombian filmmaker and Netflix partner. We are in the best hands to carry the Buendías’ story to a successful conclusion.”

args.summary:
The Netflix Tudum article announces that Part 2 (the final season) of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* will arrive in August 2026. The series is an adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize-winning magical realist novel, which has sold over 50 million copies and been translated into 40+ languages. The production is one of the most ambitious in Latin American history, filmed in Spanish in Colombia.

**Release Schedule:** The first seven episodes of Part 2 premiere on August 5, 2026, with the grand finale (Episode 8) arriving on August 26, 2026. The series totals 16 episodes (8 per part).

**Plot Overview:** The story follows the Buendía family across seven generations in the mythical town of Macondo. Part 2 picks up after the Treaty of Neerlandia, when Fernanda del Carpio arrives from Bogotá and marries Aureliano Segundo. The other twin, José Arcadio Segundo, pursues the patriarch's dream of connecting Macondo to the outside world, leading to the arrival of the railroad and banana company — which ultimately brings about the town's downfall and fulfillment of Úrsula Iguarán's curse.

**Cast & Crew:** Returning cast includes Marleyda Soto as adult Úrsula Iguarán and Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía. New cast members include Ángela Cano, Emmanuel Restrepo, and others. Directors include Laura Mora and Carlos Moreno (joining for Part 2). Alex García López directed episodes 1-3 and 7-8 of Part 1.

***One Hundred Years of Solitude*** ([Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language"): *Cien años de soledad*, Latin American Spanish: [[sjen ˈaɲos ðe soleˈðað]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Spanish "Help:IPA/Spanish")) is a [Colombian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia "Colombia") television series based on [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s 1967 novel [of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude "One Hundred Years of Solitude"). The series will run for 16 episodes on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), with the first eight released on 11 December 2024. The first part of the second season was released on 5 August 2026, while the series finale is slated to be released on 26 August 2026.

## Production

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Production")]

### Development

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Development")]

[Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") acquired the rights to *[One Hundred Years of Solitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude "One Hundred Years of Solitude")* in March 2019.[[2]](#cite_note-2) Before his death in 2014, author [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez") had refused to sell the rights to the novel as he did not believe the time constraints of a feature film were sufficient for a proper adaptation.[[3]](#cite_note-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The producers scouted several locations for filming, including [Cali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cali "Cali"), [Villavicencio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villavicencio "Villavicencio"), [Girardot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girardot,_Cundinamarca "Girardot, Cundinamarca"), [Palomino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palomino,_Colombia "Palomino, Colombia"), [Santa Marta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Marta "Santa Marta"), and [Barranquilla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barranquilla "Barranquilla").[[6]](#cite_note-Guzmán-2024-6)

> As a filmmaker, as a Colombian, it has been an honor and an enormous challenge to work on a project of the complexity and responsibility of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, always trying to understand the difference between literary and audiovisual language, to be able to construct images that contain something of the beauty, poetry and depth of a work that has impacted the entire world. We have done it with love and respect for the novel, with the help of an exceptional technical and human team.

— Director [Laura Mora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laura_Mora "Laura Mora")[[7]](#cite_note-7)

### Casting

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Casting")]

The cast was chosen through an open casting call in 2022.[[8]](#cite_note-8) The casting team saw more than 10,000 candidates for the 25 main roles.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) Only 30% of the cast were professional actors.[[10]](#cite_note-10) In addition to the main cast, 20,000 extras were selected.[[11]](#cite_note-11) The cast was partially leaked on 26 April 2023.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

### Filming

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Filming")]

Principal photography on the first part of the series took place from May to December 2023.[[13]](#cite_note-Kay-2024-13) The series was filmed entirely in Colombia,[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) specifically in [La Guajira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Guajira_Department "La Guajira Department"), [Magdalena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdalena_Department "Magdalena Department"), [Cesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cesar_Department "Cesar Department"), [Cundinamarca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cundinamarca_Department "Cundinamarca Department"), and [Tolima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tolima_Department "Tolima Department").[[16]](#cite_note-16) The fictional town of [Macondo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macondo "Macondo") was built near [Alvarado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvarado,_Tolima "Alvarado, Tolima") by 1,100 workers.[[6]](#cite_note-Guzmán-2024-6) Four versions of the town were built to depict the passage of time.[[13]](#cite_note-Kay-2024-13) The producers purchased furniture from local antique stores and had fabrics and artifacts made by local artisans for the sets.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) Filming required a crew of nearly 600 people, all from Colombia.[[17]](#cite_note-17) Netflix reported that series' production generated 225 billion [COP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombian_peso "Colombian peso") ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

Production on the second part of the series began in February 2025.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

## Release

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Release")]

A promotional display for the series at the [Guadalajara International Book Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadalajara_International_Book_Fair "Guadalajara International Book Fair") in December 2024

A teaser trailer for the first season was released on 17 April 2024.[[20]](#cite_note-20)[[21]](#cite_note-21) Promotional stills were released on 18 October.[[9]](#cite_note-Clarke-2024-9) The first two episodes premiered at the [Círculo de Bellas Artes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Círculo_de_Bellas_Artes "Círculo de Bellas Artes") in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid") on 22 November 2024.[[22]](#cite_note-22) The series' first episode screened at the [Biblioteca Vasconcelos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biblioteca_Vasconcelos "Biblioteca Vasconcelos") in [Mexico City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mexico_City "Mexico City") on 28 November 2024.[[23]](#cite_note-23) Its first two episodes were screened at the [Havana Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana_Film_Festival "Havana Film Festival") on 6 December 2024.[[24]](#cite_note-24) The first season, comprising eight episodes, was released in its entirety on Netflix on 11 December 2024.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

A trailer for the second season was released on 17 July 2026.[[26]](#cite_note-26) The second season is scheduled to be released in two parts;[[27]](#cite_note-27) the first seven episodes were released on 5 August 2026 and the series finale will be released on 26 August 2026.[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) To promote the second season, Netflix held special screenings in select cities in Colombia.[[1]](#cite_note-De_la_Fuente-2026-1)

## Reception

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Reception")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), 83% of 30 critics' reviews are positive, with an average rating of 7.9/10. The website's consensus reads: "*One Hundred Years of Solitude* faithfully realizes [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_García_Márquez "Gabriel García Márquez")'s seminal novel with sumptuous polish, making for an adaptation that is nothing short of magical."[[30]](#cite_note-30) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), it has a weighted average score of 80 out of 100, based on 16 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

Keith Watson of *[The Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Telegraph_(London) "The Telegraph (London)")* rated the series five stars out of five, calling it a "faithful but not overly reverent take on Márquez". He commended the cast's performances, specifically those of [Marleyda Soto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marleyda_Soto "Marleyda Soto") and [Claudio Cataño](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Cataño "Claudio Cataño").[[32]](#cite_note-32) Helen Coffey of *[The Independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Independent "The Independent")* called the series "pretty much perfect" and "nothing short of miraculous". She commended the series' creators for staying faithful to the source material while creating "a piece of visually gorgeous storytelling". She also commended the casting, script, cinematography, and music.[[33]](#cite_note-33) Julio Ricardo Varela of [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC") wrote that the series provides "countless moments of brilliance that prove creating art from other works of art is still possible." He commended the performances of the entire cast, especially Soto, Cataño, and Marco Antonio González, and noted the care that seemed to have gone into the series' production.[[34]](#cite_note-34) Judy Berman of *[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")* wrote, "Considering the difficulty of the assignment, it's remarkable how close Netflix's splendid *One Hundred Years of Solitude* . . . comes to recreating not just the substance, but also the kinetic spirit of the book." She wrote that the series successfully conveyed the story of the novel without oversimplifying its major themes, including the "ugly but symbolically meaningful aspects of the story, from self-harm to incest". She commended the series' production value, direction, and cinematography.[[35]](#cite_note-35)

Daniel Fienberg of *[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hollywood_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter")* called the series a "gorgeous, ambitious adaptation" of the novel that is "honorable and beautiful, if not without flaws." He noted that much of the series' content was taken verbatim from the novel, which "doesn't always work" on screen, and that "everything plays better when the show is at its most figurative and least literal." He commended García López and Mora's direction, calling the series "breathlessly beautiful at times, lyrical and alive and brimming with visual and intellectual ideas." He concluded, "*One Hundred Years of Solitude* may not be as good as *[Underground Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Underground_Railroad_(miniseries) "The Underground Railroad (miniseries)")* or even *[Station Eleven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station_Eleven_(miniseries) "Station Eleven (miniseries)")*, but it's a worthy and admirable capper for a year of often exceptional prestige adaptations."[[36]](#cite_note-36) Aramide Tinubu of *[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")* called the series "exquisitely detailed and layered in intricate symbolism" and "one of the most faithful page-to-screen adaptations in recent years." She called the performances "exceptional", but said that certain sequences felt dense. Although she found the pacing "too lackadaisical at times", she wrote, "the beauty of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* allows the viewer to absorb every intricately curated frame and moment."[[37]](#cite_note-37) Carly Lane of *[Collider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collider_(website) "Collider (website)")* called the series "a masterpiece in its own right" and wrote, "Not only does the Spanish-language series breathe new life into Márquez's supposedly unfilmable novel, but it also succeeds as a triumph of filmmaking thanks to stunning cinematography and an epic story that spans across multiple generations of the ill-fated Buendía family." She commended the visuals of Paulo Pérez and María Sarasvati, the production design of [Eugenio Caballero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenio_Caballero "Eugenio Caballero") and [Bárbara Enríquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bárbara_Enríquez?action=edit&redlink=1 "Bárbara Enríquez (page does not exist)") [[pt](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bárbara%20Enríquez "pt:Bárbara Enríquez")], and the ensemble's performance.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

Jack Seale of *[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian")* rated the series three stars out of five, writing that it "might struggle with the novel's problematic sexual politics, but it's a big, gorgeous adaptation".[[39]](#cite_note-39) Ed Potton of *[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Times "The Times")* rated the series two stars out of five, calling it "gorgeous but lethargic" and writing that it "lacks the vibrancy and energy of the novel". He commended the production design of Caballero and Enríquez, but said the series struggled to translate magic realism to the screen.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

**One Hundred Years of Solitude (TV Series) – Wikipedia Summary**

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel of the same name. Produced by Netflix and the Colombian production company Dynamo, the series is a Spanish and Wayuu-language drama/magical realism adaptation.

**Key Details:**
- **Seasons/Episodes:** 2 seasons, 15 episodes total (season 1: 8 episodes; season 2: 8 episodes)
- **Release Dates:** Season 1 premiered December 11, 2024. Season 2 Part 1 released August 5, 2026; series finale slated for August 26, 2026.
- **Creators:** Written by José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, Albatrós González, and María Camila Arias. Directed by Alex García López, Laura Mora, and Carlos Moreno.
- **Cast:** Claudio Cataño (Colonel Aureliano Buendía), Diego Vásquez (José Arcadio Buendía), Marleyda Soto (Úrsula Iguarán), Viña Machado (Pilar Ternera), Loren Sofía (Amaranta), Akima (Rebeca), Janer Villarreal (Arcadio), Moreno Borja (Melquíades), Ruggero Pasquarelli (Pietro Crespi), and others.

**Production:**
- Netflix acquired rights in March 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing a feature film was insufficient for proper adaptation.
- Filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors.
- Open casting call in 2022; more than 10,000 candidates for 25 main roles. Only 30% were professional actors; 20,000 extras were selected.
- Principal photography for Part 1: May–December 2023. Filmed entirely in Colombia (La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, Tolima). The fictional town of Macondo was built near Alvarado, Tolima by 1,100 workers, with four versions constructed to depict the passage of time.
- Production generated 225 billion COP ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy.
- Production on Part 2 began in February 2025.

**Reception:**
- Rotten Tomatoes: 83% positive from 30 critics (avg. 7.9/10). Consensus: "faithfully realizes García Márquez's seminal novel with sumptuous polish."
- Metacritic: 80/100 ("generally favorable").
- Critical praise for faithfulness to source material, performances (especially Soto and Cataño), cinematography, production design, and direction. Some criticism of pacing and literal translation of novelistic content.

**Awards:**
- Won Best Ibero-American Miniseries or TV Series at the 2025 Platino Awards.
- Claudio Cataño won Best Actor and Jairo Camargo won Best Supporting Actor at the Platino Awards.
- Multiple wins at Premios India Catalina 2025 including Best Fiction Series, Best Leading Actor/Actress, Best Supporting Actor/Actress, and Best Fiction Script.

args.summary: This is a Rotten Tomatoes page for Season 1 of "One Hundred Years of Solitude," a drama series released on December 11, 2024, on Netflix. The series is an adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's seminal novel, following seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo. It has a Tomatometer score of 87% based on 30 critic reviews, and a Popcornmeter score of 90% based on 250+ audience ratings. The critic consensus states: "One Hundred Years of Solitude faithfully realizes Gabriel García Márquez's seminal novel with sumptuous polish, making for an adaptation that is nothing short of magical." The series is in Spanish, with a cast including Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, Jerónimo Barón as Auréliano Buendía, Marco Gonzalez as José Arcadio Buendía, Leonardo Soto as José Arcadio Jr., Susana Morales as Úrsula Iguarán, and Ella Becerra as Petronila. The 8 episodes premiered on December 11, 2024. The page also includes critic reviews praising the adaptation's faithfulness and visual beauty, as well as audience reviews with mixed but generally positive reactions.
