> 					Majstorović, Stevan. 1972. Cultural policy in Yugoslavia. Paris: UNESCO.
> 				"), p. 33)

The significant role of literature under communism, brought to our attention in the paragraph above, has been well-documented by various scholars, including Andrew Wachtel, who notes that literature and writers were traditionally overvalued in Eastern Europe (2006, p. 4). However, what Majstorović likely chose to overlook in his statement is that the rising visibility of the “pre-war suppressed” Macedonia, which gained more autonomy during this period, was actually part of a broader strategy. Beginning with the 1963 Constitution, which marked a shift toward federalism, this strategy aimed to ease emerging nationalist tensions in Yugoslavia (Wachtel [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR49 "
					Wachtel, Andrew Baruch. 1998. Making a nation, breaking a nation: Literature and cultural politics in Yugoslavia. Stanford: Stanford University Press.
				"), pp. 174–175).

Coming back to Milovan Djilas, it should be mentioned that his 1953 articles, which led to his arrest, addressed the issue of self-management in Yugoslavia. In light of the political developments that followed, his call for self-management now seems “prophetic” or at least a far more viable solution. Throughout the period, official critiques emerged denouncing communism and fostering the rise of “particular nationalisms” (see Wachtel [1998](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR49 "
					Wachtel, Andrew Baruch. 1998. Making a nation, breaking a nation: Literature and cultural politics in Yugoslavia. Stanford: Stanford University Press.
				")). These tensions were evident from events such as the publication of the “Declaration Concerning the Name and the Position of the Croatian Literary Language” in March 1967, which rejected the 1954 Novi Sad Agreement on the Serbo-Croatian language and laid the groundwork for the Croatian Spring (1967–1971), and the 1986 publication of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts Memorandum, a document that emphasized alleged anti-Serb discrimination and stoked nationalist sentiment (see Križan [1994](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR27 "
					Križan, Mojmir. 1994. New Serbian nationalism and the third Balkan war. Studies in East European Thought 46:47–68.
				"), pp. 57–59).

As Slavist Edward Możejko ([1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR38 "
					Możejko, Edward. 1997. Postmodernism in the literatures of former Yugoslavia. In International postmodernism: Theory and literary practice, eds. Hans Bertens and Douwe Fokkema, 441–446. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
				"), pp. 441–446)—the author of a monograph on socialist realism—illustrates, the import of postmodernism in Yugoslavia coincided with this intensification of nationalist tendencies during the 1980s. This political backdrop adds another layer to the anti-communist East-Central European landscape: while in much of Eastern Europe postmodernism functioned as “a subversive political tool in opposition to the official literary and political dogmas” (Bertens and Fokkema [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR4 "
					Bertens, Hans, and Douke Fokkema. 1997. Introductory note. In International postmodernism: Theory and literary practice, eds. Hand Bertens and Douke Fokkema, 297–305. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
				"), p. 300), where these dogmas were purely communist, the situation in Yugoslavia was more complex. There, postmodernism and postmodern literary practices had to navigate not only communist dogmas but also the increasing _officialization_ of Serbian and Croatian nationalist discourses. Needless to say, subversiveness, by definition, presupposes the existence of a politicized literary postmodernism. However, in this case, it is a politicized postmodernism that lacks a critical dimension. More specifically, while Eastern European writers used postmodernism as an instrument to criticize their own regimes, they largely failed to extend that critique to North American capitalism, which, on the contrary, many of them embraced. Teodora Dumitru makes a similar argument regarding Romania’s 1980s Generation—a group of writers central to the development and spread of postmodernism in Romania—stating that “[g]eographically, the scope of their politics rarely transcended the nation-state, and, its substantial, American and world literature intertextually notwithstanding, their work lacks a truly global perspective let alone a critical one” (Dumitru [2018](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR13 "
					Dumitru, Teodora. 2018. Gaming the world-system: Creativity, politics, and beat influence in the poetry of the 1980s generation. In Romanian literature as world literature, eds. Mircea Martin, Christian Moraru, and Andrei Terian, 271–288. New York: Bloomsbury.
				"), p. 282).

Another perspective on the limited subversiveness of postmodernism comes from Slovenian philosopher Aleš Erjavec in his study of postmodernism in Eastern European visual arts. Erjavec distinguishes between two coexisting forms of postmodernism in former socialist countries: one uncritical and the other politicized. He further observes that in some countries, particularly those with harsher political conditions, the practice of postmodernism was significantly hindered—or, at times, nearly impossible:

> In East Germany, political repression was so strong that the only artists who succeeded in developing postmodern art were those who emigrated to West Germany […] In Poland, the political and economic crises in the 1980s were so severe that postmodernism was only a vague idea, more potent among philosophers and writers than among visual artists. The result was that there, the legacy of the nonpoliticized Conceptual Art from the 1960s remained almost intact well into the late 1980s and even into the early 1990s. In Czechoslovakia after the Prague Spring of 1968, the regime was so oppressive that very few visual artists dared to invest their works with overt political view. (2003, p. 25)

Aleš Erjavec’s insights are crucial for understanding the diversity of postmodernisms across Eastern Europe and how the specific conditions of each late socialist context shaped postmodernist practices—a point to which I will return later.

As regards the first theoretical signs of postmodernism in Yugoslavia, they can be traced back to 1982, when the Slovenian literary magazine _Sodobnost_ (Contemporaneity) initiated discussions on the topic. However, as Edward Możejko notes, Dobrilo Aranitović’s bibliography of postmodernist works, published in a 1990 issue of _Gledišta_ (Perspectives) magazine, claims that the term was first used in Yugoslavia in 1983, following the release of Predrag Palavestra’s _Kritička književnost: Alternativa postmodernizma_ (Critical Literature: The Alternative of Postmodernism) (Możejko [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR38 "
					Możejko, Edward. 1997. Postmodernism in the literatures of former Yugoslavia. In International postmodernism: Theory and literary practice, eds. Hans Bertens and Douwe Fokkema, 441–446. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
				"), p. 441). The omission of the Slovenian debate might not be as innocent as it seems. A look at the contributors to the _Gledišta_ issue on postmodernism reveals that, with few exceptions, such as Croatian painters Djuro Seder and Željko Kipke, nearly all contributors were Serbian. Moreover, as Edward Możejko points out, it is particularly striking that Slovenians are absent from this issue, especially considering that “[t]he force and breadth of the postmodernist impact in Slovenia remains unmatched in other literatures of former Yugoslavia” (p. 443), while “[i]n Serbia, the earliest accounts and explanations of postmodernism are, in fact, translations of the work of Slovene critics” (p. 444). In my view, this exclusion may reflect the gradual institutionalization of nationalist discourses, as the debates seem increasingly confined to the borders of each republic. An exception is Macedonia, where postmodern theory was imported from Belgrade and other centers in Yugoslavia (p. 445). Another one is represented by the Serbian journal _Delo_ (Opus), which published articles on postmodernist theory and art, disregarding national constraints (Lazičić [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR30 "
					Lazičić, Goran. 2022. Death of the author and birth of the nation: Literary postmodernism and nationalism in Serbia. Serbian Studies: Journal of the North American Society for Serbian Studies 33(1):21–37.
				"), pp. 28–29). Edward Możejko’s concluding remark underscores exactly this consolidation of cultural borders within what was still Yugoslavia: “If one may assume that literature sometimes serves as a harbinger of social and political changes, then postmodernism in the South-Slavic nations could be perceived as presaging the political disintegration of the country” (p. 446). In other words, the reception of postmodernism anticipates the later disintegration of the country.

Although context is crucial for understanding the early reception of postmodernism in the Yugoslav republics, the import of postmodernist theory itself often overlooked these extra-literary factors. This led to a focus on postmodernism in literature primarily as a stylistic phenomenon, or as Romanian literary critic Mircea Martin described, a “postmodernism without postmodernity” (Martin [1996](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR35 "
					Martin, Mircea. 1996. Un postmodernism fără postmodernitate [A postmodernism without postmodernity]. România literară 40:12–13.
				"), p. 13). Similarly, Dragana Obradović’s overview of the reception of postmodernism in Yugoslavia highlights a widespread neutrality toward ideological, historical, and political contexts in the scholarship across the country (2016, p. 28).

This is not to say that philosophical works were absent. For example, Fredric Jameson’s _Postmodernism, or The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism_ (1989) was translated into Slovene in 1992, and shorter references and translations of his works had already reached Yugoslavia earlier. However, there seems to have been a divide between theoretical discussions—which were often limited to translations and reviews—and literary practice (Możejko [1997](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR38 "
					Możejko, Edward. 1997. Postmodernism in the literatures of former Yugoslavia. In International postmodernism: Theory and literary practice, eds. Hans Bertens and Douwe Fokkema, 441–446. Amsterdam: Benjamins.
				"), p. 443), which, as expected, preceded the institutional import (Obradović [2016](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR39 "
					Obradović, Dragana. 2016. Writing the Yugoslav wars: Literature, postmodernism, and the ethics of representation. Toronto: Toronto University Press.
				"), p. 26). The dominant approach to postmodern literature was framed by several key theoretical concepts: Jean-François Lyotard’s “incredulity toward metanarratives” (1984), Linda Hutcheon’s “historiographic metafiction” (1988), and Brian McHale’s focus on the ontological aspects of postmodern fiction (1987). These became, I would say, canonized frameworks for reading Yugoslav postmodern literature, alongside narrative strategies such as intertextuality, self-reflexivity, parody, irony, and fragmentation, the core features of a postmodern text (see Hutcheon [1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR20 "
					Hutcheon, Linda. 1988. A poetics of postmodernism: History, theory, fiction, New York: Routledge.
				")). In short, postmodernism entered the 1990s primarily as a matter of poetics, largely detached from any engagement with late capitalism or even late socialism.

In engaging critically with Fredric Jameson’s work, Cristian Moraru rightly calls for a more nuanced contextualization of postmodernism in Eastern Europe, one that shifts the focus from late capitalism to late socialism, along with its politics and subversive elements (2001). However, what is missing from this broader picture is the resurgence of nationalism, which, though embraced by some writers and artists, remained largely unacknowledged before 1990. Aleš Erjavec highlights this shift, noting that in 1981, Sándor Pinczehelyi painted three paprikas in the Hungarian national colors—red, white, and green—and argues that “the arrival and emergence of postmodernism in socialist countries resulted in a renewed interest in traditional motifs and the use of quotations from and references to classical works from these cultures” (2003, p. 43). For instance, the nationalism embedded in Milorad Pavić’s best-known novel, _Dictionary of the Khazars_, went largely unaddressed until the late 1990s, even though the novel was published in 1984 and praised for its postmodern techniques. The author himself quickly became one of the most prominent Serbian novelists of the second half of the twentieth century. In short, during late socialism, Yugoslavia stood out among other Eastern European countries in that it allowed the consolidation of multiple nationalisms, which eventually contributed to its violent disintegration and became integrated into postmodern literary production.

In this context, I argue that the import of magical realism and postmodernism in Yugoslavia can be characterized by two key shortcomings: under-theorization and unbalanced imports. As shown earlier, Yugoslavia’s external and internal politics shaped how magical realism and postmodernism were imported. The shift in cultural focus from Latin to North America in the 1960s led to a mediated and fragmented reception of the Latin American Boom, with Jorge Luis Borges, not a true magic realist but a precursor of the genre (see Simpkins [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR43 "
					Simpkins, Scott. 1995. Sources of magic realism/ supplements to realism in contemporary Latin American literature. In Magical realism: Theory, history, community, eds. Lois Parkinson Zamora and Wendy B. Faris, 145–159. Durham: Duke University Press.
				"), p. 145), becoming central to the rebranding of the fantastic in Croatian and Serbian literary criticism, as I showed in the previous pages. While the import of magical realism coincided with changes in external politics, postmodernism arrived during a period of significant internal political transformation. However, postmodernism was mostly discussed in terms of its aesthetics. As I will show in the next section, the political dimensions of Yugoslav postmodernism only began to emerge in the late 1990s, when scholars started linking some of the literary and cinematic works of the 1980s and 1990s to the disintegration of the country.

## Towards a politics of magical realism and postmodernism in the post-Yugoslav context

Shortly before discussions about magical realism and postmodernism resurfaced in a post-Yugoslav context, Theo D’haen published a study aimed at exploring the hierarchical relationship between these concepts. While he does not attempt to de-hierarchize them, the scholar highlights their shared characteristic: both seek to decenter traditional centers of privilege related to culture, gender, class, or race (D’haen [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR12 "
					D’haen, Theo. 1995. Magic realism and postmodernism: Decentering privileged centers. In Magical realism: Theory, history, community, eds. Lois Parkinson Zamora and Wendy B. Faris, 191–208. Durham: Duke University Press.
				"), p. 195). The term “ex-centric”—the central concept in Theo D’haen’s study—derives from Hutcheon ([1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR20 "
					Hutcheon, Linda. 1988. A poetics of postmodernism: History, theory, fiction, New York: Routledge.
				"), pp. 57–73), who, in addition to drawing on works by scholars such as Derrida, Said, Nietzsche, and Foucault, refers to Lyotard’s notion that postmodernism is based on a depletion of centrality and totality (1984). However, there is evidence that suggests that these interpretations of magical realism tend to subordinate its political dimensions to those of postmodernism.

A closer examination of Alejo Carpentier’s article reveals that the “ex-centric” is framed not in terms of identity through difference, as previous discussions suggest, but rather in systemic terms. In his article “The Baroque and the Marvelous Real” (1975), Carpentier addresses the ex-centricity of Latin America. First, he distinguishes it from European Surrealism, which he sees as an intervention in the real rather than a representation of reality (Carpentier [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR6 "
					Carpentier, Alejo. 1995. The baroque and the marvelous real. In Magical realism: Theory, history, community, eds. Lois Parkinson Zamora and Wendy B. Faris, 89–108. Durham: Duke University Press.
				"), pp. 102–103), and then he argues that, unlike Surrealism, “the marvelous real […] is encountered in its raw state, latent and omnipresent, in all that is Latin American” (Carpentier [1995](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11212-025-09725-x#ref-CR6 "
					Carpentier, Alejo. 1995. The baroque and the marvelous real. In Magical realism: Theory, history, community, eds. Lois Parkinson Zamora and Wendy B. Faris, 89–108. Durham: Duke University Press.
				"), p. 104). This type of ex-centricity transcends the individual, making magical realism fundamentally incongruent with postmodernism. This open-access scholarly article by Snejana Ung, published in Studies in East European Thought (Volume 78, pp. 691–710, 2026), explores the politics of magical realism and postmodernism in (former) Yugoslavia. The author argues that although both literary movements were introduced during late socialism, their theoretical debates initially focused on aesthetic aspects. A more substantial political analysis only emerged in the late 1990s, when the destructive impact of particular nationalisms became evident following Yugoslavia's collapse.

The article traces how magical realism and postmodernism were imported into Yugoslavia. Magical realism arrived through a mediated, fragmented reception of the Latin American Boom, with Jorge Luis Borges—rather than more politically engaged magical realists—becoming a central influence. This resulted in an apolitical import that downplayed the leftist politics inherent to Latin American magical realism. Postmodernism entered Yugoslavia during the 1980s, coinciding with intensifying nationalist tendencies, and was initially discussed primarily in aesthetic terms.

The author contends that by the time these movements were analyzed politically in the late 1990s, the focus had shifted from their late socialist context to the extreme nationalisms contributing to the country's collapse. This one-sided contextualization was driven by the reception of bestsellers and blockbusters, particularly Milorad Pavić's novel "Dictionary of the Khazars" (1984) and Emir Kusturica's film "Underground" (1995). The article examines how postmodernist works came to be seen as both products of and contributors to an anti-Yugoslav, nationalist political agenda, while magical realism continued to be treated primarily as an aesthetic category for a longer period.

Key findings include: the import of magical realism and postmodernism was characterized by under-theorization and unbalanced imports; Yugoslavia's external politics (Tito-Stalin split, Non-Aligned Movement) shaped cultural exchanges; the focus on Borges over more politically engaged Latin American writers downplayed leftist politics; and the reception of postmodernism in Yugoslavia anticipated the later political disintegration of the country.

# What We Won’t Stand To See In Netflix’s Adaptation Of “One Hundred Years Of Solitude”

![Isabel Carrasco](https://i0.wp.com/culturacolectiva.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/T04B5FUBY4U-U04BPCGSGVA-f8f41f9a66fa-512.jpg?resize=150%2C150&ssl=1) by [Isabel Carrasco](https://culturacolectiva.com/en/author/isabel-carrascoculturacolectiva-com/)

[January 16, 2023](https://culturacolectiva.com/en/entertainment/movies/gabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix-series/)

in [Movies](https://culturacolectiva.com/en/entertainment/movies/)

[![What we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of one hundred years of solitude](https://i0.wp.com/culturacolectiva.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/WO4FHVPBXNBL5LDLN6CDOMHZ5E.jpg?resize=750%2C375&ssl=1 "What we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ")

What We Won't Stand To See In Netflix's Adaptation Of One Hundred Years Of Solitude](https://i0.wp.com/culturacolectiva.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/WO4FHVPBXNBL5LDLN6CDOMHZ5E.jpg?fit=1600%2C654&ssl=1)

It’s true what they say: Netflix is changing the film industry forever. And now, they even seem to be changing the book industry as well! The streaming platform giant has just acquired the adaptation rights to Gabriel García Márquez’s landmark novel One Hundred Years Of Solitude, more than 50 years after the book’s publication, and they’re going to turn it into a series. To say this is a huge deal is an understatement. García Márquez is the Colombian Nobel Literature Laureate that every Spanish speaker loves. It’s simply one of the best books ever written in Spanish.

But this isn’t huge only because of the novel’s quality. It’s a huge deal because people have been attempting to buy the book’s film rights for more than 50 years. And now, Netflix finally did it.  
All we know right now is that García Marquéz’s sons, Rodrigo and Gonzalo García, will work as executive producers on the series. And that the series will be mainly filmed in Colombia. In Spanish! The stakes are high, and the possibility of the greatest series ever is within Netflix’s reach, but so is the level of disappointment.

How do they plan to adapt this groundbreaking novel? Take this into consideration: One Hundred Years of Solitude is a family saga that tells the story of the Buendías, who arrive at a town in the middle of nowhere and experience epidemics, natural disasters, heartbreak, revolutions, industrialization, and a lot of drama over the span of one hundred years (get it?). We’re all eager to see how it will all play out, but for now, here’s some of the things Netflix should avoid:  
Read more: Was HIMYM inspired by Love in the Time of Cholera?  
 ![1552002036280 gabriel garcia marquez one hundred years of solitude netflix series - what we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ](https://i0.wp.com/img.culturacolectiva.com/content_image/2019/3/7/1552002036280-gabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix-series.gif?ssl=1 "What we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ")  
 ![1551901202333 garcia marquez cien años de soledad - what we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ](https://i0.wp.com/img.culturacolectiva.com/content_image/2019/3/6/1551901202333-garcia-marquez-cien-an%CC%83os-de-soledad.jpg?ssl=1 "What we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ")

## Casting non-Colombian actors

Hollywood has a history of putting all brown actors and characters in the same basket. Antonio Banderas, a Spaniard, became famous for playing Mexicans, and Anthony Quinn (Mexican) was hailed for playing Greek and Arab characters. But, hey, even Gwyneth Paltrow’s unbearable English accent won her an Oscar for playing a 16th century Londoner. It might not make a difference to non-Spanish speakers but to truly do justice to the adaptation, I expect an all Colombian/Latin American cast. It makes a huge difference. I don’t care how good Breaking Bad is, but those scenes in Mexico feature actors who can’t speak Spanish to save their lives! And Wagner Moura was great in Narcos… you know, for a series about crooks. But when it comes to this novel, I’m not saying I’m asking for perfection but… yeah, I’m asking for perfection.

## Making a telenovela

It’s quite tempting to make a telenovela with Latin American themes and actors. Passion is in our blood, and this book is filled with really strong emotions. And don’t forget about all the family drama. However, we can always tell the difference between drama and melodrama, the latter being something we’re fed up with. We want good acting, good directing, three-dimensional characters, and for the series to avoid all clichés at all costs. Period.  
Read: 4 Theories About The Next Breaking Bad Movie That Are Not Completely Insane  
 ![1551908101502 one hundreds years of solitude illustrated - what we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ](https://i0.wp.com/img.culturacolectiva.com/content_image/2019/3/6/1551908101502-one-hundreds-years-of-solitude-illustrated.jpg?ssl=1 "What we won't stand to see in netflix's adaptation of ")

## Trying to jam the entire novel into a few episodes

One of the frequent problems regarding adaptations is the time constraints natural to feature films. However, Netlifx has the chance to make a Game of Thrones-like adaptation. That is, an adaptation that really takes its time to put all the necessary elements from its source material into the finished product. So, Netlifx, just take your time. Not everything has to be in the series (losing things is part of the process), but just make sure everything is coherent, exciting, and just overall beautiful.

## Having non-Latino screenwriters

There’s been a trend in the way Netflix writes series. They hire American scriptwriters and then have a single Spanish speaker translate the entire thing. This is a terrible idea. You can completely tell there’s just something off about the lines in the series. I’m sure there are screenwriters in Colombia more than capable to delivering a great script. Trust us with this one.

García Márquez died quietly in his Mexico City home only five years ago, but ever since he published the novel, he remained reluctant to sell its rights, fearing it was impossible to adapt it, thinking it wouldn’t do justice to adapt it into another language, and in turn, fearing audiences would reject a series in Spanish; therefore, ruling out the possibility of a huge frustration from himself, the fans, and pretty much culture in the world. However, things are clearly changing. First, feature films are being largely overshadowed by the golden age of series. And second, audiences around the world have become more accepting of Spanish-language productions. Think of Narcos, for example, or the Academy-Award winning film, Roma, greatly accepted by audiences around the world.

With that in mind then, maybe it’s true. Perhaps it’s time to take this novel to a whole new level.

# News That Netflix Will Adapt One Hundred Years of Solitude Gets Mixed Response From Fans

By: [Jo Corona](https://www.latinorebels.com/author/ecorona/ "Posts by Jo Corona")

Mar 8, 2019

6:16 PM

The news that Netflix will be adapting literary legend Gabriel García Márquez’s most famous novel, *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, elicited a mixed range of responses from fans in the United States and the Americas, with some people being incredibly excited and others (like our founder) not as much.

> I don't think I want to see [#Cienaños](https://twitter.com/hashtag/Ciena%C3%B1os?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) on Netflix when it comes out. Have read that book so many times that how I view it my head will always been how I interpret it. But at the same time, what if the series becomes a global phenomenon? What a dilemma.
>
> — Julio Ricardo Varela (@julito77) [March 7, 2019](https://twitter.com/julito77/status/1103697787357671426?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

In general, though, readers of Gabo, as the Colombian Nobel laureate is commonly referred to in the Spanish-speaking world, agreed on one thing: expectations are not high, they are very high when it comes to seeing their beloved characters from Macondo —the isolated town where the events in the book unfold— being played out on screen. The pressure is on for Netflix to produce a series that measures up to the expectations of a readership that is fervently loyal to the book and to the Buendía family lineage.

> ¿Se imaginan el problema para organizar el casting de [#CienAñosdeSoledad](https://twitter.com/hashtag/CienA%C3%B1osdeSoledad?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) para la serie de [@NetflixLAT](https://twitter.com/NetflixLAT?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)?   
> – ¿Para qué papel vienes?  
> – El de Aureliano  
> – …
>
> — Dany Kino (@Dany\_Kino) [March 6, 2019](https://twitter.com/Dany_Kino/status/1103367978102476801?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

> I would love to see it. Netflix has to do this well, otherwise, they will be sorry, I think. This is a universally loved book. And no Banderas or Bardem, please. No Penelope Cruz as Remedios La Bella either. Let´s get primarily Latin Americans to play these characters
>
> — Pilar Marrero (@PilarMarrero) [March 7, 2019](https://twitter.com/PilarMarrero/status/1103755726256693248?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

Netflix made the announcement that it had acquired the rights to García Márquez’s masterpiece on Wednesday, what would have been the writer’s 92nd birthday. The book that popularized the literature genre of magical realism was first published in 1967, more than 50 years ago, and has been translated into 46 languages. It will be the first time it’s adapted for the screen, something that García Márquez had voiced his aversion to in the past, even though he was a consummate film lover and critic. In a column he wrote in 1982, he explained that his wish was for his readers to communicate directly to his words, “so that they will imagine the characters as they want to, and not with the borrowed face of an actor on screen.” The writer was alluding to a one million dollar offer by Mexican film director and actor to acquire the rights of the work. García Márquez shot him down: “Anthony Quinn, with or without his million dollars, will never be Coronel Aureliano Buendía to me or my readers,” he wrote, [according to the BBC](https://www.bbc.com/mundo/noticias-america-latina-47475246).

And, preceding Harvey Weinstein’s sexual abuse allegations, the film mogul [said in 2014](https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/films/news/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-was-unfilmable-its-writer-gabriel-garcia-m-rquez-said-so-9292532.html) soon after García Márquez died, that the writer had acquiesced to granting the rights of the movie to him and Giuseppe Tornatore if they agreed to film the entire book “but only release one chapter –two minutes long— each year, for 100 years.” An answer befitting to the father of magical realism. He just did not think it was possible to adapt the novel in only one or two movies.

But even though García Márquez said he did not want his seminal work being adapted to the screen, the logic behind film production has changed (see the recent Oscar-nominated [*Roma*](https://www.latinorebels.com/2019/01/24/yalitzaaparicio/)) and thus the writer’s family considered the time is ripe to finally do an adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*. García Márquez’s two sons negotiated with Netflix and will be executive producers in the upcoming project. The series will be produced entirely in Spanish and parts of it will be filmed in Colombia, two important wishes on the part of the writer’s family, who broke the news of the acquisition in an interview with the [Colombian newspaper El Tiempo](https://www.eltiempo.com/cultura/cine-y-tv/netflix-hara-una-serie-de-la-novela-cien-anos-de-soledad-de-gabriel-garcia-marquez-334516).

“Now is a good time for series,” said one of the sons, Rodrigo García Barcha in Spanish, “and with Netflix’s reach —of course— I think the work, the author, Colombia and the world of Macondo will reach a larger audience.”

> This will be phenomenal if they do it correctly. They already made the best step in that it will be completely in Spanish [#cienaños](https://twitter.com/hashtag/ciena%C3%B1os?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) [#GABO](https://twitter.com/hashtag/GABO?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw) <https://t.co/zc0UKarDNV>
>
> — Andres Villatoro (@netoduk) [March 6, 2019](https://twitter.com/netoduk/status/1103352391628394497?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw)

In the past, other García Márquez book adaptations have been “[No One Writes to the Colonel](https://variety.com/1999/film/reviews/no-one-writes-to-the-colonel-1200457626/),” directed by Arturo Ripstein in 1999, “[Chronicle of a Death Foretold](x-apple-data-detectors://7)” from 1987, or “[Love in the Time of Cholera](x-apple-data-detectors://8),” starring Spanish actor Javier Bardem.

The challenge is multifold: to honor the Nobel laureate’s work and legacy, to respect his family’s wishes, and to not let down his fan base. But there is also the question of how Netflix will decide to tackle and depict certain passages from the book, sensitive to U.S. interests abroad.

Although the novel is fictional, its climax is famously based in the 1928 massacre of United Fruit Company plantation workers at the hands of the Colombian military. On that topic, historian [Greg Grandin says](https://www.thenation.com/article/gabriel-garcia-marquez-rebel-against-form-artist-against-forces-oblivion/) that although political violence was not new to Latin America, these crackdowns manifested a different type of repression. “The terror was aimed at eliminating not just opponents but also alternatives, targeting the kind of social-democratic solidarity and humanism that powered the postwar Latin American left. Hundreds of thousands of people were disappeared and an equal number tortured. Hundreds of communities were, like Macondo, wiped off the face of the earth.”

No matter what happens with the series, here is a book extract of that scene to entice readers to pick the book up again before the series is released (tentatively in 2020):

“When José Arcadio Segundo came to he was lying face up in the darkness. He realized that he was riding on an endless and silent train and that his head was caked with dry blood and that all his bones ached. He felt an intolerable desire to sleep. Prepared to sleep for many hours, safe from the terror and the horror, he made himself comfortable on the side that pained him less, and only then did he discover that he was lying against dead people. There was no free space in the car except for an aisle in the middle. Several hours must have passed since the massacre because the corpses had the same temperature as a plaster in autumn and the same consistency of petrified foam that it had, and those who had put them in the car had had time to pile them up in the same way in which they transported bunches of bananas. Trying to flee from the nightmare, José Arcadio Segundo dragged himself from one car to another in the direction in which the train was heading, and in the flashes of light that broke through the wooden slats as they went through sleeping towns he saw the man corpses, woman corpses, child corpses who would be thrown into the sea like rejected bananas. ”

\*\*\*

*Emily Corona is a digital intern at Futuro Media. She is a journalist and translator from Mexico City, pursuing a master’s in journalism and Latin American and Caribbean studies at NYU. She tweets from [@daminijo](https://twitter.com/daminijo).*

args.summary: On March 6, 2019 (what would have been Gabriel García Márquez's 92nd birthday), Netflix announced it had acquired the rights to adapt his masterpiece "One Hundred Years of Solitude" into a series. The news received mixed reactions from fans, with many expressing both excitement and concern about how the beloved novel will be translated to screen. The book, first published in 1967 and translated into 46 languages, will be adapted for the screen for the first time. García Márquez had previously opposed adaptations, famously rejecting a $1 million offer from Anthony Quinn in 1982, and later jokingly suggesting to Harvey Weinstein that a film adaptation should release one two-minute chapter per year for 100 years. However, García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García Barcha and Gonzalo García Barcha, negotiated with Netflix and will serve as executive producers. The series will be produced entirely in Spanish and filmed partially in Colombia. Key concerns from fans include: honoring Gabo's legacy, casting primarily Latin American actors (avoiding stars like Antonio Banderas, Javier Bardem, or Penélope Cruz), and how the series will depict sensitive scenes such as the 1928 United Fruit Company massacre, which is a climactic passage in the novel. The article includes a lengthy excerpt from the book describing the massacre's aftermath from the perspective of José Arcadio Segundo.

# 2 Years Later, The Return Of Netflix's One Hundred Years of Solitude Is Only 1 Month Away

![Netflix's logo in front of the poster of One Hundred Years of Solitude part two](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/netflix-s-logo-in-front-of-poster-of-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-part-two-1.jpg?&fit=crop&w=1600&h=900)

It's a golden age for seeing books on screen, with a wave of Netflix releases based on iconic novels, ranging from contemporary titles like Harlan Coben’s *I Will Find You* to classics such as the upcoming *Pride and Prejudice* adaptation slated for 2026, which became some of the platform's most talked-about productions. However, readers will be even more spoiled, as the series based on one of history’s greatest books is set to reach its conclusion in just a month.

Hailed as a literary masterpiece by Nobel Prize in Literature laureate Gabriel García Márquez, [***One Hundred Years of Solitude***](https://screenrant.com/db/tv-show/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-2024/) stands as one of the biggest classic novels worldwide, selling millions of copies since 1967. Sadly, it appeared on the list of banned books in U.S. school districts in the 2023 and 2025 periods, citing its explicit sexual content and profanity, [as reported by PEN America](https://pen.org/nobel-prize-winners-banned/). But beyond censorship, *One Hundred Years of Solitude* was also long considered unadaptable, even by the author himself, since García Márquez famously rejected several offers to turn the book into a movie.

With its intricate character relationships and a narrative deeply rooted in Colombian history, it was an insurmountable challenge to translate the book's magic. It wasn't until 2024 that *One Hundred Years of Solitude*'s potential was grasped not as a movie but as a series that provided the necessary time to immerse viewers in the town of Macondo with the approval of García Márquez’s family and entirely filmed in Colombia with local actors. The second season of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* is hitting Netflix on August 5, 2026, but the adaptation has already set the bar high for its finale.

## What Makes One Hundred Years of Solitude One of Netflix's Greatest Book-to-Screen Adaptations

![Colonel Aureliano Buendia from the Netflix series with a book cover for One Hundred Years of Solitude](https://static0.srcdn.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/colonel-aureliano-buendia-from-the-netflix-series-with-a-book-cover-for-one-hundred-years-of-solitude.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2)

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* explores the turbulent generations of the Buendía family, beginning with José Arcadio and his wife, Úrsula Iguarán. The biggest difference in Netflix's adaptation is that its first sequence covers the very end of the story, including symbolism for readers, while also giving newcomers a heads-up about the cyclical nature of the family. The novel is quite dense, with very little dialogue. It spans 100 years, and the Buendía family has a habit of passing down names from generation to generation, making the chronology hard to understand for some readers as well as distinguishing the characters.

While the actors bring faces to the characters, the series adapted the novel's unique structure by employing narration, which helps viewers follow the events while also cleverly filling in the gaps in the story's time jumps, making it more accessible. Although *One Hundred Years of Solitude* is the kind of story that loses some charm outside the written page, shaped around magical realism, where the link between the extraordinary and reality tends to be subtle and enigmatic, the adaptation spares no effort in portraying the elements that defined Macondo, such as its weird customs, superstitions, or even its violence.

With landscapes of almost divine beauty, the series remains faithful to the novel's political, erotic, and esoteric elements. But even if *One Hundred Years of Solitude*'s adaptation doesn't quite match the novel's impact, specifically its metaphorical tone, which cloaks events, so viewers can use their imagination, the series succeeds in capturing a style steeped in the novel's spirit. It hooks the viewer with the urge to uncover the characters' fates, effectively expressing the work's themes of isolation, emotional wounds, and the unconscious patterns that lead to obsessions and abuse with foreshadowing and visual elements that give it a unique touch.

# 26 TV Shows Based on Books for Your Streaming (and Reading!) Pleasure

Swap chapters for episodes with these shows inspired by literary favorites. * * *

By Mary Sollosi July 9, 2026  Link copied to clipboard Share   

[Film adaptations are great](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/movies-based-on-books-netflix), but sometimes nothing can do a book justice quite like a full-blown TV series. It provides all the visual possibilities of a movie along with the added benefits of a long runtime and a chapter-style, episodic structure. (The Victorians basically consumed Dickens novels like 19th-century TV dramas, after all.)

Shows inspired by books span genres, from legal series like[_The Lincoln Lawyer_](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/the-lincoln-lawyer) to thrillers like [_You_](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/you)_,_ fantasies like[_The Witcher_](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/the-witcher)_,_ and period dramas like [_Little House on the Prairie_](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/little-house-on-the-prairie), to name a few. And while audiences are watching them around the world, these adaptations can also spark renewed interest in their source material, with books [returning to bestseller lists](https://about.netflix.com/en/news/celebrating-world-book-day-how-netflix-adaptations-are-driving-bestseller) years or sometimes even decades after they originally hit shelves.

We’ve rounded up a list of Netflix series that are based on books — classic and modern, fiction and nonfiction, happy and scary, funny and sad. Add these titles to your queue to find your newest bookish favorite.

### 3 Body Problem

![Image 5](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQUPlsykJU9djmVfHUEy_gcqfY7dQhJH45u8UducBl-MdVFGKEZ_1uCCDwp0OX2fDhih0pu6OqBktwHTucsIKlqHuG5vyZHqaR9rlTIG6UisZLeRkVbdhDrMfnqLaNKs93pRP3-jv5bRgRAu1kQ.jpg?r=857)

Based on the best-selling novels by Cixin Liu,[this epic drama](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/3-body-problem-teaser-release-date) spans decades and continents. The eight-episode series _3 Body Problem_ imagines what happens when a young scientist makes a bold decision in 1960s China that will have major global implications over the ensuing decades. In the present day, a group of brilliant physicists, baffled by recent anomalies in their research, team up with a hardened investigator (Benedict Wong) to reckon with the consequences.

### Agatha Christie's Seven Dials

![Image 7](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQR6Vw-fjgKGJgUSLuEtPV4kBylKA8d6vP_pH9e-dP_H99y0hz2ksBwi7eZY5g_6q9-iuHH6RJl0ed97AGFRJhB39hEjbOKVZzwoKHNfSVK3VjXhOyNF3IrQuwTt0YzHciprHi-cxSoCrKbb1zg.jpg?r=008)

The morning after a party at a lavish country house, Lady Eileen “Bundle” Brent (Mia McKenna-Bruce) is shocked to discover Gerry Wade (Corey Mylchreest) still in bed, even as seven alarm clocks go off inside his room. But Gerry isn’t sleeping — he’s dead, and Bundle is determined to solve the mystery of who is responsible for his untimely end. Helena Bonham Carter and Martin Freeman also star in the three-part adaptation of the Queen of Crime’s novel.

When the young detective investigates the shocking case herself, she uncovers truths that many would prefer were left buried.

### Boots

Surviving boot camp is one thing, but doing so when being gay in the military was illegal is another. This life-affirming dramedy follows closeted Cameron (Miles Heizer) and his best friend, Ray (Liam Oh), as they get thrown into the tough and unpredictable world of the 1990s US Marine Corps. They join a diverse group of recruits, and together, they discover their true selves while navigating the intense environment. The eight-episode series is inspired by former US Marine Greg Cope White’s memoir, _The Pink Marine_.

### Bridgerton

![Image 13](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQXFu5jY2HUT4vYBANDYaM5afOoLLijiXV_o9vDtleXOtFrQRc5D09HjDCDXvB3szSj6ko-c3TXIOJd1rGYAZqHUTZq_d3KQpCyOKXOhETANXQhVMihxk_1p58CJbM9kTtG09-mNHJUez7vBLXg.jpg?r=e8a)

Based on Julia Quinn’s period romance novels and produced by Shonda Rhimes, the Regency-era series introduces audiences to the titular family and its eight siblings. Its inaugural season kicks off the matchmaking with the eldest Bridgerton daughter, Duchess Daphne Basset (Phoebe Dynevor), as she navigates the dos and don’ts of the social season — courtship protocol, dating etiquette, and the scandal sheets penned by Lady Whistledown. Each subsequent season follows the love story of another Bridgerton sibling, including Anthony (Jonathan Bailey), Colin (Luke Newton), and Benedict (Luke Thompson).

### Death by Lightning

![Image 15](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQTBSbv6lLtO27IzJIpOAqXLhAeIBiIpTuf9AALwunetC6ey2kLg6d5OT9e4ZPNWTLH2hZ6QaSy-l2oemuRa8hTiPCTpEq5ymas6XWTRODcLyCgjxqbkFxTp9ke8dg4wRUmMI_SDdQbSiDfYapA.jpg?r=c3b)

This limited series stars Michael Shannon as James Garfield, the underdog congressman who became the 20th US president in 1881. Based on Candice Millard’s nonfiction book _Destiny of the Republic: A Tale of Madness, Medicine, and the Murder of a President,_ the four episodes chronicle Garfield’s improbable rise and abrupt fall at the hands of Charles Guiteau (Matthew Macfadyen), Garfield’s fanatical admirer and eventual assassin. Betty Gilpin, Nick Offerman, Bradley Whitford, and Shea Whigham [also portray real-life figures](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/death-by-lightning-cast-guide).

### FOREVER

![Image 17](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQaf6ZB280UsBpoCZ-BQtjy_CjhWnRuxAO0fII7FoYW7qYKRHo9f5-e6bnbmm7AOBdpDdykFQquaCm7b6G0SFjh96zVZXzXGZ0llSjI129LxfbZTxRIwfviYuBci8Q7wB4dJFDpdYwN3-aO_rog.jpg?r=5bd)

You never forget your first love. This eight-episode romance follows Keisha (Lovie Simone) and Justin (Michael Cooper Jr.), childhood friends who meet again as teenagers, their lives having diverged significantly in the interim. Even while struggling under the pressures of athletic competition, college admissions, and ambitious parents, they forge a powerful bond that may or may not be able to sustain past high school, but is sure to change them both forever. The acclaimed adaptation of the Judy Blume book is the brainchild of Mara Brock Akil ([_Girlfriends_](https://www.netflix.com/title/70157416?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum), [_The Game_)](https://www.netflix.com/title/70157205?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum).

### The Haunting of Hill House

![Image 19](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQeyEbNItYjT_QyAt_OT2Jy8l-hN4_oLUMr5yUBW-hNl3fC9LiNVseK5ECJ3DbXhHyvYrDa-wSEUcVJIuNeyaMXSM5iyhY6b4qEb8VBntl6sNWFFLBnSe1xj0B75WBhHgbMH_mPBuWnTKPuo62A.jpg?r=b11)

Get spooked with these creepy tales from [Mike Flanagan](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/mike-flanagan-shows-movies), who adapted Shirley Jackson’s _The Haunting of Hill House_ for this show and Henry James’_The Turn of the Screw_ for its follow-up,[_The Haunting of Bly Manor_](https://www.netflix.com/title/81237854?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum). Flanagan succeeded that pair of eerie tales with an adaptation of Christopher Pike’s[_The Midnight Club_](https://www.netflix.com/title/81112336?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum), which follows a group of hospice patients who like to tell each other scary stories late at night, as well as the Gothic horror series[_The Fall of the House of Usher_](https://www.netflix.com/title/81414665?trackId=259776131&trkId=259776131&src=tudum),[inspired by the work of Edgar Allan Poe](https://www.netflix.com/tudum/articles/the-fall-of-the-house-of-usher-poe-references).

### HIS & HERS

![Image 21](https://dnm.nflximg.net/api/v6/BvVbc2Wxr2w6QuoANoSpJKEIWjQ/AAAAQVBmchQBtSYnmSLvUyHzvoxqCv6SY_iHBvnYFxJAseP0Ztg_39Nu0Zlrmv1DAQtv62cJM28RFRtlLKlCgsWZnJN3HXCauK6g1FC3R7fo2ReI5AOOIWAM0YvnFXSvgoZ-psBjFR0OQ_QzxCfmzQ.jpg?r=7ec)

An unreliable narrator makes for a good mystery, but in this adaptation of Alice Feeney’s psychological thriller, there are two. In this twisty thriller series, Tessa Thompson plays Anna, a reporter, opposite Jon Bernthal as Jack, a detective. The two are married but estranged, and when a body is discovered in their sleepy Georgia town, they compete to solve the case — with each believing the other is a prime suspect. Pablo Schreiber, Crystal Fox, Marin Ireland, and Sunita Mani are also part of the six-episode mystery.

args.key_excerpts: "Film adaptations are great, but sometimes nothing can do a book justice quite like a full-blown TV series. It provides all the visual possibilities of a movie along with the added benefits of a long runtime and a chapter-style, episodic structure. (The Victorians basically consumed Dickens novels like 19th-century TV dramas, after all.)", "While audiences are watching them around the world, these adaptations can also spark renewed interest in their source material, with books returning to bestseller lists years or sometimes even decades after they originally hit shelves.", "The French thriller Lupin is faithful to its source material more in spirit than in letter, but therein lies its brilliance."
args.summary:
This Netflix Tudum article (published July 9, 2026) lists 26 TV shows based on books available on Netflix. It argues that TV series can do justice to books better than films due to longer runtime and episodic structure. The article notes that these adaptations can drive renewed interest in source material, with books returning to bestseller lists years after publication. The shows span genres including legal dramas, thrillers, fantasies, and period dramas.

Listed shows with key details:
- **3 Body Problem** (2024, 1 season, TV-MA) - Based on Cixin Liu's novels; epic drama spanning decades and continents.
- **Agatha Christie's Seven Dials** (2026, 3 episodes, TV-14) - Starring Mia McKenna-Bruce, Helena Bonham Carter, Martin Freeman.
- **A Good Girl's Guide to Murder** (2024, TV-MA) - Based on Holly Jackson's YA mystery; Emma Myers stars.
- **Boots** (2025, 8 episodes, TV-MA) - Based on Greg Cope White's memoir "The Pink Marine"; about a closeted gay man in 1990s US Marine Corps.
- **Bridgerton** (2020, 4 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Julia Quinn's novels; Shonda Rhimes-produced Regency-era romance.
- **Death by Lightning** (2025, limited series, TV-MA) - Based on Candice Millard's "Destiny of the Republic"; about President Garfield's assassination.
- **FOREVER** (2025, 8 episodes, TV-MA) - Based on Judy Blume's novel; created by Mara Brock Akil.
- **The Haunting of Hill House** (2018, 10 episodes, TV-MA) - Mike Flanagan adaptation of Shirley Jackson's novel.
- **HIS & HERS** (2026, limited series, TV-MA) - Based on Alice Feeney's thriller; Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal star.
- **The Leopard** (2025, limited series, TV-MA) - Based on Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa's classic novel.
- **The Lincoln Lawyer** (2022, 4 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Michael Connelly's books; renewed for 5th season.
- **Little House on the Prairie** (2026, 8 episodes, TV-PG) - Based on Laura Ingalls Wilder's books.
- **Lord of the Flies** (2026, TV-MA) - Based on William Golding's classic; adapted by Jack Thorne.
- **Lupin** (2021, 3 parts, TV-MA) - French thriller inspired by Maurice Leblanc's gentleman thief character.
- **Man on Fire** (2026, 7 episodes, TV-MA) - Based on A.J. Quinnell's book series; Yahya Abdul-Mateen stars.
- **The Night Agent** (2023, 3 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Matthew Quirk's novel; spy thriller.
- **One Hundred Years of Solitude** (2024, 2 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Gabriel García Márquez's novel; filmed in Colombia in Spanish.
- **ONE PIECE** (2023, TV-14) - Live-action adaptation of Eiichiro Oda's manga.
- **The Perfect Couple** (2024, 6 episodes, TV-MA) - Based on Elin Hilderbrand's novel; Nicole Kidman stars.
- **The Queen's Gambit** (2020, limited series, TV-MA) - Based on Walter Tevis's 1983 novel; won 11 Emmys.
- **RIPLEY** (2024, limited series, TV-MA) - Based on Patricia Highsmith's crime classic; Andrew Scott stars.
- **Survival of the Thickest** (2023, 3 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Michelle Buteau's autobiographical essays.
- **Sweet Magnolias** (2020, 5 seasons, TV-14) - Based on Sherryl Woods' 11-book series.
- **Vladimir** (2026, limited series, TV-MA) - Rachel Weisz stars; adapted from Julia May Jonas's novel.
- **The Witcher** (2019, 4 seasons, TV-MA) - Based on Andrzej Sapkowski's novels; animated movies and prequel series also exist.

# Netflix’s ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ Is a Cinematic Miracle

Magical Macondo comes to life even as Colombia suffers tragedy

[Dr. Carlos Flores](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/author/carlos-flores/ "Dr. Carlos Flores")      [2 Comments](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/streaming/netflixs-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-is-a-cinematic-miracle/#comments)  [Ángela Cano](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/angela-cano/), [book adaptation](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/book-adaptation/), [Carla Baratta](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/carla-baratta/), [Claudio Cataño](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/claudio-catano/), [Colombia](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/colombia/), [Dynamo](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/dynamo/), [Gabriel Garcia Marquez](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/gabriel-garcia-marquez/), [Julián Román](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/julian-roman/), [Latin American cinema](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/latin-american-cinema/), [Laura Mora](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/laura-mora/), [Laura Taylor](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/laura-taylor/), [Licinia Alzate](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/licinia-alzate/), [Macondo](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/macondo/), [magical realism](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/magical-realism/), [Marleyda Soto](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/marleyda-soto/), [Netflix](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/netflix/), [One Hundred Years of Solitude](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/one-hundred-years-of-solitude/), [Streaming](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/streaming/), [Television Review](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/tag/television-review/)

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* returns to Netflix with a devastating second season: a triumph of visual arts and literary storytelling over the current mediocrity of Hollywood. And in the middle of a doomscrolling culture, where Nolan’s insipid, soulless The Odyssey is conquering the world; where a Spider-Man whose flat, sadly stupid plot — recycling its already recycled story — is praised by critics; and where the industry’s great revitalizing phenomenon, Obsession, amounts to little more than a bundle of scenes ripped from TikTok, witnessing the grand cinematic spectacle presented by this second season, in the most glorious, poetic, impeccable way, feels like an act of absolute and vehement rebellion. An act of courage and, above all, of respect and love for the glorious experience of putting a mythical and unique story on screen — not merely to be enjoyed, but to be felt, lived, experienced.

Three years ago, I showed not only skepticism but [total rejection](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/television/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-adaptation/) toward the profane idea of adapting the book I hated so much, written by that Colombian Nobel Prize winner whose magical realism condemned future generations of Latin American storytellers to the repetition of fantastical little-town fables, and I firmly took my stand against Netflix. Two years later, when *One Hundred Years of Solitude* debuted on Netflix in 2025, I not only [had to swallow every single one of my words](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/television/surprise-the-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-tv-adaptation-is-magically-great/), I even reconciled with the book. And today, after watching the first seven episodes of the second season — released by Netflix on August 5, with a final episode still to come on August 26 — I have laughed and cried, my skin has crawled, and I have ended up applauding what is, without a doubt, one of the most impressive achievements in the history of Latin American cinema. Does this sound bombastic? Absolutely. Does it do justice to what I have seen on screen? Absolutely.

![](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/CADS_S2_Meme2_R-300x200.jpg)

*Courtesy Netflix*

And Netflix — together with production company Dynamo — has delivered seven colossal one-hour episodes that, taken individually, reach a cinematic standard rarely, if ever, achieved by Latin American cinema. The first season of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* — received with skepticism by critics and audiences alike — started slowly. Very slowly. The first episodes felt like trying to push an elephant across the Sahara, only to eventually find an oasis. It presented a visual spectacle, sprinkled with magic — which, in the end, wasn’t that much magic — and characters leaping from the pages of the immortal novel to ascend into the heavens of streaming.

And so, the foundation of Macondo was told: the town that José Arcadio Buendía — dreamer, leader, and patriarch of an entire universe — and his wife and cousin, that colossal force of nature named Úrsula Iguarán, built from mud and cane at the edge of a river of clean water. It was a season that went in crescendo, just as Macondo itself grew, through challenges, wars, suffering, and celebration. And with four generations of Buendías breathing in the Caribbean heat, the first season ended as something very difficult to surpass. But boy, was it surpassed.

In this continuation, the cards have changed. There is no slow beginning. There are no elephants to drag. There is effort, attention, and dedication required, yes. That is what this series demands from its audience, which is a kick in the ass to the industry’s current dynamic, which asks you to keep track of Easter eggs, read “things you need to know before watching…,” scour Reddit for clues about what you are about to see, stripping away that old, visceral sensation of surrendering yourself to a movie or series and allowing yourself to be surprised. From the very first episode, “The Armistice,” director Laura Mora — responsible for five of the seven episodes, as well as the grand, feature-length finale on August 26 — delivers a masterclass that fuses camera work, production design, and music to inject us into the open veins of a Macondo suffocated by the stench of death brought by war.

![](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/CADS_108-SC858_S-19_R-208x300.jpg)

*Marco Antonio González as*  
*José Arcadio Buendía and*  
*Susana Morales as Úrsula*  
*Iguarán ; Courtesy Netflix.*

Mora’s great achievement is maintaining an effective rhythm despite the complications of the story, and blending “magical realism” with a visual approach that does not trigger that instinctive rejection or reveal the hand of special effects. There is, as with all good drama, an exception —  in the fourth episode “ThereHad Come an Innocent Train,” Remedios the Beauty ascends to the heavens, carried away by a powerful wind while hanging freshly washed sheets out to dry. And well, the truth is: there was no way to make that believable. The series moves like a heavy machine. This is far from a good binge. Here, it is good to breathe, to let what you have seen settle in your mind before continuing with the great journey of Macondo’s growth and eventual downfall.

But direction can be masterful, and if the actors don’t provide enough flesh, the result is helpless, empty. Yet, the cast of *One Hundred Years of Solitude* match the production’s technical achievements. The performances of Claudio Cataño, as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, and Marleyda Soto, as Úrsula Iguarán, who from the earliest episodes — as in much of the previous season — carry the weight of the series on their shoulders, deserve not only recognition but awards at galas packed with Hollywood stars. These two deserve to be named national heroes of Colombia.

Here, you don’t see actors or actresses: you see Aureliano, you see Úrsula. You see them, feel them, suffer with them, criticize them, accompany them… and bid them farewell. The episode depicting Colonel Aureliano Buendía’s death — on October 11, my birthday, thanks, Gabo — drags you into a memorable goodbye. And Úrsula, in her passage into the afterlife, leaves us with the stillness of an indomitable woman who was the bastion of a lineage and whose retirement is deserved. These are moments of high cinema.

To this pair we can add Laura Taylor and Carla Baratta, playing Fernanda del Carpio as a teenager and an adult, respectively. Beautiful, rigid, and pathologically puritanical, Fernanda steals an episode with the most colossal temper tantrum I have ever seen. Indeed, it may be the platonic ideal of a man imagining his wife exploding over something.

![](https://bookandfilmglobe.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/CADS_108-SC857_C-174_R-300x208.jpg)

*Akima as Rebeca; Courtesy Netflix.*

Julián Román who plays Fernanda’s husband, Aureliano Segundo, also takes on the role of Aureliano’s twin, José Arcadio Segundo. Román devours the screen with the brothers’ duality: the warrior against the dreamer. Ángela Cano and Licinia Alzate luminously, profoundly portray Petra Cotes — Aureliano’s true love — at different stages of her life. The list goes on and on, as members of the Buendía family enter and leave a world that shines before eventually becoming dull and drowned in darkness.

And Macondo grows. It modernizes with the arrival of the railroad, which fulfills its founder’s dreams but with development also brings destruction. The establishment of the banana company and the domination of the “American empire” mark Macondo’s extinction. And there is one scene. One scene that sells the entire series: the Banana Massacre. More than three thousand striking workers seeking to establish a union are gunned down. The solemnity, honor, and humanity with which the director tears open the entrails of the conflict between the cruelest violence — all inspired by a very real tragedy that occurred in Colombia in 1928 — and the helplessness of the humble, of those who have no voice to protect them… What we see here, the staging, has nothing to envy *Schindler’s List*. This stands on its own merits as an achievement of contemporary artistic creation.

A great flood lasting four years plunges us into the torment of the protagonists. Everything beautifully and brutally photographed. Here we see the big canvas. It is not only the Buendía lineage that is condemned but Latin America writ large. The magic of our grandmothers’ stories struggles against our conflicted realities. *One Hundred Years of Solitude* moves towards the end of the second — and final — season with one last breath of hope. After a cruel flood has washed everything away, can we start anew with the closing chapter of an epic where speaking with the dead has been as ordinary as screwing your aunt, when Aureliano Babilonia confronts us with the manuscripts of the old gypsy Melquíades and the lineages finally come to an end.

A Colombian woman once told me that one could live and die without ever having seen this series, but that no one could live and die without having read *One Hundred Years of Solitude*. After this second season, I have to correct her, the spirit of Gabriel García Márquez also lives and breathes through Mora’s miraculous Macondo.

## The Legacy of One Hundred Years of Solitude

Before diving into the film itself, it’s important to understand the cultural and literary weight that One Hundred Years of Solitude carries. Published in 1967, García Márquez’s novel is often credited with popularizing magical realism worldwide, intertwining supernatural elements seamlessly with everyday life. The story chronicles the Buendía family across several generations in the fictional town of Macondo, capturing themes of time, memory, and solitude.
