# Guía completa del reparto y personajes de la serie de Cien años de soledad en Netflix

Tras una prolongada espera, el elenco oficial de la anticipada apuesta del streaming ya está aquí. Te contamos todo al respecto.

Por [Miguel Vicencio](/personaje/miguel-vicencio)

Además de ser uno de los trabajos que más destacan de la carrera de **Gabriel García Márquez**, **Cien años de soledad** también es un estandarte de excelencia literaria alrededor del mundo. Con un Premio Nobel de Literatura, el escritor colombiano se colocó como uno de los máximos exponentes del realismo mágico.

**La trama de la historia** es bien conocida: acompaña la vida y aventuras de la familia Buendía, fundadores del pueblo ficticio de **Macondo**, durante un siglo completo. La novela ha vendido 50 millones de copias con traducciones en 46 idiomas. Ahora, gracias a **Netflix**, [vemos esta historia como una serie](https://www.vogue.mx/estilo-de-vida/articulo/macondo-netflix-cien-anos-de-soledad) que regresa con una segunda parte este 5 de agosto.

Este es el **reparto y los personajes.**

## Cien años de soledad (Serie de Netflix): Reparto completo y personajes

* **Claudio Cataño es el coronel Aureliano Buendía adulto**
* **Jerónimo Barón es Aureliano Buendía niño**
* **Santiago Vásquez es Aureliano Buendía joven**
* **Marleyda Soto es Úrsula Iguarán de adulta**
* **Susana Morales es Úrsula Iguarán de joven**
* **Viña Machado es Pilar Ternera**
* **Moreno Borja es Melquíades en sus inicios**
* **Ruggero Pasquarelli es Pietro Crespi**
* **Ella Becerra es Petronila**
* **Marco González es José Arcadio Buendía de joven**
* **Diego Vásquez es José Arcadio Buendía de adulto**
* **Thiago Padilla es José Arcadio niño**
* **Edgar Vittorino es José Arcadio joven**
* **Leonardo Soto es José Arcadio adulto**
* **Luna Ruíz es Amaranta Buendía niña**
* **Loren Sofía Paz es Amaranta Buendía de joven**
* **Nicole Montenegro es Rebeca niña**
* **Laura Sofía Grueso es Rebeca niña joven**
* **Carlos Suárez es Aureliano Iguarán**
* **Cristal Aparicio es Remedios Moscote**
* **Jairo Camargo es Apolinar Moscote**
* **Jacqueline Arenal es Leonor Moscote**
* **Julian Román es los gemelos Jose Arcadio Segundo y Aureliano Segundo**
* **Carla Baratta es Fernanda del Carpio**
* **Ángela Cano es Petra Cotes**
* **María Adelaida Puerta es Amaranta Úrsula**
* **Juanita Molina es Meme**
* **Daniela Reyes es Remedios, la bella**

Formado por una mezcla entre actores naturales y profesionales, **el reparto de Cien años de soledad** ya fue revelado, y a continuación te decimos quiénes serán los responsables:

Claudio Cataño es el coronel Aureliano Buendía adulto

Claudio Cataño es Aureliano Buendía en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

Virginia Casta, Mil colmillos y Nadie sabe para quién trabaja son algunos de los títulos en los que el actor nacido en Bogotá ha participado en el pasado. Sin embargo, esta vez **podremos verlo como el Coronel Aureliano Buendía** **en su versión adulta,** en donde ya consolidado como coronel a través de 32 guerras civiles, es una de las piezas que cambiaron el destino de Macondo.

Jerónimo Barón es Aureliano Buendía niño

Este es el reparto de la adaptación de Cien años de soledad.

Cortesía.

Además de ser uno de los personajes centrales de la historia, **Aureliano Buendía** destaca por poseer habilidades sobrenaturales que van desde la predicción de eventos futuros, hasta manipular objetos con la mente. Su personalidad puede definirse como firme y de carácter inquebrantable. **Jerónimo Barón**, el talento detrás de proyectos como Sound of Freedom, Memoria y Primate, interpreta a **Aureliano Buendía de niño**, una versión que nos permitirá conocer más sobre su vida con sus padres Úrsula Iguarán y José Arcadio Buendía.

Santiago Vásquez es Aureliano Buendía joven

Santiago Vázquez es Aureliano Buendía adolescente en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

**Santiago Vásquez** se une al reparto como **Aureliano Buendía durante su adolescencia**, cuando sus intereses políticos comenzaron a tomar forma y las habilidades mágicas que poseía comienzan a transformarse en una sed por hacer las cosas a su modo.

Marleyda Soto es Úrsula Iguarán de adulta

Marleyda Soto es Úrsula Iguarána en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

**Marleyda Soto**, la actriz de entregas como Perro come perro, Los silencios, Oscuro animal y Cienaga oscura, le da vida a una versión mayor de la matriarca, quien después de la fundación de Macondo, dedica sus días a preservar el orden en su familia y velar por el interés de quienes la rodean bajo una mano firme.

Susana Morales es Úrsula Iguarán de joven

Susana Morales es Úrsula Iguarána en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

Además de ser la prima y esposa de José Arcadio Buendía, **Úrsula Iguarán** también es la matriarca de la familia, entre sus cualidades, los esfuerzos por sacar adelante a su descendencia tienen gran repercusión en el éxito de esta misma y son clave para la trama. Para retratar el personaje, **Susana Morales** ha sido fichada en el proyecto como una versión joven de Úrsula, mientras

Viña Machado es Pilar Ternera

Viña Machado es Pilar Ternera en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

**Viña Machado**, la modelo y actriz colombiana, se adentra bajo la piel de **Pilar Ternera**, una mujer con habilidades para adelantarse ante el futuro que dirige un prostíbulo y con quien José Arcadio y Aureliano tienen a dos hijos que se integran a la familia.

Moreno Borja es Melquíades en sus inicios

Moreno Borja es Melquíades en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

Gracias a cintas como Carmen y Lola, El verano que vivimos y El universo de Óliver, el actor nominado al Premio Goya por Mejor Actor Revelación ha manifestado su talento ante la cámara y para sumar un nuevo éxito a su portafolio, **podremos verlo como Melquíades**, **un gitano que visita Macondo** cada año para poner a la venta inventos provenientes de todo el mundo. Este es un personaje clave para la historia, pues además de desafiar la lógica y aportar la magia que caracteriza el sello de **García Márquez**, es quien lleva el registro de la historia de la familia Buendía y sabe el destino de la misma.

Ruggero Pasquarelli es Pietro Crespi

Ruggero Pascuarelli es Pietro Crespi en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

En la novela, **Pietro Crespi** es el motivo por el cual existe una ruptura en la relación entre Amaranta y Rebeca, pues ambas comparten una relación con el hombre como un punto en común. Al igual que en el relato, en donde es de origen italiano, el actor que lo interpreta también cumple el requisito, es así como **Ruggero Pasquarelli**, el cantante y actor de Soy Luna y Violetta se suma al reparto para darle vida a Pietro.

Ella Becerra es Petronila

Ella Becerra es Petronila en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano /Netflix

**Ella Becerra** ha participado en proyectos como El paseo de Teresa, El gran Bingo, Dulce amor, y Mi casa es tu casa, aunque en esta ocasión **asumirá el papel de Petronila**, una mujer que deberá enfrentar el desamor y la pérdida que acompañan a la vida.

Marco González es José Arcadio Buendía de joven

Marco Antonio González es José Arcadio joven en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

Considerado como un erudito cuya pasión por la ciencia y la alquimia lo ayudaron a impulsar su trayectoria como fundador del pueblo de Macondo, **José Arcadio Buendía** es el patriarca de la familia de la que todo parte, y esta vez será **Marco González** el responsable de interpretar al patriarca en el proyecto en su versión de joven.

Diego Vásquez es José Arcadio Buendía de adulto

Diego Vásquez es José Arcadio Buendía en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

Al igual que Marco, **Diego Vásquez** también **interpreta a Jose Arcadio Buendía**, sin embargo, lo hace en una etapa más adulta del personaje, lo cual nos permite explorar su vida tras la fundación de Macondo y la consolidación de su familia, así como los intereses cambiantes con la llegada de los años.

Thiago Padilla es José Arcadio niño

Gracias a su espíritu aventurero, **José Arcadio**, **el primer hijo de Úrsula Iguarán y José Arcadio Buendía**, ha sorprendido a su familia en más de una ocasión. Desde tener una relación con una mujer mayor, hasta viajar por todo el mundo para alejarse de sus problemas, el primogénito no deja de causar conflictos a lo largo de la historia. **Thiago Padilla** lo interpreta de niño para representar su origen dentro del núcleo familiar de los Buendía.

Edgar Vittorino es José Arcadio joven

El intérprete colombiano de Centauro, Vivir sin permiso, Nieva en Benidorm y Bajo Cero retoma el papel de **José Arcadio en su etapa juvenil**, donde despierta su interés por conocer el mundo y viajar alrededor de él, alejándose de todo y emprendiendo diversas aventuras.

Leonardo Soto es José Arcadio adulto

El intérprete colombiano, **Leonardo Soto**, es José Arcadio en una etapa más madura, donde se enfrentará a nuevos retos que podrían conducirlo a un abrupto final.

Luna Ruíz es Amaranta Buendía niña

Luna Ruiz es Amaranta de niña en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González /Netflix

**Luna Ruíz se une al reparto como Amaranta**, la hija menor de José Arcadio Buendía y hermana de Rebeca. Ruíz se encarga de darle vida en sus años de infancia.

Loren Sofía Paz es Amaranta Buendía joven

Loren Sofía Paz es Amaranta de grande en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

**Loren Sofía Paz también sostiene el rol de Amaranta** en la juventud, donde complica su relación con Rebeca tras interesarse en el mismo hombre, dando pie así a uno de los conflictos secundarios que forman parte del relato.

Nicole Montenegro es Rebeca niña

Nicole Montenegro es Rebeca de niña en Cien años de soledad.Mauro González/Netflix

**Nicole Montenegrole da vida a Rebeca**, una huérfana que llega a Macondo durante la niñez y es adoptada por José Arcadio y Úrsula. Desde el inicio, destaca por ser introvertida y temerosa, **Nicole Montenegro** asume el rol del personaje en su niñez.

Laura Sofía Grueso es Rebeca joven

Laura Grueso es Rebeca de grande en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

**Laura Sofía Grueso** también interpreta a Rebeca, sin embargo, lo hace durante una etapa más madura, en donde el tiempo ha forjado su interés por Pietro Crespi y una fractura en la relación con su hermana, Amaranta, se da gracias a ello.

Carlos Suárez es Aureliano Iguarán

Por otro lado, **será Carlos Suárez quien le dé vida a Aureliano Iguarán**, uno de los miembros de la familia, quien se enfrenará al constante cambio de los años y deberá encontrar la forma de navegarlos sin perderse a sí mismo en el proceso.

Cristal Aparicio es Remedios Moscote

Cristal Aparicio es Remedios en Cien años de soledad.Pablo Arellano / Netflix

La actriz colombiana, conocida por entregas como Sonido de la libertad, le da vida a **Remedios Moscote**, la hija de Apolinar y esposa de Aureliano Buendía, con quien se casa desde temprana edad en consecuencia de acuerdos políticos en Macondo.

Jairo Camargo es Apolinar Moscote

El actor responsable por estar detrás de títulos como Pedro el escamoso y Palabra de ladrón, encarna a **Apolinar Moscote**, el padre de Remedios y cabeza del partido conservador que impregna en las entrañas de Macondo.

Jacqueline Arenal es Leonor Moscote

Anteriormente, Jacqueline Arenal se ha incorporado a proyectos como Pálpito, Los Reyes, y El Siglo de las Luces, y esta vez la vemos como **Leonor Moscote**, esposa de Apolinar y madre de Remedios.

Julian Román es los gemelos Jose Arcadio Segundo y Aureliano Segundo

Julián Román interpreta a Jose Arcadio Segundo y Aureliano Segundo, hijos de Arcadio y Santa Sofía de la piedad. El actor le da vida a los dos gemelos idénticos, que a pesar de su parecido, toman caminos muy distintos y se convierten en una de las claves para el desarrollo de la segunda parte de la historia.

Carla Baratta es Fernanda del Carpio

La actriz y modelo venezolana de *Mayans M.C.* y *Prueba de Fe* interpreta a Fernanda del Carpio, una aristócrata que llega a la familia Buendía tras su matrimonio con Aureliano Segundo para imponer una visión conservadora en el hogar.

Ángela Cano es Petra Cotes

Ángela Cano, la actriz de Frontera Verde y Ritmo Salvaje **es Petra Cotes**, un interés amoroso de Aureliano Segundo, con quien comparte una dinámica que lo hace explorar fuera de su matrimonio.

María Adelaida Puerta es Amaranta Úrsula

María Adelaida Puerta de *El capo* y *La mariposa* **es Amaranta Úrsula**, descendiente de los Buendía. Destaca por su educación en el extranjero, donde vivió por un tiempo antes de regresar a Macondo para intentar devolverle la magia que alguna vez tuvo.

Juanita Molina es Meme

La actriz y cantante de *Romina poderosa* y *Betty la fea, la historia continúa* **es Meme**, la hija de Fernanda del Carpio y Aureliano Segundo. Es conocida por su espíritu libre y valentía, que rechaza la idea de estar encasillada. Protagoniza un romance que la marca para siempre.

Daniella Reyes es Remedios, la bella

Daniella Reyes interpreta a Remedios, la bella, un personaje marcado por su belleza. Es considerada como un alma pura e inocente, despierta el deseo en los hombres que la rodean pero mantiene su distancia. En medio del caos, es la representación de la pureza.

Ver más

[Cien años de soledad estrena su segunda parte. Estos son todos los detalles](/estilo-de-vida/articulo/macondo-netflix-cien-anos-de-soledad)

Por [Karina González Ulloa](/personaje/karina-gonzalez-ulloa) y [Fernanda Pérez Sánchez](/personaje/fernanda-perez-sanchez)

## ¿Cómo se buscó al reparto de Cien años de soledad?

De acuerdo con la información revelada por Netflix, **la búsqueda del reparto de Cien años de soledad** fue como ninguna otra, pues inició en Colombia en junio de 2022 con más de 10 mil perfiles han sido revisados para el fichaje. De igual manera, el reparto está conformado por un 70% de actores naturales que debutan en pantalla y tan solo 30% de talentos profesionales.

Asimismo, la búsqueda encabezada por las directoras de casting de títulos como La casa de Papel y Dolor y gloria, Yolanda Serrano y Eva Leira, fue acompañada por el sistema que Maria Juliana Casadiego y Carlos Medina crearon con la finalidad de encontrar autenticidad en los perfiles, anticipando así a más de 20 mil extras en la pantalla para el final de la serie.

En el tráiler oficial, solo vemos una parte de los personajes. Lo que indica que tras el estreno de la serie, los miembros del **reparto** continuarán revelándose en cada episodio.

This article from Vogue México provides a comprehensive guide to the cast and characters of Netflix's adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude). The series, based on the Nobel Prize-winning novel that has sold 50 million copies in 46 languages, follows the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo. The article details the full cast list, with actors playing different age versions of key characters.

The main cast includes:
- Claudio Cataño (adult Colonel Aureliano Buendía), Jerónimo Barón (child), Santiago Vásquez (young)
- Marleyda Soto (adult Úrsula Iguarán), Susana Morales (young)
- Marco González (young José Arcadio Buendía), Diego Vásquez (adult)
- Viña Machado as Pilar Ternera, Moreno Borja as Melquíades, Ruggero Pasquarelli as Pietro Crespi
- Various actors portray José Arcadio, Amaranta, Rebeca, and other family members across different ages
- Julián Román plays the twin brothers José Arcadio Segundo and Aureliano Segundo
- Carla Baratta as Fernanda del Carpio, Ángela Cano as Petra Cotes, María Adelaida Puerta as Amaranta Úrsula, Juanita Molina as Meme, and Daniela Reyes as Remedios, la bella

The casting process began in Colombia in June 2022, reviewing over 10,000 profiles. The cast is 70% natural actors (debuting on screen) and 30% professional talent. The casting directors were Yolanda Serrano and Eva Leira. The series has a second part releasing on August 5.

args.key_excerpts: "Macondo ya llegó! Conoce los rostros colombianos que darán vida a 'Cien años de soledad' en Netflix, desde el lente del talentoso Ruven Afanador.", "Que maravilloso que en Netflix la gente al rededor del mundo podrá conocer otra faceta de Colombia, no solamente Narcos! Vivo en Australia y Ahora puedo decir: vean cien años de soledad, premio Novel de Colombia." - Sandra Londono, "No obstante el mérito cinematográfico y de producción audiovisual, era realmente imposible que una película logrará siquiera aproximarse al virtuosismo literario del libro." - Luis Fernando García Cerón, "Me siento orgullosa de ser colombiana... obra que ahora la podemos no sólo leer y recrearla en nuestras mentes, sino también saborearla de a poquitos viéndola en la pantalla!" - Rocío Morales
args.summary:
This is a Facebook post from Marca Colombia (www.colombia.co) dated December 11, 2024, announcing the arrival of the Netflix adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude). The post highlights that Colombian faces will bring the story to life, photographed by Ruven Afanador. The post celebrates this as a showcase of Colombian talent and magic under the hashtags #ElPaísDeLaBelleza and #OrigenColombiano.

The post generated significant engagement with 2.1K reactions, 82 comments, and 280 shares. Notable comments include:

- Sandra Londono (from Australia) expresses pride that Netflix viewers worldwide can see another side of Colombia beyond "Narcos," recommending people watch "Cien años de soledad."
- Luis Fernando García Cerón notes that while the film adaptation has cinematic merit, it cannot fully capture the literary virtuosity and poetic narrative of the book, and suggests reading the book first.
- Gloria Teresa Romero shares that she has watched 4 episodes and loves it more each time, recalling the book she read twice.
- Rocío Morales expresses pride in being Colombian, calling the adaptation "goodísima" (very good) and visually well-crafted with superb character adaptations.

This is the IMDb news page for Gonzalo García Barcha, son of Gabriel García Márquez and executive producer on Netflix's adaptation of "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The page contains a chronological feed of news articles about the series, which is a two-part limited series adaptation of García Márquez's 1967 Nobel Prize-winning novel. 

Key details about the series:
- Part 1 (8 episodes) premiered December 11, 2024, on Netflix
- Part 2 (7 episodes) premieres August 5, 2026, with an 8th Grand Finale episode on August 26, 2026
- Directed by Laura Mora and Alex García López
- Filmed entirely in Colombia in Spanish, produced by Dynamo
- One of the most ambitious audiovisual projects in Latin American history, employing mostly unknown Colombian actors and over 20,000 extras
- The series was supported by García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha, who serve as executive producers — the author had previously resisted adaptations
- "One Hundred Years of Solitude" was nominated for Breakthrough Drama Series at the 2025 Gotham TV Awards

The page also includes articles about the Gotham TV Awards (2025 nominations and winners), with "Adolescence" leading nominations, and coverage of the series' locations, reviews, and development history.

# One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel García Márquez

Decades of family drama and magical realism unfold in this sprawling epic set in a fictional Colombian town.

![One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel García Márquez](https://images.ctfassets.net/qpn1gztbusu2/4JwMQzZppPmqfQLMi5uoOP/4620c9e9b438fc0e67bca179c617996f/gabriel-garcia-marquez-one-hundred-years-of-solitude.png?fm=jpg&w=1920&q=70)

## Summary

Gabriel García Márquez's *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, first published in 1967, is widely considered one of the most significant novels of the 20th century. This sweeping saga chronicles seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo, weaving together elements of magical realism, Colombian history, and universal themes of love, war, and the cyclical nature of time. The novel sold millions of copies worldwide, won numerous awards, and helped García Márquez secure the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. Though García Márquez resisted film adaptations during his lifetime, Netflix announced in 2019 that it is developing the first-ever screen adaptation as a Spanish-language TV series.

## Plot

The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional town of Macondo. It begins with José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán founding Macondo after leaving their hometown due to José Arcadio’s killing a man. In Macondo, the Buendías experience many fantastical events over the decades, including annual visits from gypsies who bring new inventions and technologies.

As Macondo grows and becomes connected to the outside world, the town experiences political turmoil, including rigged elections and civil war. Colonel Aureliano Buendía, José Arcadio's son, leads rebel forces in numerous failed uprisings. Later, an American fruit company establishes a banana plantation nearby, leading to economic growth and labor unrest. The novel depicts a massacre of striking banana workers, which is then erased from the town's memory.

Throughout the generations, the Buendía family is plagued by incest, solitude, and fantastical occurrences like levitation and alchemy. Characters are often driven to madness or obsession. By the end, the once-prosperous Macondo has fallen into ruin. The last Buendía, Aureliano, decodes ancient parchments that tell the family's history just as a prophesied windstorm wipes the town off the map, fulfilling the fate that had been foretold for the Buendías since the beginning.

## Themes

Cyclical nature of time and history

Solitude and isolation

Magic and reality intertwined

Family legacy and fate

Political and social upheaval

Love and passion

Memory and forgetting

## Setting

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* takes place primarily in the fictional town of Macondo, located in an isolated jungle region of Colombia. Macondo is founded in the early 19th century by José Arcadio Buendía and his wife Úrsula Iguarán after they flee their hometown. The story spans approximately 100 years, chronicling the town's growth from a small settlement to a bustling banana plantation, and its eventual decline and destruction.

Initially cut off from the outside world, Macondo slowly becomes connected to broader Colombian society as the 19th century progresses. Key historical events like civil wars, the arrival of new technologies, and the establishment of American fruit companies shape the town's development. The Buendía family home serves as the narrative's central setting, with its rooms and courtyards witnessing generations of family drama.

While grounded in Colombia's history, Macondo also exists in a realm of magical realism. Fantastical events occur alongside everyday life, blurring the lines between reality and myth. The town's physical and temporal isolation allows it to develop its own insular culture and legends. By the novel's end, Macondo has transformed from a place of hopeful new beginnings to one of decaying solitude, mirroring the Buendía family's own trajectory.

## Characters

**José Arcadio Buendía**: Patriarch of the Buendía family and founder of Macondo. A curious and impulsive man who becomes obsessed with scientific pursuits and eventually goes insane.

**Úrsula Iguarán**: Matriarch of the Buendía family. A strong-willed woman who lives to be more than 100 years old and holds the family together through multiple generations.

**Colonel Aureliano Buendía**: Second son of José Arcadio and Úrsula. A solitary figure who leads numerous failed rebellions and fathers 17 sons by different women.

**Amaranta**: Daughter of José Arcadio and Úrsula. A bitter spinster who rejects multiple suitors and carries unresolved guilt throughout her life.

**Remedios the Beauty**: Granddaughter of José Arcadio and Úrsula. An ethereal beauty whose otherworldly nature causes the deaths of men who desire her.

**Aureliano Segundo**: Great-grandson of José Arcadio and Úrsula. A jovial hedonist who amasses and loses a fortune through his relationship with his mistress, Petra Cotes.

**Fernanda del Carpio**: Wife of Aureliano Segundo. A haughty aristocrat who imposes strict rules on the Buendía household.

**Aureliano Babilonia**: Last of the Buendía line. The illegitimate son of Meme who decodes Melquíades' prophecies as Macondo is destroyed.

**Melquíades**: A mysterious gypsy who brings technological marvels to Macondo and leaves behind prophetic parchments that foretell the family's fate.

## Quick facts

It took Gabriel García Márquez 18 months of writing seven days a week to complete his masterwork, *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

García Márquez wrote the novel after a five-year period where he had not published any new works.

The novel was first published in Spanish in 1967 and has since been translated into more than 46 languages.

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* has sold more than 50 million copies worldwide.

García Márquez claims the novel's style was inspired by the way his grandmother used to tell stories.

Time in the novel is cyclical rather than linear. Events and character traits repeat across generations, creating a sense that history is destined to repeat itself. This reflects García Márquez's view of Latin American history.

The fictional town of Macondo is based on García Márquez's hometown of Aracataca, Colombia.

The novel alludes to real events in Colombian history, including civil wars, the arrival of new technologies, and the infamous “Banana Massacre” of 1928. These are woven into the fictional narrative of Macondo and the Buendías.

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* popularized the literary style known as magical realism.

Pablo Neruda called *One Hundred Years of Solitude* “the greatest revelation in the Spanish language since *Don Quixote*."

The novel was a major factor in García Márquez being awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.

García Márquez refused to sell the film rights to the novel for many years, believing this epic work could not be properly adapted.

 In March 2019, Netflix acquired the rights to *One Hundred Years of Solitude* and, with the support of García Márquez’s family, began developing a Spanish-language TV series. Shot on location in Colombia, with the author's son as an executive producer, the series is slated to release in December 2024.

## About the Author

Gabriel García Márquez was a Colombian novelist, short-story writer, screenwriter, and journalist who became one of the most significant authors of the 20th century. Born in 1927 in Aracataca, Colombia, García Márquez drew inspiration from his grandparents' storytelling and the vibrant culture of the Caribbean coast. He began his career as a journalist before achieving worldwide fame as a pioneer of magical realism with his 1967 novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

García Márquez's writing style blended the fantastic with the mundane, using vivid imagery and deadpan delivery to create richly imagined worlds. Many of his works are set in the fictional village of Macondo and explore themes of solitude, family, and the cyclical nature of history. His other acclaimed novels include *Love in the Time of Cholera*, *Chronicle of a Death Foretold*, and *The Autumn of the Patriarch*. In 1982, García Márquez was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

García Márquez died in 2014 at the age of 87 in Mexico City, where he had lived for many years. His death was mourned around the world, with the Colombian president calling him “the greatest Colombian of all time.” He left behind a rich literary legacy that continues to captivate readers and influence writers worldwide.

# Gabriel Garcia Marquez’s ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ to be Adapted Into Netflix Series

By Peter White, Deadline

Published  March 6, 2019, 11:39 a.m. ET

![Gabriel Garcia Marquez](https://decider.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/gabriel-garcia-marquez.jpg?quality=75&strip=all&w=978&h=652&crop=1)

Photo: Getty Images

See more of our coverage in your search results.

 [Add Decider on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=decider.com)

[Netflix](https://decider.com/platform/netflix/) is to adapt Gabriel García Márquez’s literary classic *One Hundred Years of Solitude* into a Spanish-language series.

The SVOD service has acquired the rights to develop the novel, which was first published in 1967 and has sold over 50M copies.

García Márquez’s sons Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo García Barcha will serve as executive producers on the series, which will be filmed mainly in Colombia.

The book, delving deep into magical realism, tells the story of the multi-generational Buendia family, whose patriarch Jose Arcadio Buendia founded Macondo, a fictional town in Colombia.

It marks the first time that García Márquez’s book will be adapted for screen as the author, who died in 2014, refused to sell the film rights.

Sylvie Rabineau at WME, attorney Shelley Surpin, and the Agencia Literaria Carmen Balcells represented the author’s estate in the deal.

“For decades, our father was reluctant to sell the film rights to *Cien Años de Soledad* because he believed that it could not be made under the time constraints of a feature film, or that producing it in a language other than Spanish would not do it justice,” said Garcia. “But in the current golden age of series, with the level of talented writing and directing, the cinematic quality of content, and the acceptance by worldwide audiences of programs in foreign languages, the time could not be better to bring an adaptation to the extraordinary global viewership that Netflix provides. We are excited to support Netflix and the filmmakers in this venture, and eager to see the final product.”

“We are incredibly honored to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world,” added Francisco Ramos, Vice President, Spanish Language Originals for Netflix. “We know our members around the world love watching Spanish-language films and series and we feel this will be a perfect match of project and our platform.”

[Business](https://www.forbes.com/business/)[Hollywood & Entertainment](https://www.forbes.com/hollywood-entertainment/)

# One Hundred Years Of Solitude: Macondo Is Making Its Way To Netflix

By[Bedatri Choudhury](https://www.forbes.com/sites/bedatrichoudhury/ "https://www.forbes.com/sites/bedatrichoudhury/"),

Former Contributor.

This article is more than 7 years old.

Close on the heels of the phenomenal success of *Roma*, Netflix has just announced another exciting Spanish language original project! The internet entertainment service has acquired rights to Gabriel García Márquez’s 1967 groundbreaking novel, *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, and will be turning the novel into a new series. The novel follows the multi-generational Buendía family of the fictional Colombian town, Macondo through a myriad of fascinating characters including the family patriarch José Arcadio Buendía, and this is the first on-screen adaptation of the novel.

![FILE - In this March 6, 2014 file photo, Colombian Nobel Literature laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez... [+] greets fans and reporters outside his home on his 87th birthday in Mexico City. (AP Photo/Eduardo Verdugo, File)](https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/f215f2c4cbdc4e9ba3c4ea8f6ccaf19d/960x0.jpg?fit=scale)

FILE - In this March 6, 2014 file photo, Colombian Nobel Literature laureate Gabriel Garcia Marquez greets fans and reporters outside his home on his 87th birthday in Mexico City. (AP Photo/Eduardo Verdugo, File)

ASSOCIATED PRESS

In his lifetime, García Márquez turned down several adaptation requests because he believed that the magical realist novel was too complex to be condensed into a feature film; he also believed that any non-Spanish language would fail to do justice to the novel’s plot. 

His sons Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo García Barcha have, however, agreed to serve as the executive producers on the Netflix series. They believe that in the recent years, short series have been able to attract viewers while being able to produce excellent content. “With the level of talented writing and directing, the cinematic quality of content, and the acceptance by worldwide audiences of programs in foreign languages, the time could not be better to bring an adaptation to the extraordinary global viewership that Netflix provides,” Rodrigo Garcia emphasized. Sylvie Rabineau at WME, attorney Shelley Surpin, and the Agencia Literaria Carmen Balcells represented the author’s estate in the deal. Though no casting or budget details were announced, it is known that the series will be filmed entirely in Colombia.

Netflix, of course, is no stranger to investing in producing non-English content for its worldwide audience base; the French political drama *Marseille*, the Brazilian dystopian thriller *3%*, and the Korean comedy *My Only Love Song* are all successful examples of the company’s dedicated engagement with international content. Their specific and consistent interest in Spanish language content from various Spanish-speaking countries is especially evident through eclectic shows like *Narcos: Mexico* (Mexico), *Las chi**cas del cable* (Spain), and *Edha* (Argentina).

According to a [recent survey commissioned by the Publishers Association and produced by Frontier Economics](https://www.forbes.com/sites/adamrowe1/2018/07/11/why-book-based-films-earn-53-more-at-the-worldwide-box-office/#4e65401b306f), film adaptations of books gross 44% more at the U.K. box office and almost 53% more worldwide, than films made from original screenplays. In the last few years, Netflix has been dedicatedly producing several book-to-screen adaptations such as *A Series of Unfortunate Incidents, Alias Grace*, and *The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society*.

This announcement comes only a few days after Hollywood director Steven Spielberg made the now-debated decision to use his clout to have the Academy not consider films, that are released on streaming sites, for the Oscars. This news comes in barely weeks after another Netflix Spanish language original, *Roma* was nominated for both Best Film and Best Foreign Film at this year’s Oscars.  
  
“We are incredibly honored to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world,” said Francisco Ramos, Vice President, Spanish Language Originals for Netflix.

Notably, the announcement comes on the celebrated author's birthday. García Márquez, who passed away in 2014, would've turned 92 today.

# Netflix To Adapt Gabriel García Márquez’s Literary Classic ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’ Into Spanish-Language Series

![]()

By [Peter White](https://deadline.com/author/peter-white/)

## [Peter White](https://deadline.com/author/peter-white/)

Executive Editor, Television

#### More Stories By Peter

## Services to share this page.

![](https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/rexfeatures_6731307d.jpg?w=681&h=383&crop=1)

[Netflix](https://deadline.com/tag/netflix/) is to adapt Gabriel García Márquez’s literary classic *One Hundred Years of Solitude* into a Spanish-language series.

The SVOD service has acquired the rights to develop the novel, which was first published in 1967 and has sold over 50M copies.

García Márquez’s sons Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo García Barcha will serve as executive producers on the series, which will be filmed mainly in Colombia.

The book, delving deep into magical realism, tells the story of the multi-generational Buendia family, whose patriarch Jose Arcadio Buendia founded Macondo, a fictional town in Colombia.

It marks the first time that García Márquez’s book will be adapted for screen as the author, who died in 2014, refused to sell the film rights.

Netflix has acquired the rights to develop Gabriel García Márquez's literary classic "One Hundred Years of Solitude" into a Spanish-language series. The novel, first published in 1967, has sold over 50 million copies. This marks the first time the book will be adapted for screen, as the author (who died in 2014) had previously refused to sell the film rights. 

García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo Garcia and Gonzalo García Barcha, will serve as executive producers on the series, which will be filmed mainly in Colombia. The book tells the multi-generational story of the Buendia family and their founding of the fictional Colombian town of Macondo, exploring magical realism.

Rodrigo Garcia explained that his father was reluctant to sell the film rights because he believed it couldn't be done under the time constraints of a feature film, or in a language other than Spanish. However, the current golden age of series, with quality writing, directing, and global audience acceptance of foreign-language programming, makes the time right for adaptation. Francisco Ramos, Vice President of Spanish Language Originals for Netflix, expressed honor at being entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of this timeless Latin American story.

**One Hundred Years of Solitude (TV Series) – Wikipedia Summary**

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel of the same name. Produced by Netflix and the Colombian production company Dynamo, the series is a Spanish and Wayuu-language drama/magical realism adaptation.

**Key Details:**
- **Seasons/Episodes:** 2 seasons, 15 episodes total (season 1: 8 episodes; season 2: 8 episodes)
- **Release Dates:** Season 1 premiered December 11, 2024. Season 2 Part 1 released August 5, 2026; series finale slated for August 26, 2026.

- **Cast:** Claudio Cataño (Colonel Aureliano Buendía), Diego Vásquez (José Arcadio Buendía), Marleyda Soto (Úrsula Iguarán), Viña Machado (Pilar Ternera), Loren Sofía (Amaranta), Akima (Rebeca), Janer Villarreal (Arcadio), Moreno Borja (Melquíades), Ruggero Pasquarelli (Pietro Crespi), and others.

**Production:**
- Netflix acquired rights in March 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing a feature film was insufficient for proper adaptation.
- Filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors.
- Open casting call in 2022; more than 10,000 candidates for 25 main roles. Only 30% were professional actors; 20,000 extras were selected.
- Principal photography for Part 1: May–December 2023. Filmed entirely in Colombia (La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, Tolima). The fictional town of Macondo was built near Alvarado, Tolima by 1,100 workers, with four versions constructed to depict the passage of time.
- Production generated 225 billion COP ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy.
- Production on Part 2 began in February 2025.

**Reception:**
- Rotten Tomatoes: 83% positive from 30 critics (avg. 7.9/10). Consensus: "faithfully realizes García Márquez's seminal novel with sumptuous polish."
- Metacritic: 80/100 ("generally favorable").
- Critical praise for faithfulness to source material, performances (especially Soto and Cataño), cinematography, production design, and direction. Some criticism of pacing and literal translation of novelistic content.

**Awards:**
- Won Best Ibero-American Miniseries or TV Series at the 2025 Platino Awards.

Key adaptation challenges included: organizing the novel's nonlinear narrative chronologically, handling approximately 50 significant characters, and translating the novel's tone and magical realism. Major creative decisions included: giving Úrsula Iguarán Buendía the point of view to drive the story, accepting the need for a narrator (despite initial resistance), and focusing on dramatic character arcs rather than just sequence of events. Key points covered include:

1. **Colombia or Bust**: García Márquez's family, particularly his son Rodrigo Garcia, agreed to the adaptation when Netflix proposed using Spanish language and Colombian talent. The family felt the timing was right given the rise of serialized storytelling and global acceptance of subtitles.

2. **Dynamo's Global Experience**: Colombia's leading production company Dynamo (known for "Narcos," "Monos," "Gemini Man") was tapped to support the entire production process.

5. **Casting Macondo**: Starting June 2022, a nationwide search reviewed over 10,000 candidates to cast 25 lead roles across seven generations of the Buendía family. 97% of the cast are Colombian actors. The series finale features nearly 20,000 extras.

6. **Landscapes**: Filmed across 15 Colombian towns, capturing the country's geographic diversity. A team of 16 specialists led by Martha Duque imported dozens of native plant species to create an authentic ecosystem.

7. **Recreating Historical Colombia**: Over three years of research went into costumes, sets, plants, food, and music. Composer Juancho Valencia leads the music team focusing on traditional Colombian folk sounds.

8. **Accurate Century-Long Rendering**: Four distinct versions of Macondo were built, including an 8,611-square-foot recreation of the Buendía house. Over 200 artisans created more than 90 detailed structures.

9. **Costume Design as Ethnography**: Costume designer Catherine Rodriguez ("Embrace of the Serpent") and her team created 40,000 garments from scratch, 97% using Colombian-origin textiles for Season One (spanning 1850-1900).

10. **Colombian Talent Pool**: Colombian filmmaker Laura Mora ("The Kings of the World") directed three episodes of Season One and five of Season Two, alongside Carlos Moreno. --- SOURCE 2: The Cinematography of "One Hundred Years of Solitude" ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=54gtS4kt8iw

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage features a transcript of a "Sight, Sound & Story" panel discussion hosted by Manhattan Edit Workshop, moderated by Josh Apter, focusing on the cinematography of Netflix's adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The panelists are cinematographers Paulo Pérez (episodes 1-3 and 7-8) and María Sarasvati Herrera (episodes 4-6), both of whom are Colombian and deeply connected to the source material.

Key points from the discussion:

- **Background & Preparation**: Both cinematographers read the novel in school (it's required reading in Colombia). Pérez studied at the film school García Márquez founded in Cuba. The production involved extensive research with historians and experts.

- **Production Design**: The entire town of Macondo was built from scratch on a farm four hours from Bogotá, Colombia. The Buendía house was constructed inside a large tent/hanger on the farm. Sets were built three or four different times to show the town's evolution. The production used a mix of natural and artificial light, including LED balloons on the ceiling, large lights (18K and T lights) on cherry pickers, and cranes for lighting to simulate sunrises and sunsets. Over 300 lights were used.

- **Visual Approach**: The camera serves as the narrator (like Melquíades writing the story). For episodes 1-3, the camera is handheld, alive, and moving constantly to represent the circular nature of the story and break time and space. The magical realism is depicted as everyday, natural occurrences, done mostly in-camera without VFX (only the flying carpet and donkey were VFX; the levitating priest and ghost were real/physical).

- **Long Takes**: Many scenes were shot as single, continuous takes lasting 2-3 minutes. Examples include: a three-minute shot following a naked boy through Macondo (shot 7-8 times), a shot using a rotating floor (tornamesa) to show the house aging 10 years in a single take, and a shot following Remedios through the house with lighting changing from sunrise to sunset to night to sunrise.

- **Division of Labor**: Pérez worked with director Alex García López on the first block (episodes 1-3, innocence, building civilization) and the third block (episodes 7-8, war). Herrera worked with director Laura Mora on the second block (episodes 4-6, older characters, religion, government, politics). They maintained constant communication to ensure continuity across the series.

- **Color Palette**: Pre-color grading was done but changed when Herrera's block required different colors. Colors have political meaning (blue and red representing conflicting parties). The look evolved with the story—from innocence to government/religion to destruction.

- **Challenges**: Working with children (limited to 6-hour shooting days), coordinating 100-300 extras, managing 360-degree shots with costume and makeup changes on the fly, and the physical demands on the Steadicam operator (30+ kg camera rig). Pérez's director often came up with new ideas the morning of shooting, requiring constant adaptation.

- **The Ghost (Prudencio)**: The murdered character appears as a recurring physical presence representing guilt, appearing multiple times throughout the series without any special effects or halos.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We built everything from zero that was like a dream to build my condo three or four times and to design how we are going to shoot it, how we can imagine that for a book that everybody say that you cannot film that." — Paulo Pérez, "What was very important is that the magic realism is part of the everyday life it happens in a natural way so we didn't want to do VFX, we wanted that all the things happen in front of the camera." — Paulo Pérez, "Our visual approach to the project it was the movement, the movement to break the time and the space." — Paulo Pérez, "The camera is alive, this camera is the voice of the book." — Paulo Pérez, "We had to keep talking about it because we didn't want two different movies in one series." — María Sarasvati Herrera

URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magical_realism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Magical realism (also called magic realism or marvellous realism) is a style of fiction and art that presents a realistic view of the world while incorporating magical elements, often blurring the lines between speculation and reality. It is commonly found in novels and dramatic performances, and is distinguished from fantasy by its use of substantial realistic detail to make a point about reality, rather than separating from it. The term originated in 1925 with German art critic Franz Roh (magischer Realismus) to describe a painterly style known as Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity). It was later applied to literature, particularly Latin American literature, by writers such as Gabriel García Márquez, Isabel Allende, Jorge Luis Borges, Alejo Carpentier, and others. Key characteristics include: fantastical elements in a real-world setting, authorial reticence (withholding explanations of magical events), plenitude (abundance of disorienting detail), hybridity (multiple planes of reality), metafiction, heightened awareness of mystery, and political critique. The genre often mixes history and fantasy, and is seen as a subversive form that challenges socially-dominant forces. Major works include García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) and Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949). Notable authors span multiple languages and cultures, including English (Neil Gaiman, Salman Rushdie, Alice Hoffman), Russian (Mikhail Bulgakov), Japanese (Haruki Murakami), Chinese (Mo Yan), Polish (Olga Tokarczuk), and Bengali (Nabarun Bhattacharya) writers.
</summary>

# Summary of The Paris Review: "Gabriel García Márquez, The Art of Fiction No. 69"

This webpage from The Paris Review (Issue 82, Winter 1981) contains a lengthy interview with Nobel Prize-winning author Gabriel García Márquez, conducted by The Paris Review. The interview took place over three late-afternoon sessions at his studio in San Angel Inn, Mexico City, with his two sons assisting with translation.

**Key topics covered in the interview:**

1. **On Journalism vs. Interviewing**: García Márquez expresses discomfort with tape recorders during interviews, noting they make him defensive. As a journalist himself, he never used tape recorders for interviews, preferring long conversations followed by writing from memory. He recounts his famous series about a shipwrecked sailor, published under the sailor's name, which wasn't recognized as his work until after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

2. **Journalism as His True Profession**: He states, "I've always been convinced that my true profession is that of a journalist." He now enjoys being able to choose topics that interest him, having achieved financial independence through novels. He cites John Hersey's *Hiroshima* as an exceptional piece of journalism.

3. **Novel vs. Journalism**: He argues there is no fundamental difference between journalism and fiction: "The sources are the same, the material is the same, the resources and the language are the same." The key difference: "In journalism just one fact that is false prejudices the entire work. In contrast, in fiction one single fact that is true gives legitimacy to the entire work."

4. **Writing Process**: He describes writing much more slowly now than in his newspaper days, sometimes producing only a short paragraph of four or five lines in a good day's work.

5. **Early Influences and Beginnings**: He started by drawing cartoons. Reading Kafka's *The Metamorphosis* was a revelation—"the first line almost knocked me off the bed." He later read Joyce's *Ulysses* and learned the technique of interior monologue. The American Lost Generation writers helped him connect literature to life.

6. **The Bogotazo (April 9, 1948)**: The assassination of political leader Gaitan and the ensuing riots in Bogotá were pivotal. He realized his short stories had nothing to do with the reality of his country.

7. **Return to Aracataca (1950-51)**: Visiting his birthplace with his mother to sell his childhood home was transformative. He felt he was "experiencing it as if I were reading it" and realized everything had literary value. This led to his first novel, *Leaf Storm*.

8. **On Reality vs. Imagination**: He insists that "there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality." The Caribbean reality, he says, "resembles the wildest imagination."

9. **Writing for an Audience**: He writes for specific friends, but after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, he no longer knows who among millions of readers he is writing for, which "upsets and inhibits" him.

The page also includes an interview with Yan Lianke (The Art of Fiction No. 269) about Chinese censorship, rural life, and literary freedom, as well as numerous other contents from Issue 82 and subsequent issues.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Variety article by Anna Marie de la Fuente provides ten key insights into the making of Netflix's ambitious series adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize-winning novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The production was a massive collaborative effort employing nearly 900 crew members, primarily Colombian, alongside 150 skilled artisans and thousands of extras. More than 850 local suppliers contributed to constructing the legendary town of Macondo from the ground up.

Key points covered include:

1. **Colombia or Bust**: García Márquez's family, particularly his son Rodrigo Garcia, agreed to the adaptation when Netflix proposed using Spanish language and Colombian talent. The family felt the timing was right given the rise of serialized storytelling and global acceptance of subtitles.

2. **Dynamo's Global Experience**: Colombia's leading production company Dynamo (known for "Narcos," "Monos," "Gemini Man") was tapped to support the entire production process.

3. **Colombia's Incentives**: Netflix leveraged Colombia's 35% CINA tax rebate for international productions. "One Hundred Years of Solitude" is the largest project to use this incentive, and Season 2 (currently filming) also taps it.

4. **Finding Macondo**: Oscar-winning production designer Eugenio Caballero ("Pan's Labyrinth") spent two years researching locations. They built Macondo from scratch in Ibagué, four hours from Bogotá, featuring a backlot — unprecedented in Latin America.

5. **Casting Macondo**: Starting June 2022, a nationwide search reviewed over 10,000 candidates to cast 25 lead roles across seven generations of the Buendía family. 97% of the cast are Colombian actors. The series finale features nearly 20,000 extras.

6. **Landscapes**: Filmed across 15 Colombian towns, capturing the country's geographic diversity. A team of 16 specialists led by Martha Duque imported dozens of native plant species to create an authentic ecosystem.

7. **Recreating Historical Colombia**: Over three years of research went into costumes, sets, plants, food, and music. Composer Juancho Valencia leads the music team focusing on traditional Colombian folk sounds.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage features a transcript of a "Sight, Sound & Story" panel discussion hosted by Manhattan Edit Workshop, moderated by Josh Apter, focusing on the cinematography of Netflix's adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The panelists are cinematographers Paulo Pérez (episodes 1-3 and 7-8) and María Sarasvati Herrera (episodes 4-6), both of whom are Colombian and deeply connected to the source material.

Key points from the discussion:

- **Background & Preparation**: Both cinematographers read the novel in school (it's required reading in Colombia). Pérez studied at the film school García Márquez founded in Cuba. The production involved extensive research with historians and experts.

- **Production Design**: The entire town of Macondo was built from scratch on a farm four hours from Bogotá, Colombia. The Buendía house was constructed inside a large tent/hanger on the farm. Sets were built three or four different times to show the town's evolution. The production used a mix of natural and artificial light, including LED balloons on the ceiling, large lights (18K and T lights) on cherry pickers, and cranes for lighting to simulate sunrises and sunsets. Over 300 lights were used.

- **Visual Approach**: The camera serves as the narrator (like Melquíades writing the story). For episodes 1-3, the camera is handheld, alive, and moving constantly to represent the circular nature of the story and break time and space. The magical realism is depicted as everyday, natural occurrences, done mostly in-camera without VFX (only the flying carpet and donkey were VFX; the levitating priest and ghost were real/physical).

- **Long Takes**: Many scenes were shot as single, continuous takes lasting 2-3 minutes. Examples include: a three-minute shot following a naked boy through Macondo (shot 7-8 times), a shot using a rotating floor (tornamesa) to show the house aging 10 years in a single take, and a shot following Remedios through the house with lighting changing from sunrise to sunset to night to sunrise.

- **Division of Labor**: Pérez worked with director Alex García López on the first block (episodes 1-3, innocence, building civilization) and the third block (episodes 7-8, war). Herrera worked with director Laura Mora on the second block (episodes 4-6, older characters, religion, government, politics). They maintained constant communication to ensure continuity across the series.

- **Color Palette**: Pre-color grading was done but changed when Herrera's block required different colors. Colors have political meaning (blue and red representing conflicting parties). The look evolved with the story—from innocence to government/religion to destruction.

- **Challenges**: Working with children (limited to 6-hour shooting days), coordinating 100-300 extras, managing 360-degree shots with costume and makeup changes on the fly, and the physical demands on the Steadicam operator (30+ kg camera rig). Pérez's director often came up with new ideas the morning of shooting, requiring constant adaptation.

- **The Ghost (Prudencio)**: The murdered character appears as a recurring physical presence representing guilt, appearing multiple times throughout the series without any special effects or halos.
</summary>

**Aracataca** - García Márquez's childhood hometown where he was born in 1927 and lived until age 8 with his grandparents. The house is now a museum. Elements from his childhood here directly inspired the novel: his grandfather's gold fish-making inspired Aureliano Buendía's fish; his grandmother's candied animals inspired Úrsula Iguarán's; the train station, river, and central square all feature in the book. The town is filled with Macondo-themed signs, murals, and statues.

**Ciénaga** - A town 60km north of Aracataca on the Caribbean coast. It served as the backdrop for the Banana Massacre of 1928 (when striking United Fruit Company workers were gunned down by the Colombian army), which García Márquez dramatized in the novel. The nearby Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta (UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, Colombia's largest swamp) inspired the "great swamp" crossed by the gypsy Melquiades.

**Riohacha and La Guajira** - The region where the novel's characters originate before founding Macondo. García Márquez's own ancestors relocated from here. His grandmother told him fantastical tales about pirate raids and the levitating priest who inspired Father Nicanor Reyna. The Wayúu people, who feature prominently in the novel as servants Visitación and Cataure, are indigenous to this region, and García Márquez learned some Wayuunaiki as a child.

The article quotes García Márquez: "The truth is that there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>

But it eventually became One Hundred Years of Solitude due to the perpetual loneliness that all the characters experienced" – Donal Ramos., "It's a book that's always on my nightstand. Every time I read it, I identify with it more and more" – Aracataca resident Emilia Salcedo., "What García Márquez describes [in the novel] is what is known in Colombia as The Banana Massacre" – Local guide Yeiner Mendoza., "The truth is that there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality" – Gabriel García Márquez.
