**Emir Kusturica** ([Serbian Cyrillic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbian_Cyrillic_alphabet "Serbian Cyrillic alphabet"): Емир Кустурица, pronounced [[ě.mir ˈku.stu.ri.tsa]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian "Help:IPA/Serbo-Croatian"); born 24 November 1954) is a [Serbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia")[[2]](#cite_note-Britannica-2)[[3]](#cite_note-homeland-3)[[4]](#cite_note-4) [film director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_director "Film director"), [screenwriter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Screenwriter "Screenwriter"), [actor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actor "Actor"), [film producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_producer "Film producer") and [musician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musician "Musician"). Kusturica has been an active filmmaker since the 1980s.[[2]](#cite_note-Britannica-2)

He has competed at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") on five occasions and won the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") twice (for *[When Father Was Away on Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Father_Was_Away_on_Business "When Father Was Away on Business")* and *[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_(1995_film) "Underground (1995 film)")*), as well as the [Best Director prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Best_Director_Award_(Cannes_Film_Festival) "Best Director Award (Cannes Film Festival)") for *[Time of the Gypsies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_of_the_Gypsies "Time of the Gypsies")*. Kusturica has won a [Silver Bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jury_Grand_Prix "Jury Grand Prix") at the [Berlin Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Film_Festival "Berlin Film Festival") for *[Arizona Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Dream "Arizona Dream")*, a [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") at the [Venice Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival") for *[Black Cat, White Cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cat,_White_Cat "Black Cat, White Cat")* and a Golden Lion for Best First Work for *[Do You Remember Dolly Bell?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_You_Remember_Dolly_Bell%3F "Do You Remember Dolly Bell?")* [[5]](#cite_note-5). He has also been made a [Commander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commander "Commander") of the French [Ordre des Arts et des Lettres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordre_des_Arts_et_des_Lettres "Ordre des Arts et des Lettres").[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-7) Kusturica has been a member of the [Academy of Sciences and Arts of the Republika Srpska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_and_Arts_of_the_Republika_Srpska "Academy of Sciences and Arts of the Republika Srpska") since 9 November 2011.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Among other accolades, Kusturica became a [UNICEF ambassador](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF_Goodwill_Ambassador "UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador") in 2002 and eight years later he was made a chevalier of the [Legion of Honour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Honour "Legion of Honour") in France.

Kusturica has also been recognized for his projects in [town-building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrićgrad "Andrićgrad"). Since the mid-2000s, Kusturica's primary residence has been in [Drvengrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drvengrad "Drvengrad"), a town built for his film *[Life Is a Miracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Is_a_Miracle "Life Is a Miracle")*, in the [Mokra Gora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mokra_Gora "Mokra Gora") region of Serbia. He had portions of the historic village reconstructed for the film.[[9]](#cite_note-9) He published an autobiography "Smrt je neprovjerena glasina" ('Death Is an Unverified Rumour') in 2010, which was followed by four other books.[[2]](#cite_note-Britannica-2)

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Kusturica was born in [Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo"), the son of Murat Kusturica, a [journalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalist "Journalist") employed at Sarajevo's Secretariat of Information, and Senka ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") Numankadić), a court secretary.[[10]](#cite_note-10) Emir grew up as the only child of a [Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Islam in Bosnia and Herzegovina") [secular](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_and_secularism "Islam and secularism") family[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) in [Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo"), the capital of [PR Bosnia and Herzegovina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Republic_of_Bosnia_and_Herzegovina "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina"), then a constituent republic within [FPR Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia").[[13]](#cite_note-NYTHalpern-13) As he writes in 1993, his father's mother was "strongly tied to Muslim rites" while his father "did not belong to any cult, he was not religious at all".[[12]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-12) Kusturica primarily defined himself as [Yugoslavian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavs "Yugoslavs") at least until the year 2000.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

A lively youth, Kusturica was by his own admission a borderline [delinquent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juvenile_delinquency "Juvenile delinquency") while growing up in the Sarajevo neighbourhood of Gorica.[[15]](#cite_note-Kustu_bio-15) Through his father's friendship with the well-known director [Hajrudin "Šiba" Krvavac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hajrudin_Krvavac "Hajrudin Krvavac"), Kusturica, aged seventeen, got a small part in Krvavac's *[Walter Defends Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Defends_Sarajevo "Walter Defends Sarajevo")*, a 1972 [partisan film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partisan_film "Partisan film") funded by the Yugoslav state.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

## Work

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

In 1978, Kusturica graduated from the [film school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_and_TV_School_of_the_Academy_of_Performing_Arts_in_Prague "Film and TV School of the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague") (FAMU) at the [Academy of Performing Arts in Prague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Performing_Arts_in_Prague "Academy of Performing Arts in Prague"), which is why he is sometimes considered a part of the *[Prague film school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praška_filmska_škola "Praška filmska škola")*, an informal group of Yugoslav film directors who studied at FAMU and shared similar influences and aesthetics. After graduating from FAMU, Kusturica began directing made-for-TV [short films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film") in Yugoslavia.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### 1980s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1980s")]

He made his feature film debut in 1981 with *[Do You Remember Dolly Bell?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Do_You_Remember_Dolly_Bell%3F "Do You Remember Dolly Bell?")*, a coming-of-age drama that won the prestigious [Golden Lion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Lion "Golden Lion") for Best First Work at [that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/38th_Venice_International_Film_Festival "38th Venice International Film Festival")'s [Venice Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Film_Festival "Venice Film Festival"). The same year, at age 27, he became a lecturer at the newly established [Academy of Performing Arts in Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Performing_Arts_in_Sarajevo "Academy of Performing Arts in Sarajevo"), a job he held until 1988. He was also art director of Open Stage Obala (*Otvorena scena Obala*). [*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Kusturica's second feature film, *[When Father Was Away on Business](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Father_Was_Away_on_Business "When Father Was Away on Business")* (1985), earned a *[Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or")* at [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Cannes_Film_Festival "1985 Cannes Film Festival") and five Yugoslav movie awards, as well as a nomination for an American [Academy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Awards "Academy Awards") for Best Foreign Film. In 1989 he earned more accolades for *[Time of the Gypsies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_of_the_Gypsies "Time of the Gypsies")*, a film about [Romani culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_society_and_culture "Romani society and culture") and the exploitation of their youth. In 1989 he was a member of the jury at the [16th Moscow International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/16th_Moscow_International_Film_Festival "16th Moscow International Film Festival").[[18]](#cite_note-Moscow1989-18)

### 1990s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1990s")]

Kusturica continued to make highly regarded films into the next decade, including his American debut, the absurdist comedy *[Arizona Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Dream "Arizona Dream")* (1993).

He won the [Palme d'Or](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palme_d'Or "Palme d'Or") for his black comedy epic *[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_(1995_film) "Underground (1995 film)")* (1995), based upon a scenario of [Dušan Kovačević](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dušan_Kovačević "Dušan Kovačević"), a noted Serbian playwright.[[19]](#cite_note-19) *Underground* was partly financed by state-owned [Yugoslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FR_Yugoslavia "FR Yugoslavia") television. It recounted the history of Yugoslavia from World War II until [the conflicts during the 1990s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslav_Wars "Yugoslav Wars"). Bosnian and French critics claimed the film contained pro-Serb propaganda.[[20]](#cite_note-guardian-20)[[21]](#cite_note-nytimes-21) [Sarajevo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarajevo "Sarajevo")-born novelist [Aleksandar Hemon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandar_Hemon "Aleksandar Hemon"), who emigrated to the United States before the war, said *Underground* downplayed [Serbian atrocities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia_in_the_Yugoslav_Wars "Serbia in the Yugoslav Wars") by presenting "the Balkan war as a product of collective, innate, savage madness."[[22]](#cite_note-22) French philosopher and writer [Alain Finkielkraut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alain_Finkielkraut "Alain Finkielkraut"), a supporter of the Croatian president [Franjo Tuđman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franjo_Tuđman "Franjo Tuđman") during the 1990s,[[23]](#cite_note-23) denounced the Cannes Film Festival's jury award, saying *it was honouring a creator with a thriving imagination* and that the jury *praised a version of the most hackneyed and deceitful Serb propaganda.*[[21]](#cite_note-nytimes-21) It was later revealed that Finkielkraut had not seen the film before writing his criticism.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)

French philosopher [Bernard-Henri Lévy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard-Henri_Lévy "Bernard-Henri Lévy") made a film criticizing *Underground*.[[20]](#cite_note-guardian-20) In a discussion with Levy, the Slovenian philosopher [Slavoj Žižek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavoj_Žižek "Slavoj Žižek") said: *I hope we share another point, which is – to be brutal – hatred of [director] Emir Kusturica.* Underground *is one of the most horrible films that I've seen. What kind of Yugoslav society do you see in Kusturica's* Underground*? A society where people fornicate, drink, fight – a kind of eternal orgy.*[[27]](#cite_note-27)

Emir Kusturica taught Film Directing at Columbia University's Graduate Film Division.

In 1998, he won the Venice Film Festival's Silver Lion for Best Direction for *[Black Cat, White Cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cat,_White_Cat "Black Cat, White Cat")*, a farcical comedy set in a Gypsy ([Romani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_people "Romani people")) settlement on the banks of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube"). The music for the film was composed by the Belgrade-based band [No Smoking Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/No_Smoking_Orchestra "No Smoking Orchestra").

### 2000s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2000s")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/09/Emir_Kusturica_Bruxelles05.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emir_Kusturica_Bruxelles05.jpg)

Emir Kusturica in Brussels, during the Philippe Rotthier awards, November 2005.

In 2001, Kusturica directed *[Super 8 Stories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_8_Stories "Super 8 Stories")*, a documentary road and concert movie about [The No Smoking Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_Kusturica_&_The_No_Smoking_Orchestra "Emir Kusturica & The No Smoking Orchestra"), of which he is a band member.[[28]](#cite_note-28) He was appointed *President of the Jury* of the [2005 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Cannes_Film_Festival "2005 Cannes Film Festival"). His film *[Maradona by Kusturica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maradona_by_Kusturica "Maradona by Kusturica")*, a documentary on [Argentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentine "Argentine") football star [Diego Maradona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Maradona "Diego Maradona"), was released in Italy in May 2007. It premiered in France during the Cannes Film Festival in 2008. His film *[Promise Me This](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promise_Me_This "Promise Me This")* premiered at the [2007 Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Cannes_Film_Festival "2007 Cannes Film Festival").[[29]](#cite_note-cannes-2007.com-29) In June 2007, Kusturica directed the music video to [Manu Chao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manu_Chao "Manu Chao")'s single "[Rainin in Paradize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainin_in_Paradize?action=edit&redlink=1 "Rainin in Paradize (page does not exist)")", from the latter's *[La Radiolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Radiolina "La Radiolina")* album.

In 2002 Kusturica became a [UNICEF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNICEF "UNICEF") National Ambassador for Serbia.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

Since January 2008 he has organized the annual private [Küstendorf Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Küstendorf_Film_Festival "Küstendorf Film Festival"). Its first installment was held at [Drvengrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drvengrad "Drvengrad")/Küstendorf, a village built for his film *[Life Is a Miracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Is_a_Miracle "Life Is a Miracle")*, from 14 to 21 January 2008.[[31]](#cite_note-31) His next film, *Cool Water*, is a comedy set against the background of a [Middle East conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East_conflict "Middle East conflict"). Filming started in November 2010 in Germany.

### 2010s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2010s")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/Kusturica%2C_Zelenovi%C4%87%2C_Mihalkov.jpg/250px-Kusturica%2C_Zelenovi%C4%87%2C_Mihalkov.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kusturica,_Zelenović,_Mihalkov.jpg)

Kusturica with [Nikita Mikhalkov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikita_Mikhalkov "Nikita Mikhalkov") (2014)

[Andrej Nikolaidis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrej_Nikolaidis "Andrej Nikolaidis"), a [Montenegrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montenegrins_(ethnic_group) "Montenegrins (ethnic group)") writer and columnist, criticized Kusturica for appearing to agree with [Slobodan Milošević](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slobodan_Milošević "Slobodan Milošević")'s propaganda during the [Bosnian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War"). Kusturica sued Nikolaidis and the *Monitor* newspaper for civil damages at the Supreme Court of Montenegro. In the end, Nikolaidis was ordered to pay $6,490 to Kusturica for calling the famed director a "media star of Milosevic's war machinery".[[32]](#cite_note-32) The judge ruled that the evidence was not credible enough.[[33]](#cite_note-The_case_of_Kusturica-33) In the end Nikolaidis and the paper were fined 12,000 euros for breaking the code of journalism by calling Kusturica "stupid, ugly and corrupt" in the article.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

In October 2010, Kusturica withdrew from the jury of [Antalya Golden Orange Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/47th_Antalya_ "47th Antalya ") after being publicly criticized and accused by Turkish director [Semih Kaplanoğlu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semih_Kaplanoğlu "Semih Kaplanoğlu") and Turkey's minister of culture [Ertuğrul Günay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ertuğrul_Günay "Ertuğrul Günay") over his alleged remarks and opinions about the [Bosnian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnian_War "Bosnian War").[[35]](#cite_note-abc-35) The criticism of Kusturica was started by an organization called the Turkish-Bosnian Cultural Federation as soon as Kusturica was announced as a jury member.[[36]](#cite_note-36) Turkish media reported that Kusturica repeatedly downplayed the number of people killed and the rape of Muslim women during the war.[[35]](#cite_note-abc-35) The daily newspaper *[Milliyet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milliyet "Milliyet")* said Kusturica denied the allegations.[[35]](#cite_note-abc-35) Public sentiment in Turkey and in Serbia was such that a couple of days after Kusturica left Turkey, there were unsubstantiated news reports by Serbian [tabloids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabloid_journalism "Tabloid journalism") claiming that a mob of Turkish youths in [Antalya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya "Antalya") physically assaulted Swiss actor Michael Neuenschwander (in town to promote his movie *180° – Wenn deine Welt plötzlich Kopf steht*) because they mistook him for Kusturica due to apparent physical resemblances between the two.[[37]](#cite_note-37) Later, Neuenschwander's press agent said there was no physical assault and that Neuenschwander was verbally abused by a small group.[[38]](#cite_note-38) Kusturica later commented on the incident:

> I did receive a sincere apology from the mayor of Antalya [Mustafa Akaydın](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mustafa_Akaydın "Mustafa Akaydın") over what happened. Essentially, I became collateral damage in the ongoing political fight between the central powers from the ruling coalition in Istanbul and the municipal authorities in Antalya where the local power is held by a [social-democrat party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_People's_Party "Republican People's Party"). But regardless of everything, this is completely unacceptable on a basic level – when you're an invited guest somewhere, your hosts simply cannot behave in this manner. And this run-in I had was with a part of Turkish society, the part that consists of highly-evolved primitives. I am not a politician and I'm not obliged to comment on and dissect every crime or genocide around the world. And then I got very angry and I told them if they're so sensitive about genocide it would be much better for them to publicly condemn the [genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") they committed against the [Armenian people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians "Armenians"), before having a go at me with accusatory statements. I clearly condemned the crimes in Bosnia, but the 'problem' is that I condemned the crimes committed by all sides, which makes me incompatible with the strategy they have for Bosnia.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

At the [64th Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_Cannes_Film_Festival "2011 Cannes Film Festival"), held 11–22 May 2011, Kusturica presided over the jury of the *[Un Certain Regard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Un_Certain_Regard "Un Certain Regard")* section of the festival's official selection. On 14 May, in [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes "Cannes"), he was invested with the insignia of Chevalier of the [Legion of Honour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legion_of_Honour "Legion of Honour"), France's highest decoration.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

In September 2012, Kusturica accepted an offer to be the head juror of the first [Saint Petersburg International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Petersburg_International_Film_Festival "Saint Petersburg International Film Festival"). During the festival he also performed for the residents and guests of Saint Petersburg with his band The No Smoking Orchestra.

Kusturica was awarded the [Order of St. Sava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_St._Sava "Order of St. Sava"), First Class, for his "selfless care and presentation of the Serbian nation in the world", on 12 May 2012.[[41]](#cite_note-41)

During the last months of 2013, Kusturica started shooting a documentary on the life of Uruguayan president [José Mujica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Mujica "José Mujica"), whom he considers "the last hero of politics".[[42]](#cite_note-docukusturica-42) *El Pepe: A Supreme Life* was released in 2018.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

### 2020s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2020s")]

Kusturica announced that he will be filming his next project in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"). The film will be based on works of Russian writers [Dostoyevski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Dostoevsky "Fyodor Dostoevsky"), [Gogol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Gogol "Nikolai Gogol") and [Tolstoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leo_Tolstoy "Leo Tolstoy").[[44]](#cite_note-44) It is titled *Just One More Time*.[[45]](#cite_note-45) He was also planning to direct, in 2024, *The Engineer of Easy Walks* to be shot in [Sochi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sochi "Sochi").[[46]](#cite_note-46)

### Acting

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Acting")]

After numerous film cameo appearances over the years, Kusturica's first sizable acting role was in *[The Widow of St. Pierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Widow_of_St._Pierre "The Widow of St. Pierre")*, a 2000 movie by director [Patrice Leconte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrice_Leconte "Patrice Leconte"), as a convict on the French island colony of [Saint Pierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Pierre_and_Miquelon "Saint Pierre and Miquelon").

In 2002, Kusturica appeared as an electric guitar player/security specialist in *[The Good Thief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Good_Thief_(film) "The Good Thief (film)")*, directed by [Neil Jordan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neil_Jordan "Neil Jordan").

In the French movie *[L'affaire Farewell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farewell_(2009_film) "Farewell (2009 film)")* (2009), he played the role of a [KGB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KGB "KGB") agent, Colonel Sergei Gregoriev.

In *[On the Milky Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/On_the_Milky_Road "On the Milky Road")* (2016), he played Kosta, a milkman and falconer.

## Musical career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Musical career")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/An_image_of_Emir_Kusturica.jpg/250px-An_image_of_Emir_Kusturica.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:An_image_of_Emir_Kusturica.jpg)

Kusturica performing with [The No Smoking Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_Kusturica_&_The_No_Smoking_Orchestra "Emir Kusturica & The No Smoking Orchestra") in March 2017.

In mid-1986, thirty-one-year-old Kusturica started playing [bass guitar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_guitar "Bass guitar") in [Zabranjeno Pušenje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zabranjeno_Pušenje "Zabranjeno Pušenje"),[[47]](#cite_note-47) a Sarajevan punk/garage rock outfit and part of the [New Primitivism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Primitivism "New Primitivism") movement.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] Kusturica, an already established and celebrated Palm d'Or-winning film director, joined the band just after Zabranjeno Pušenje frontman [Nele Karajlić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nele_Karajlić "Nele Karajlić") had caused a media scandal[[48]](#cite_note-48) that led to his legal prosecution on the verbal offence grounds and the band being shadow banned in the Yugoslav media, all of which hurt its commercial prospects and led to three of the six members leaving the group.[[49]](#cite_note-49)

Kusturica ended up playing bass on three track from the band's third studio album *[Pozdrav iz zemlje Safari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pozdrav_iz_zemlje_Safari "Pozdrav iz zemlje Safari")* and composing one of the songs as well as directing a [music video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_video "Music video") for the track "Manijak" off the album. Though never fully involved in the band's day-to-day activities, Kusturica left Zabranjeno Pušenje in 1988 once the filming of *[Time of the Gypsies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_of_the_Gypsies "Time of the Gypsies")* began.

Kusturica returned to the group in the late 1990s following the *[Black Cat, White Cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Cat,_White_Cat "Black Cat, White Cat")* film and the band's name changed to [Emir Kusturica & The No Smoking Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_Kusturica_&_The_No_Smoking_Orchestra "Emir Kusturica & The No Smoking Orchestra"). In 1999, the No Smoking Orchestra recorded a new album, *Unza Unza Time*, produced by the Universal record company, as well as a music video, directed by Emir Kusturica. The band has been touring internationally since 1999. The musician and composer [Goran Bregović](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goran_Bregović "Goran Bregović") has composed music for three of Kusturica's films: *[Time of the Gypsies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_of_the_Gypsies "Time of the Gypsies")*, *[Arizona Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Dream "Arizona Dream")*, which featured [Iggy Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iggy_Pop "Iggy Pop"); and *[Underground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underground_(1995_film) "Underground (1995 film)")*.

## Writing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Writing")]

### *Death is an Unverified Rumour*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Death is an Unverified Rumour")]

Kusturica's autobiography, *Death is an Unverified Rumour* (Смрт је непровјерена гласина / *Smrt je neprovjerena glasina*), was published in October 2010 in Belgrade by [Novosti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novosti_a.d. "Novosti a.d."). The launch took place on 26 October during the Belgrade Book Fair and was attended by [Nele Karajlić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nele_Karajlić "Nele Karajlić"), [Dušan Kovačević](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dušan_Kovačević "Dušan Kovačević"), foreign minister [Vuk Jeremić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vuk_Jeremić "Vuk Jeremić"), [Vojislav Koštunica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vojislav_Koštunica "Vojislav Koštunica"), etc.[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52) Initially released only in [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia"), Montenegro, and [Republika Srpska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republika_Srpska "Republika Srpska"), the book's first printing of 20,000 copies quickly sold out. The second printing of 32,000 copies was out in November and it too sold within weeks. On 8 December, the third printing in 40,000 copies was out[[53]](#cite_note-53) and promoted a day later at Belgrade's [Dom Sindikata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dom_Sindikata "Dom Sindikata").[[54]](#cite_note-54) In February 2011, a fourth printing with further 10,000 copies was out and soon the sale of the 100,000th book was announced.[[55]](#cite_note-55) The final number of copies sold by the publisher was 114,000.[[56]](#cite_note-blic.rs-56)

Translations were published in Italy (translated by Alice Parmeggiani) on 30 March 2011 under the title *Dove sono in questa storia* ("Where am I in this Story"),[[57]](#cite_note-57) in France by [JC Lattès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JC_Lattès "JC Lattès") on 6 April 2011 as *Où suis-je dans cette histoire ?*,[[58]](#cite_note-58) and in Germany in September 2011 as *Der Tod ist ein unbestätigtes Gerücht*.[[59]](#cite_note-59) In 2012, the book was published in Bulgaria as *Cмъpттa e нeпoтвъpдeн cлуx*, in Greece as *Κι εγώ πού είμαι σ' αυτή την ιστορία;*, in Romania as *Unde sunt eu în toată povestea asta*, and in Hungary as *Hogy jövök én a képbe?*.

### *Hundred Pains*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Hundred Pains")]

Kusturica's second book was a novel, *Hundred Pains* (Сто јада / *Sto jada*), released in Serbia on 24 April 2013 by Novosti a.d.[[56]](#cite_note-blic.rs-56)[[60]](#cite_note-60) in the initial printing of 35,000 copies. On 6 June, the second printing came out in the circulation of 25,000.[[61]](#cite_note-61) The book's translated form was released in France in January 2015 by JC Lattès as *Étranger dans le mariage*.

### *Why Did I Need This*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Why Did I Need This")]

His third book, a diary titled *Why Did I Need This* (Шта ми ово треба / Šta mi ovo treba) was published in October 2018 and for the first time presented at the [Belgrade Book Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade_Book_Fair "Belgrade Book Fair").[[62]](#cite_note-62)

### *Vidiš li da ne vidim*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Vidiš li da ne vidim")]

In 2022, Kusturica published a book titled *Vidiš li da ne vidim.*[[63]](#cite_note-63) The main protagonists of the book are the author and his friend and Austrian Nobel laureate novelist [Peter Handke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Handke "Peter Handke").

### *Kada mrtve duše marširaju*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Kada mrtve duše marširaju")]

His fifth book, *Kada mrtve duše marširaju* (*When the dead souls march*) was published in 2023.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

## Other endeavors

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Other endeavors")]

### Drvengrad

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Drvengrad")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Drvengrad.jpg/250px-Drvengrad.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Drvengrad.jpg)

[Drvengrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drvengrad "Drvengrad")

[Drvengrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drvengrad "Drvengrad") (meaning 'Wooden Town') is a traditional village that Kusturica built for his film *[Life Is a Miracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Life_Is_a_Miracle "Life Is a Miracle")*. It is located in the [Zlatibor District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zlatibor_District "Zlatibor District") near the city of [Užice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Užice "Užice"), two hundred kilometers southwest of Serbia's capital, [Belgrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade "Belgrade"). It is located near [Mokra Gora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mokra_Gora "Mokra Gora") and [Višegrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Višegrad "Višegrad"), best known for [Yugoslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yugoslavs "Yugoslavs") [Ivo Andrić](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivo_Andrić "Ivo Andrić")'s novel, *[The Bridge on the Drina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bridge_on_the_Drina "The Bridge on the Drina")*.[[65]](#cite_note-65)

### *Time of the Gypsies* punk opera

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Time of the Gypsies punk opera")]

During 2007, Kusturica and Nele Karajlić prepared a punk opera, *Time of the Gypsies*. The initial idea came five years earlier in 2002 from Kusturica's collaborator [Marc di Domenico](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marc%20di%20Domenico "fr:Marc di Domenico") while the support of the [Paris Opera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Opera "Paris Opera") director [Gerard Mortier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerard_Mortier "Gerard Mortier") got the project rolling. Basing the production on his eponymous 1988 film, Kusturica wrote the [libretto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libretto "Libretto") by adapting the story of the Gypsy youth from the Balkans relocating to Italy in order to obtain money for his ill sister's surgery. The director cast young Serbian folk singers Stevan Anđelković and Milica Todorović in the roles of Perhan and Azra, respectively, while the experienced Karajlić took the role of Ahmed Đida. The music in the original movie had been composed by [Goran Bregović](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goran_Bregović "Goran Bregović"); however, since Kusturica and he have not been on speaking terms since the late 1990s, those pieces could not be used.[[66]](#cite_note-bloomberg-2007-66) The all-new score was composed by Dejan Sparavalo of the No Smoking Orchestra.

The premiere took place in June 2007, at the [Opéra Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opéra_Bastille "Opéra Bastille") in Paris, to positive reviews.[[66]](#cite_note-bloomberg-2007-66)[[67]](#cite_note-67)[[68]](#cite_note-68) Following the vast open stage of Bastille, the show was performed in smaller arenas. In March 2008, the production was staged in Paris' [Palais des congrès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palais_des_congrès_de_Paris "Palais des congrès de Paris").[[69]](#cite_note-69)

In fall 2010, the production was staged in Belgrade at [Sava Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sava_Center "Sava Center").

On 29 June 2012, the opera was staged in [Banja Luka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banja_Luka "Banja Luka") at the [City Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banja_Luka_City_Stadium "Banja Luka City Stadium"), for the very first time under the open skies, with 10,000 people in attendance.[[70]](#cite_note-70) This was followed with the July staging in [Cartagena, Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartagena,_Spain "Cartagena, Spain"), as part of [La Mar de Músicas de Cartagena](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/La%20Mar%20de%20Músicas%20de%20Cartagena "es:La Mar de Músicas de Cartagena").[[71]](#cite_note-71)

Future staging of the punk opera is scheduled for August 2013 in [Krasnodar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krasnodar "Krasnodar"), [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), during Kubana Festival.[[72]](#cite_note-72)

### Küstendorf Film and Music Festival

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Küstendorf Film and Music Festival")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Novak_Djokovic_in_Andricgrad.jpg/250px-Novak_Djokovic_in_Andricgrad.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Novak_Djokovic_in_Andricgrad.jpg)

Kusturica with [Novak Djokovic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novak_Djokovic "Novak Djokovic") in [Andrićgrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrićgrad "Andrićgrad") (2014)

Since 2008, Drvengrad hosts the annual [Küstendorf Film and Music Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Küstendorf_Film_and_Music_Festival "Küstendorf Film and Music Festival"),[[73]](#cite_note-73) which showcases films and music from all around the world as well as a competition programme for student [short films](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_film "Short film"). The festival is known for not having a [red carpet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_carpet "Red carpet") as well as none of the popular Hollywood festival artifacts.

### Andrićgrad

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Emir_Kusturica&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Andrićgrad")]

On 28 June 2011 Kusturica started the construction project of [Andrićgrad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrićgrad "Andrićgrad") (also known as *Kamengrad*, meaning *Stone Town*), located

Emir Kusturica (born 24 November 1954 in Sarajevo) is a Serbian film director, screenwriter, actor, producer, and musician. He has been active since the 1970s and is one of the most acclaimed European filmmakers, having won the Palme d'Or at Cannes twice (for *When Father Was Away on Business* in 1985 and *Underground* in 1995), the Best Director prize at Cannes for *Time of the Gypsies* (1989), a Silver Bear at Berlin for *Arizona Dream* (1993), and a Golden Lion at Venice for *Black Cat, White Cat* (1998). He is also a Commander of the French Ordre des Arts et des Lettres and a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour.

Kusturica grew up in a secular Muslim family in Sarajevo and graduated from the FAMU film school in Prague in 1978. His feature debut *Do You Remember Dolly Bell?* (1981) won the Golden Lion for Best First Work at Venice. His 1995 film *Underground* sparked controversy, with some critics accusing it of pro-Serb propaganda. In the late 1990s, he joined (and later fronted) The No Smoking Orchestra. He has also written five books, including the autobiography *Death is an Unverified Rumour* (2010). Since the mid-2000s, his primary residence has been Drvengrad, a traditional village he built for his film *Life Is a Miracle* in Serbia. He also founded the Küstendorf Film and Music Festival and built Andrićgrad. He has been a UNICEF ambassador since 2002. His political views, including support for Slobodan Milošević-era positions and Vladimir Putin, have been controversial.

<webpage_content>
# [Science Fiction and Other Suspect Ruminations](https://sciencefictionruminations.com/)

## Reviews of Vintage Science Fiction (pre-1985)

# A Film Rumination: Underground, Emir Kusturica (1995)

/ [Joachim Boaz](https://sciencefictionruminations.com/author/sciencefictionruminations/)

9.5/10 (Masterpiece)

Winner Palm d’Or Cannes 1995

Seldom, if ever, have I been so enamored with a movie. Emir Kusturica weaves a poignant, comic, vicious, madcap, sprawling, and physics defying cinematic experience deftly intertwined

with the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states.

Brief Plot Summary

Two friends build a massive underground weapons making complex to protect their town from the German invasion in WWII while they join the communist guerilla fighters.  Both fall for the same woman — an actress who helps the Germans and also has a bungling/comical German lover. Eventually, one friend is injured and remains underground while the other rises up through the ranks of the Tito regime (and adapts an elaborate system to convince those still hidden underground that WWII is still being waged).  I best not spoil the rest!

Most criticism of the film I’ve read revolves around Kusturica’s interpretation historical events. Although I’m not Serbian or Bosnian but I do have some basic knowledge concerning the break-up of the Yugoslavia, WWII, and the Serbian atrocities inflicted on various other ethnic groups in the region.

Emir Kusturica was so badgered by attacks concerning his glossing over of the real issues of the succession (ethnic cleansing etc…) that he was forced into voluntary film retirement (thankfully that did not last long) because of the hostile reaction he received at home even though he won the prestigious Palm de’Or at Cannes in 1995.

I do not have a clear rebuttal, but I can say that this exclusion should not condemn him. The monumental task of embodying the history of a country, the feelings of a people, into an extended family over 60 years cannot and should not include everything. A WWII movie about the invasion of Normandy most likely will not address the Holocaust — neither will a movie about German U-boat captains address the Nazi invasion of Russia in any depth. The material which he covers for a Hollywood director would be material for tons of movies. His concentration on a single family (and the history that eddies around them) excludes discussion of atrocities for to quote Kusturica, “they were not all bad.”

This statement is depressing in the context of the movie itself for it is hard for the audience to sympathize with anyone. Those that are truly innocent are either mentally handicapped or hidden underground and brainwashed with Tito propaganda.

That is the chilling part of the film and I feel it is the crux of his message. Many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, but in the context of the extreme isolation of Tito’s regime and WWII these actions are definitely not to be forgiven but perhaps, understood in context to a greater degree.

The acting is impeccable. Miki Manojlovic is my personal favorite portraying the alcoholic womanizing and eventually fiercely loyal husband. The chemistry between him and his best friend (Lazar Ristovski) is exceptional as is the love triangle with Mirjana Jokovic (an amazing actress). Slavko Stimac plays the mentally slow Ivan and his journey through the tunnels in search of his chimpanzee friend is harrowing and frightening.

My favorite element of Emir Kusturica’s films is his use of magical realism. This element is normally used by South American writers, and Italo Calvino and Borges in Europe but rarely is it used in Cinema. If used poorly it can seem corny and contrived. Emir is the master of using the technique, for example, the glorious Underground wedding scene with the bride connected to the wheeled wooden arm. Only in the beginning is this moving contraption seen, in all other shots the bride is actually flying around the room, over the tables. The effect is stunning. Many stories thrive off of unexplained, unscientific, elements that the characters themselves are oblivious too. The grenade exploding in the suitcase, the detaching island, the underwater scenes, etc…

The movie is LONG. The scenes are madcap.  The cinematography is spectacular. The music is exceptional, infectious and crawls farther and farther into your skull edging you on to some conclusion — simply put, either you love it or hate it. The movie is also heart wrenching (perhaps the symbolism is occasionally heavy handed) while being astoundingly funny — a dichotomy paramount for his message. It explores the joys of family, of love, and the terror of events and feelings (war, lust) that might seem out of an individual’s control. A cinematic masterpiece.

args.key_excerpts: "Seldom, if ever, have I been so enamored with a movie. Emir Kusturica weaves a poignant, comic, vicious, madcap, sprawling, and physics defying cinematic experience deftly intertwined with the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states.", "The monumental task of embodying the history of a country, the feelings of a people, into an extended family over 60 years cannot and should not include everything.", "Many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, but in the context of the extreme isolation of Tito's regime and WWII these actions are definitely not to be forgiven but perhaps, understood in context to a greater degree.", "Emir is the master of using the technique [magical realism], for example, the glorious Underground wedding scene with the bride connected to the wheeled wooden arm.", "The movie is also heart wrenching (perhaps the symbolism is occasionally heavy handed) while being astoundingly funny — a dichotomy paramount for his message."
args.summary:
This is a review of Emir Kusturica's 1995 film "Underground" (winner of the Palm d'Or at Cannes 1995), rated 9.5/10 and called a "Masterpiece" by the reviewer Joachim Boaz. The film is a sprawling, madcap cinematic experience that intertwines the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states through the story of two friends who build an underground weapons complex during WWII. One friend remains hidden underground while the other rises through Tito's regime, maintaining the fiction that the war is still ongoing.

The review addresses criticism of Kusturica's interpretation of historical events, particularly accusations of glossing over Serbian atrocities. The reviewer defends the film, arguing that a single film cannot encompass all aspects of a country's history, and that Kusturica's focus on a single family necessarily excludes discussion of some atrocities. The reviewer notes that the film's chilling message may be about how many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, actions that should be understood in context. The film is praised for its impeccable acting, magical realism (a technique rarely used in cinema), spectacular cinematography, and exceptional music. The reviewer describes it as both heart-wrenching and astoundingly funny—a cinematic masterpiece.

The comments section includes a lengthy discussion about the political controversy surrounding Kusturica, including accusations of Serb nationalism, the role of French intellectual Alain Finkelkraut, and the complex nature of ethnicity and nationalism in the former Yugoslavia. The author also discusses Kusturica's other films and the film "Four Friends" by Steve Teisch as a possible template.

# On Underground (Emir Kusturica, 1995)

by [David Bezmozgis](https://brickmag.com/author/david-bezmozgis/)

### From [*Brick* 108](/product/brick-108)

![](https://brickmag.com/wp-content/uploads/Brick108_Cover_FINAL.jpg)

Brick 108 Winter 2022

In April of 2020, a friend called me from Los Angeles to tell me that Chris had killed himself. Someone had found him in his Venice apartment. We had all gone to film school together in the late 1990s—I somewhat incidentally, the others more intentionally. Chris was from working-class Palo Alto, darkly handsome, a talented muralist, of Polish and Italian lineage, the oldest of two brothers. Film school and Los Angeles don’t tend to be cradles of virtue, but I don’t remember Chris ever being petty or cruel.

The spring before we started film school, Emir Kusturica, the Bosnian Serbian director, won the Palme d’Or at Cannes for his film *Underground*, a great, raucous, three-hour saga that tracked from the opening salvos of World War II in the Balkans to the Bosnian War that obliterated even the concept of Yugoslavia. Kusturica previously made *Time of the Gypsies* and followed with *Black Cat, White Cat*, films that were so lush, kinetic, and narratively outrageous that they teased the line between a faithful representation of reality—repudiating sanitized and formulaic Hollywood—and an incorrigible embrace of the absurd. I remember those films as revelations, works of art that showed what was possible. Chris loved *Underground* in particular.

Hoping to evoke his presence, I rewatched the film recently. I hadn’t seen it in twenty-five years. The story is a love triangle between two friends, Marko and Blacky, grifters who’ve allied with Tito’s communist resistance, and Natalija, the star of the Belgrade stage. At first Marko and Blacky seem practically indistinguishable from each other, but when Marko usurps Natalija from Blacky, he reveals him-self to be duplicitous in a way Blacky is not. Marko orchestrates an elaborate ruse to convince Blacky and others hiding from the Nazis that the war isn’t over. They live for twenty years in a cellar, manufacturing arms for the resistance and awaiting orders to emerge and liberate their country. Meanwhile, Marko becomes a hero of the Tito regime, celebrated for his socialist-realist doggerel. If history is either tragedy or farce, Kusturica chooses farce without denying the tragedy. Terrible things happen, people are tortured and killed, or die of illness, mishap, or by their own hand, but Kusturica is a master of tone and keeps the film mostly buoyant. The action is slapstick. A brass band provides frenzied accompaniment for scenes of banquet and battle. Like a great writer who seizes an opportunity in every sentence, Kusturica fills each frame with something bold and emotionally arresting. The hero of the film is ultimately Blacky since he personifies its spirit: though he suffers betrayal, disappointment, and loss, he succumbs to neither cynicism nor despair.

I saw Chris in Blacky, and not just because he physically resembled the actor who played the part. They shared qualities of exuberance, generosity, and charisma. Or that is how I remembered Chris. I hadn’t seen or spoken to him in two years before he died. Another friend learned that a failed business venture had obliged him to sell his grandfather’s farm, that a childhood ailment had come back to plague him, and that he had been hospitalized in a psychiatric ward for a time. And yet my naive response to seeing the film was that if Chris had only watched it again it could have banished the darkness and kept him alive.

If this is a fantasy, it is a fantasy shared by the film itself. *Underground* concludes by doing something that only film can, bringing the dead back to life. The final scene is another banquet. The brass band plays. All of Blacky’s departed relatives and friends are at the table. All is forgiven but not forgotten, Blacky tells Marko and Natalija, as the grassy promontory on which they are perched breaks away and drifts out to sea.

---

**David Bezmozgis** is the author of *Natasha and Other Stories*, *The Free World*, *The Betrayers*, and *Immigrant City*. He has written and directed two feature films and was a screenwriter on the animated feature, *Charlotte*. David lives in Toronto and is the creative director of the Humber School for Writers.

# Cinco años, 18 versiones y una novela que “no se agota en una lectura”: así trabajaron las guionistas de ‘Cien años de soledad’

## Natalia Santa y Camila Brugés, las escritoras colombianas de la serie basada en la obra de García Márquez, cuentan la adaptación de una historia que se consideraba imposible de llevar a la pantalla

Las escritoras **Natalia Santa** y **Camila Brugés**, responsables del guion de la adaptación de la novela de **Gabriel García Márquez** para Netflix, llevan más de cinco años dentro de Macondo. No como lectoras —ya lo eran desde antes—, sino con la tarea de desmenuzar cada página y traducir al lenguaje audiovisual una obra que muchos consideran inadaptable. La segunda parte de ***Cien años de soledad***fue estrenada esta semana con siete episodios que narran el declive del linaje Buendía y la caída de Macondo. El gran final, un episodio especial con formato de largometraje, llegará el **26 de agosto**.

En entrevista con el diario El Tiempo de Colombia, **Santa** y **Brugés** describieron el proceso de trabajo sobre una novela que, según sus propias palabras, “no se agota con las lecturas”. La conversación giró en torno a los desafíos de la fidelidad, las decisiones sobre qué contar y qué suprimir, y la manera en que su condición de mujeres influyó —de forma orgánica, no programática— en las elecciones narrativas de la serie.

PUBLICIDAD

La premisa que guió el trabajo fue la fidelidad. No una reinterpretación libre, sino una traducción. “Nos pidieron **una adaptación muy fiel**. Entonces ya no es percibir el libro desde tu propia lectura, no es tomar una fracción y transformarla. Es traducir todo a otro lenguaje, intentando mantener la fidelidad y haciendo honor a una obra que ya sabemos lo que representa en Colombia y en Latinoamérica”, explicó **Natalia Santa** al diario colombiano.

Esa fidelidad tuvo un costo particular: enfrentarse a los pasajes más oscuros e incómodos de la novela sin esquivarlos. **Camila Brugés** señaló que el proceso de desglose reveló capas que la lectura corriente tiende a suavizar. “Al desglosar la novela te das cuenta de **lo oscura que es**. No es que uno pensara que Gabo era ligero, pero siento que se me había olvidado lo denso que es, en muchas capas: a nivel psicológico de los personajes, de las relaciones familiares, de lo político”, afirmó.

PUBLICIDAD

**García Márquez** apareció en la conversación como una presencia viva, no como un monumento. **Santa** recordó que cada regreso al texto abría nuevas lecturas: “Habiéndolo leído tantas veces, de repente decía: esto no lo había visto, esto revela otra capa, otro símbolo. Está tejido de tal manera que siempre que vuelves, descubres algo”. Su primera lectura, añadió, había estado atravesada por la dimensión mítica del relato; la relectura para el guion le reveló la precisión histórica de la novela. Para **Brugés**, ese reencuentro tuvo un efecto concreto sobre su valoración del autor. “El respeto que le tengo como autor, después de hacer esto, es mucho mayor. Siento que estuvo atravesado por **un momento de iluminación”**, dijo en la entrevista con el diario colombiano.

![Cien años de soledad, temporada 2 - Netflix](https://www.infobae.com/resizer/v2/B3S7PGGMY5EZFGSJDCMBMROKDQ.jpg?auth=103114020d768ebf61a6b93b8a6081bbb8b6286077faff03f21154d7957b07f9&smart=true&width=350&height=233&quality=85)

La pregunta sobre la mirada femenina detrás de la serie generó respuestas matizadas. **Natalia Santa** fue tajante respecto a la relación entre las guionistas y la obra original: “Yo no creo que le aportemos nada a García Márquez. La novela es grande y es brillante”. Pero reconoció que el equipo —integrado también por la directora **Laura Mora**, diseñadoras de producción y vestuario, y productoras— tomó decisiones desde una perspectiva contemporánea. El tratamiento del matrimonio infantil y otras formas de violencia presentes en el texto exigió discusiones sobre cómo representarlas sin caer en la censura. “Tomamos decisiones, no desde la censura, sino desde una reinterpretación del ahora”, precisó ante el diario bogotano.

PUBLICIDAD

**Camila Brugés** matizó esa posición: “Como somos mujeres, de repente hay cosas que nos importan más, que marcaron las decisiones de qué dejábamos adentro y qué afuera. No creo que sea una serie con **una mirada explícitamente femenina**, pero tampoco es una serie sin esa mirada”.

El proceso de escritura también implicó aprender a soltar. **Santa** describió el momento del cierre no como una decisión artística, sino como una imposición del cronograma de producción: “Siempre va a haber, al menos de mi parte, la sensación de que hubiera podido hacer más, revisar más, hacer esta escena desde otro lugar”. **Brugés** lo resumió con precisión: “En la versión 18 de cada guion, ya te quieres ir”. Ambas coincidieron en que el guion es solo el primer estadio de una creación colectiva que se reescribe en el rodaje y otra vez en el montaje.

PUBLICIDAD

Sobre el impacto de la primera temporada, El Tiempo recogió un dato que las guionistas celebraron: en Colombia, las editoriales reportaron un **aumento del 300%** en las ventas de la novela tras el estreno de la serie en diciembre de 2024. Para **Brugés**, ese efecto era uno de los objetivos implícitos del proyecto: “Si asumimos que va a haber mucha gente que nunca va a llegar al libro, quizás podamos ser una puerta”.

args.summary:
This Infobae article reports on an interview with Colombian screenwriters Natalia Santa and Camila Brugés, who adapted Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude) for Netflix. The writers spent over five years working on the adaptation, which many considered impossible to translate to screen. The second part of the series was recently released with seven episodes covering the decline of the Buendía lineage and the fall of Macondo, with a feature-length finale scheduled for August 26.

The screenwriters emphasized their commitment to fidelity—a "very faithful adaptation" that translates the novel to audiovisual language rather than reinterpreting it freely. They noted that breaking down the novel revealed its darkness: psychological depth, complex family relationships, and political dimensions. Both writers expressed renewed respect for García Márquez, describing the work as "tejed" (woven) such that each reading reveals new layers and symbols.

Regarding the female perspective, Santa stated the team added nothing to García Márquez but made contemporary decisions about how to represent uncomfortable elements like child marriage and violence. Brugés noted that being women influenced which elements were included or excluded, though the series lacks an "explicitly feminine perspective." The writing process involved 18 versions of each script, and the writers acknowledged that screenwriting is only the first stage of a collective creation that continues through filming and editing.

Following the first season's release in December 2024, Colombian publishers reported a 300% increase in novel sales. Brugés expressed hope that the series could serve as a gateway for viewers who might never read the book.

# “El tema de ‘Cien años de soledad’ es la repetición”. Entrevista a Camila Brugés y Natalia Santa

Dos de las guionistas de la serie de próximo estreno hablan sobre el proceso para llevar a la pantalla la novela de Gabriel García Márquez.

[porPaulina Barros Reyes Retana](https://letraslibres.com/author/paulina-barros-reyes-retana/ "View all posts by Paulina Barros Reyes Retana")

4 diciembre 2024

[AÑADIR A FAVORITOS](# "Bookmark This")

Please login to bookmark[*Close*](# "Click to close bookmark panel/modal")

La creación de contenidos para la televisión en Latinoamérica ha tenido un boom en los últimos años, de la mano de las plataformas de *streaming*. Dentro de esta ola, la atención se ha volcado sobre las obras literarias de esta región. Sea por la voracidad inherente de este medio por las historias o sea por el derecho natural que tiene nuestra literatura y lo que se cuenta en ella a ocupar un lugar en la pantalla, las adaptaciones de novelas a series o películas están en boga.

Una de las que más curiosidad genera en estos días es *Cien años de soledad*, novela emblemática del escritor colombiano Gabriel García Márquez, y una de las obras maestras de la literatura hispanoamericana y universal. La serie, una producción de Netflix dirigida por Alex García López y Laura Mora, se estrena el 11 de diciembre en esa plataforma. Con dos partes de ocho capítulos cada una, los retos de adaptar el libro no eran pocos: la imaginación desbordada que contiene, los años y años acumulados en la historia que narra, la poesía de su lenguaje y, en general, el sello del realismo mágico, el movimiento literario del que García Márquez fue exponente.

El esfuerzo por llevarlo a buen puerto es evidente en los primeros capítulos de la serie, que pude ver antes del estreno. Los personajes son retratados con complejidad, la trama se cuenta de forma precisa y acotada para adecuarse a la estructura dramática de este lenguaje, los valores de producción visten la historia y recrean un mundo que, si bien no es el Macondo de mi imaginación, ni quizá tampoco el que cada lector tiene la libertad de crear en su cabeza, es un Macondo coherente con el universo de esta ficción. En pocas palabras, la serie se sostiene por su propio pie. Si no alcanza los vuelos metafóricos y poéticos de la novela es, quizá, porque no es su intención. La televisión pone el acento en brindar entretenimiento, es el lugar que ocupa en la vida cultural de la sociedad y así fue concebida desde su origen. Cumplir con ese cometido sin renunciar a la calidad, a la profundidad y a la belleza es motivo de celebración.

Para transitar el camino de una obra narrativa de esa envergadura a una obra audiovisual para la pantalla chica, se ha de seguir un camino largo y sinuoso, uno que tiene su punto de partida en la escritura. Dos de las guionistas de *Cien años de soledad*, Camila Brugés y Natalia Santa, abren en esta entrevista una ventana a este proceso. Ambas son colombianas y con una proyección internacional de su oficio: Camila tiene una trayectoria multidisciplinaria, interesada en las distintas formas del *storytelling*, mientras que Natalia se ha concentrado en el guionismo y la dirección audiovisual.

**Al hacer una adaptación de una obra de narrativa a una audiovisual, necesariamente hay que hacer un proceso de depuración: elegir entre lo que queda fuera y lo que se va a conservar. También de síntesis: cómo acoplar significado en los elementos dramáticos con los que se elige jugar. ¿Qué decisiones fundamentales tomaron para abordar estos dos procesos en la escritura de la serie?**

Natalia Santa (NS): Cuando nosotras llegamos al proyecto ya había varías cosas definidas. José Rivera, otro de los guionistas, hizo una primera propuesta de adaptación, haciendo un análisis muy complejo para hacer lineal, cronológica, la historia, que en el libro no es así; en el libro va y vuelve, todo el tiempo está pasando de años y temporalidades. Él hizo el gran trabajo de poner todo en orden, y se te abren unas puertas de entender cosas que a la mejor antes no entendías, de ver qué cosas de pronto sobran –no en la novela, por supuesto– a la hora de adaptarla, qué hace falta fortalecer, qué se cuenta muy bien como está en la novela y qué definitivamente hay que ayudarle para ponerlo en el lenguaje audiovisual desde un lugar que tenga sentido y sea coherente con una estructura de dieciséis episodios de una hora cada uno, cómo tomar todos esos elementos y ponerlos.

![](https://letraslibres.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/CADS-EP01-SCN34-00608_R_V4-1024x683.jpg)

Escena de *Cien años de soledad*. Cortesía de Neflix.

A la hora de decidir está siempre la pregunta de qué es esencial contar y cuáles son los personajes que deben contarlo: Úrsula, como uno de los personajes principales, por supuesto el coronel Aureliano Buendía. Personajes que tienen mucho peso en la historia, pero que además están vivos por mucho tiempo, transitan por buena parte de la historia. Tienen mucha fuerza, entonces ponemos en ellos los temas principales.

**En *Cien años de soledad* el manejo del lenguaje tiene un gran peso. En la traducción de la poesía del lenguaje escrito al audiovisual, ¿qué tomaron como brújula?**

Camila Brugés (CB): Ese fue uno de los retos más grandes, aceptar que había un punto en el que la voz de García Márquez en esa novela era intraducible a menos de que usáramos sus propias palabras, porque una de las cosas hermosas es su forma de usar el lenguaje. En lo audiovisual, nosotras podíamos encontrar en la historia, en el arco dramático, en sucesos, cosas muy específicas, pero el reto era emular el tono. Descubrimos muy prontamente que usar el narrador, que usa apartados de la novela verbatim, era la forma más efectiva de lograrlo. A menos que alguien lo diga, el narrador o los personajes, no tenemos cómo escuchar esa voz y darle ese tono. Para nosotras era importante que el resto de la serie –con las herramientas audiovisuales, sonoras, la música, la actuación– capturara un poco de esa poesía, pero usar el narrador fue una brújula para anclarnos a ella.

Y también lo usamos en la construcción de diálogos. Hay pocos diálogos en la novela, pero intentamos mantenerlos, y basarnos en ellos para construir la oralidad de cada uno de los personajes. Además, tomamos partes del narrador de la novela y los pusimos en boca de alguno de los personajes.

![](https://letraslibres.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/CADS-EP01-SCN05-01783_R_V2-1024x709.jpg)

Escena de *Cien años de soledad*. Cortesía de Neflix.

**¿Qué significado tiene para ustedes el realismo mágico y cómo lo acomodaron en la serie?**

NS: El realismo mágico no es un concepto de Gabriel García Márquez, él no dijo “me inventé el realismo mágico y esto es un estilo”. Para nosotras, lo que se ha llamado realismo mágico –y él lo dijo muchas veces– es mucho lo que pertenece a la idiosincrasia de esa zona de donde él es, su abuela era de la Guajira, de una etnia indígena que tiene mucha influencia en esa zona, y muchas de las historias y de los mitos que se contaban, que contaba su abuela, están en la novela. Eran parte de la realidad de estos lugares del Caribe, es decir que no era algo extraordinario ni fantasioso, estaba en la cotidianeidad. Y así es como él lo expone; lo aparentemente extraordinario, como que Remedios la Bella ascienda, o que llegue la peste del insomnio –que de hecho llega con los indígenas guajiros a Macondo–, se ve desde un lugar de normalidad, cotidiano. Para nosotras era muy importante conservar esto, que esa magia, ese mito y esta convivencia con la muerte y con los espíritus fuera parte del mundo. Eso, contrastado con una radiografía muy poderosa de Colombia, la historia de violencia que hemos vivido por años, queríamos que en lo narrativo tuvieran el mismo peso.

![](https://letraslibres.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/CADS-EP03-SCN41-06081_R-1024x683.jpg)

Escena de *Cien años de soledad*. Cortesía de Neflix.

**La temática de *Cien años de soledad* tiene tintes filosóficos: el tiempo mítico, circular, donde el destino de cada individuo parece escrito –¿condenado?– desde mucho antes de nacer. Para ustedes, ¿cuál es el tema de la novela, el núcleo temático que intentaron plasmar en la serie?**

CB: Hay varios temas, pero uno que permea todos los temas y todas las capas es la imposibilidad de cambiar. Esta es una historia que en muchos aspectos nos habla de generaciones que se repiten. Se repiten en su incapacidad de amar, pero se repiten también en cómo los hombres terminan perdidos por sus obsesiones. A diferencia del patriarca que se pierde en obsesiones luminosas, se enloquece pero se ilumina, el resto de sus hijos se pierden en la violencia. Y si la generación del coronel Aureliano Buendía, y su sobrino Arcadio se pierde en la violencia, la siguiente generación vuelve a perderse en obsesiones, esta vez de progreso: hombres obsesivos que traen desgracias, que traen tragedias, que le entregan su vida a esas ideas. Entonces yo creo que es la repetición. La imposibilidad de ver más allá de esas obsesiones, de esos miedos. ~

args.summary:
This is an article from Letras Libres (dated December 4, 2024) featuring an interview with screenwriters Camila Brugés and Natalia Santa about the Netflix adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude). The series, directed by Alex García López and Laura Mora, premiered on December 11, 2024, on Netflix, with two parts of eight episodes each.

Key points from the interview:
- Screenwriter José Rivera first organized the novel's non-linear timeline into a chronological structure, which became the foundation for the adaptation.
- The writers used the novel's own language verbatim through a narrator to preserve García Márquez's poetic voice, as they found it otherwise untranslatable to audiovisual media.
- The "magical realism" is treated not as fantasy but as a reflection of the actual worldview of Colombia's Caribbean region, where myth, death, and spirits coexist with everyday reality.
- The central theme identified is "the impossibility of change" and generational repetition — characters are doomed to repeat the same mistakes (obsessions, violence, misguided progress) across generations.
- Úrsula and Colonel Aureliano Buendía were prioritized as essential characters because they live through much of the story and carry its main themes.

args.summary:
Peninsula Podcast Colombia hosted an episode (released Dec 16, 2024) featuring three screenwriters of the Netflix series "Cien años de soledad" (based on Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize-winning novel), which premiered on December 11, 2024. The screenwriters—Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, and María Camila Arias—discussed the challenges of adapting the novel, which has sold over 50 million copies, been translated into more than 40 languages, and remains culturally relevant 56 years after publication.

Key points from the conversation:
- The adaptation process involved a linear narrative structure (unlike the novel's non-linear timeline), 16 episodes divided into two seasons, and a Colombian writing team that took over from an initial script by Puerto Rican screenwriter José Rivera.
- María Camila Arias created a foundational analysis document that identified key themes, character arcs, and essential elements for the adaptation.
- The writers emphasized the novel's political and historical dimensions—particularly Colombia's recurring cycle of violence and the banana plantation massacre—as central to the series.
- Significant decisions were made regarding sensitive topics: the marriage of Aureliano to the child Remedios was handled with care, making Aureliano's awareness of the problematic nature of the relationship explicit, and adjusting Pilar Ternera's role to avoid complicity in child marriage.
- Female characters, especially Úrsula and Amaranta, were given greater depth and dimension than in the novel, with the writers exploring their motivations and traumas.
- The adaptation process involved extensive research, collaboration with directors, and an "archaeological" approach—finding clues in the novel to reconstruct scenes and dialogue that García Márquez only suggested.
- The writers aimed to create a series that works both for readers of the novel and newcomers who haven't read the book.
- Favorite characters among the writers: Amaranta, Arcadio, and Fernanda del Carpio—with Amaranta noted as a complex, bitter character whose pain the writers came to understand and empathize with.

<webpage_content>
# [La Cuarta CR](/)

# Guionista de 'Cien años de soledad' nos habla sobre Macondo y la herida del amor

### Camila Brugés reflexiona sobre su experiencia en la adaptación de la obra de García Márquez, la soledad como raíz de la violencia y la necesidad de crear historias universales desde la sensibilidad

[La Cuarta CR](https://substack.com/@lacuartacr)

*Por: Jorge Arturo Mora*

Cuando recibió la llamada de Netflix, Camila Brugés dijo que sí “como una loca, porque es una llamada que uno no espera recibir”, recuerda hoy entre risas.

La plataforma la invitaba a un viaje tan descomunal como inevitable: ser parte del equipo de escritura de la adaptación de *Cien años de soledad* para Netflix. Una empresa titánica, destinada al éxito si se tomaban las decisiones correctas (lo cual ocurrió), pero también a las expectativas imposibles.

El resultado, sin embargo, ha sido profundamente gratificante, tanto para la crítica como para el público. Y también para quien escribe estas líneas: una obra redonda, un homenaje visual sólido y conmovedor a una novela fundacional.

Desde la producción se planteó una apuesta arriesgada: narrar la historia de manera cronológica. Fue entonces cuando se convocó a Camila, junto a los guionistas Albatros González, Natalia Santa y María Camila Arias. Todas personas colombianas, todas llamadas a reescribir y traducir desde la entraña una historia que, como pocas, ha atravesado los corazones del mundo entero.

Sobre ese reto monumental, y sobre la pulsión íntima que implicó habitar Macondo desde adentro, Camila Brugés conversó con *La Cuarta CR*. Habló del amor como herida fundacional, del vértigo de escribir sobre un país imposible, y de la necesidad urgente de contar historias que resistan al ruido.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

# **Armar una historia trascendental**

Camila se preguntaba: “¿qué puedo aportar yo a algo tan inmenso?”. Lo dice entre risas y con una humildad palpable desde la pantalla de Zoom, desde Ciudad de México.

Brugés cuenta que su carrera artística comenzó desde el teatro y la danza, mundos que han formado su particular sensibilidad. A lo largo de su carrera ha escrito y dirigido obras de teatro y documentales, como el corto *Niña José*, seleccionado en festivales como Shnit, Bogoshorts y FICSUR en 2018, y fue guionista de la serie documental *Maestros*, dirigida por Sergio Cabrera.

Comenzó escribiendo para Vista Productions/RCN TV y Sony Colombia – Teleset, y ha desarrollado ideas de cine y series para Dynamo Producciones. Fue parte del *writers room* de *Frontera Verde*, serie original de Netflix estrenada en 2019, así como con Exile Content, co-desarrolló la adaptación de la novela *Diez Mujeres* de Marcela Serrano, y fue guionista principal de *Fuentes Humanas*, serie de Amazon Studios.

Ella confirma que su “sensibilidad plástica” fue esencial en la sala de escritores. Asegura que tuvo un lugar desde donde pensar las imágenes y escenas, que ese lugar era su particular sensibilidad. Y también sintió una profunda responsabilidad: “sentí que tenía que corresponder a Colombia, a mi país”.

Pero ese país no es uno solo: “Colombia es muy diversa. No tenemos una identidad unificada, por nuestros acentos, regiones, culturas. El colombiano no es una sola cosa. Pero *Cien años de soledad* nos identifica a todos a través de Macondo. La segunda parte de la novela coincide con eventos históricos del país, lo que también permite esa identificación. Y más allá de Colombia, países como Costa Rica o toda Centroamérica pueden reconocerse en los relatos de las bananeras o en los procesos de colonización presentes en la obra. Macondo es espejo”, afirma la guionista..

Camila afirma que:

> “Hay una verdad que baja Gabo: la imposibilidad del ser humano de amar, porque no entendemos el amor. Lo ponemos en la mirada del otro, en el amor romántico. Y en esa incapacidad de amar nos quedamos solos. En medio de esa soledad y esa confusión, si le agregas el capitalismo con su sistema violento, divisorio y desigual, pues los seres humanos no tenemos cómo actuar si no es desde el lugar más oscuro del espíritu. Porque el sistema nos obliga a alienarnos y a vernos como otros. Eso es la sociedad de hoy. Eso es lo que pasa en Macondo”.

Uno de sus temas preferidos es ese punto de intersección: la incapacidad de amar y cómo de ahí nace toda la oscuridad.

> “La violencia deriva de esa herida. Una familia piensa más en una maldición que en el amor profundo de la pareja original. Úrsula trata fatal a Arcadio, el bastardo, y por esa ausencia de amor él se convierte en un tirano de su propio pueblo. Todo parte desde ese lugar. Ahí está el germen de la novela. Es su mensaje más profundo. Todas las historias, manifiesta o no, están hablando del amor”.

Para ella, las historias se vuelven universales cuando sus personajes contienen luces y sombras, cuando comprendemos sus heridas.

> “Todos tienen heridas profundas que explican comportamientos nefastos. Es la herida del abandono. Aureliano Buendía, el coronel, es un personaje que atraviesa todo: de niño introspectivo a orfebre sensible, a coronel sanguinario que lucha por la justicia y luego ataca a su propio pueblo. Termina como un viejo patético que nadie quiere escuchar. Pero si ves todo ese camino, no podrías juzgarlo. No es un villano. Es un hombre supremamente herido. Por eso es poesía pura”.

Camila cree que todavía se pueden crear obras universales:

> “*Cien años de soledad* es infinita. Si hay escritores que no renuncien, que se pregunten por el lenguaje y la vida, sí se puede. El problema son los lectores. Que no existan. Pero mientras haya quienes resistan, quienes digan: no voy a ceder a la literatura rápida ni a los videos verticales de diez segundos, habrá lugar. Artistas que no piensen sólo en el mercado. Siempre hay que pensar en el fondo de las cosas”.

Y añade con esperanza:

> “Las nuevas generaciones me entusiasman. Están desconectándose. Vuelven a los celulares sin internet. Hay una pulsión por bajar la velocidad. Esa ola viene con esta crisis de salud mental. Reconocer que la velocidad nos tiene sacados de onda. Es un buen signo”.

***Pronto sabremos más***

La serie Cien años de Soledad concluirá con dos temporadas. La producción de la segunda temporada comenzó en febrero de este año. Aún no hay fecha de estreno, pero Camila asegura que está segura que el público quedará satisfecho.

“Queremos cumplir con quienes nos regalan su tiempo para ver esta serie. No puedo adelantar detalles, pero se le ha dotado de ganas y de mucha sensibilidad este tramo final. Para mí, es aún mejor que la primera temporada”, concluye.

args.summary:
This is an interview conducted by La Cuarta CR with Camila Brugés, a Colombian screenwriter who was part of the writing team for Netflix's adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's *Cien años de soledad* (One Hundred Years of Solitude). Brugés, whose background includes theatre, dance, and documentary work (including the short film *Niña José* and the series *Maestros*, *Frontera Verde*, and *Fuentes Humanas*), was recruited alongside fellow Colombian writers Albatros González, Natalia Santa, and María Camila Arias. The adaptation took the risky approach of telling the story chronologically.

Key themes from the interview:

- **Macondo as a universal mirror**: Brugés argues that Macondo reflects not just Colombia's diverse identities but also broader Latin American experiences, including colonial processes and banana republic histories.
- **Love as a foundational wound**: She argues that the novel's deepest message is about humanity's inability to love, which leads to solitude and violence. She points to Úrsula's mistreatment of Arcadio—born from a lack of love—as the seed of his tyranny.
- **Complex characters**: Brugés emphasizes that the novel's universality comes from its characters' deep wounds, which explain even their worst actions. Colonel Aureliano Buendía is not a villain but a deeply wounded man.
- **The possibility of universal art today**: She believes timeless, universal stories can still be created if writers resist market pressures and fast-paced, shallow content. She notes optimism about younger generations seeking slower, more meaningful engagement.
- **Second season**: The series will conclude with two seasons. Production of Season 2 began in February 2025 (no release date yet). Brugés says the second season is even better than the first.
