--- SOURCE 1: 'One Hundred Years of Solitude': How It Was Crafted in Colombia ---
URL: https://variety.com/2025/tv/news/netflix-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-shooting-in-colombia-1236278697

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Netflix's "One Hundred Years of Solitude," the streaming service's most ambitious series in Latin America, injected over $52 million (225 billion Colombian Pesos) into the Colombian economy. The adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize-winning 1967 novel employed approximately 900 Colombian crew members, 150 artisans, thousands of extras, and worked with over 850 suppliers to build the mythical town of Macondo from scratch. Season One generated over 100,000 hotel nights in Ibagué during filming.

Produced by Colombian powerhouse Dynamo ("Narcos," "Echo 3"), the two-part Spanish-language series about the Buendía family utilized the CINA incentive—a 35% tax rebate on location shoot expenses for international projects. Colombia also benefits from the Colombia Film Fund (FFC), providing cash rebates covering 40% of audiovisual services and 20% of logistical costs. The year 2024 is set to break records for Colombian theatrical releases, with 74 local films expected.

The series was led by predominantly Colombian department heads, with 98% of the production team from Colombia. Gabriel García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García, served as executive producers. The author had previously opposed adaptation but mused it could work if done in many hours, in Spanish, and in Colombia.

Building the Macondo set in Tolima involved constructing roads, drainage systems, and electricity across 5,812,506 square feet (133.4 acres). The production faced significant challenges, including filming an exodus across nearly half of Colombia—from the Páramo de Chingaza to mangrove swamps on the Magdalena/La Guajira border.

Female Colombian talent dominated across departments, including co-director Laura Mora, executive producers Carolina Caicedo and Juliana Flórez Luna, and lead actresses Marleydo Soto (as Úrsula) and Susana Morales (as younger Úrsula). The scriptwriting team organized the novel's non-linear narrative chronologically and expanded on implied moments from the text. Season Two is currently filming, also utilizing the CINA incentive.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I believe what we've accomplished here is the ability to distill many of the lessons we've learned from previous projects... If we compare it to our previous projects, we almost always had to bring department heads from abroad... now, to some extent, we've managed to have mostly Colombian department heads. I think for me, that has been one of the most rewarding aspects." - Andrés Calderón, Dynamo co-founder-CEO, "'One Hundred Years' is a testament to what Latin Americans can accomplish when they get together with a single purpose... I would say that 98% of the people who made this show are from Colombia." - Paco Ramos, Netflix VP of Latin American Content, "My father didn't want to have it adapted... he preferred that the book live in the imagination of the reader... But he did sometimes muse that if it could be done in many hours and in Spanish and in Colombia, he would consider it." - Rodrigo García, executive producer and son of Gabriel García Márquez, "We didn't alter the novel's written scenes; instead, we focused on two areas: First, organizing the non-linear narrative... Second, expanding on implied moments... We interpreted these to create scenes and conversations that captured the story's essence and poetic tone." - Camila Brugés, co-writer
</key_excerpts>

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel of the same name. Produced by Netflix and the Colombian production company Dynamo, the series is a Spanish and Wayuu-language drama/magical realism adaptation.

**Key Details:**
- **Seasons/Episodes:** 2 seasons, 15 episodes total (season 1: 8 episodes; season 2: 8 episodes)
- **Release Dates:** Season 1 premiered December 11, 2024. Season 2 Part 1 released August 5, 2026; series finale slated for August 26, 2026.
- **Creators:** Written by José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, Albatrós González, and María Camila Arias. Directed by Alex García López, Laura Mora, and Carlos Moreno.
- **Cast:** Claudio Cataño (Colonel Aureliano Buendía), Diego Vásquez (José Arcadio Buendía), Marleyda Soto (Úrsula Iguarán), Viña Machado (Pilar Ternera), Loren Sofía (Amaranta), Akima (Rebeca), Janer Villarreal (Arcadio), Moreno Borja (Melquíades), Ruggero Pasquarelli (Pietro Crespi), and others.

- Netflix acquired rights in March 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing a feature film was insufficient for proper adaptation.

- Open casting call in 2022; more than 10,000 candidates for 25 main roles. Only 30% were professional actors; 20,000 extras were selected.
- Principal photography for Part 1: May–December 2023. Filmed entirely in Colombia (La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, Tolima). The fictional town of Macondo was built near Alvarado, Tolima by 1,100 workers, with four versions constructed to depict the passage of time.

**Awards:**

The series is a two-part limited series spanning over 16 hours, with Part 1 (8 episodes) premiering December 11 on Netflix. The adaptation was made with the blessing of Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García and Gonzalo García Barcha, who serve as executive producers. Directors Alex García López and Laura Mora helm Part 1.

**Plot:** The story begins in mid-19th century Colombia with forbidden love between cousins José Arcadio Buendía (Marco Antonio González) and Úrsula Iguarán (Susana Morales). After José kills a man for mocking their marriage, the couple flees and eventually founds the village of Macondo. Over generations, the Buendía family grapples with incest, sibling rivalries, illegitimate children, mental illness, self-harm, and political turmoil including Colombia's Thousand Days War.

**Key highlights:**
- Described as "one of the most faithful page-to-screen adaptations in recent years"
- Features cinematography by Paulo Pérez and María Sarasvita, production design by Bárbara Enríquez and Eugenio Caballero
- Notable performances: Marleyda Soto as elder Úrsula, Claudio Cataño as adult Aureliano, Nicole Montenegro and Laura Grueso as Rebeca, Diego Vásquez as older José
- The series is praised for its exquisite detail, layered symbolism, and willingness to let scenes breathe
- Some criticism: pacing is "too lackadaisical at times" and "a bit dense"
- The review notes that the series unpacks every layer of the novel with "wealth of detail and profound eloquence"

It is widely considered one of the most significant novels of the 20th century, chronicling seven generations of the Buendía family in the fictional Colombian town of Macondo. The novel blends magical realism with Colombian history, covering themes of love, war, solitude, and the cyclical nature of time. It has sold over 50 million copies worldwide, been translated into more than 46 languages, and was a major factor in García Márquez winning the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.

The setting is the fictional town of Macondo, isolated in the Colombian jungle, spanning approximately 100 years. Major characters include patriarch José Arcadio Buendía, matriarch Úrsula Iguarán, Colonel Aureliano Buendía, and the mysterious gypsy Melquíades.

Notable facts: García Márquez wrote the novel in 18 months working seven days a week; the novel's style was inspired by his grandmother's storytelling; the town of Macondo is based on his hometown of Aracataca, Colombia. ---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

**1. Rights Acquisition — How Netflix Obtained the Rights**

Netflix acquired the rights to Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude* in March 2019, marking the first-ever screen adaptation of the novel. The deal was negotiated through attorney Shelley Surpin and the Agencia Literaria Carmen Balcells [Source: The Hollywood Reporter, 2019]. 

For decades, García Márquez was reluctant to sell the film rights. According to his son Rodrigo García: "For decades our father was reluctant to sell the film rights to *Cien Años de Soledad* because he believed that it could not be made under the time constraints of a feature film, or that producing it in a language other than Spanish would not do it justice" [Source: Rodrigo García, via multiple outlets including Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Netflix press release, 2019]. 

The novel had long been considered "unadaptable." García Márquez himself was on record doubting that any film could faithfully recreate Macondo's complexity [Source: The Arts Fuse, 2025]. The author was concerned that an adaptation for the screen would reduce the reader's creativity, as they would imagine characters, events, and places in a more personal way (reading the novel) than when presented on the screen, explained Alvaro Santana-Acuna [Source: The Hollywood Reporter, 2019]. García Márquez also believed a screen adaptation would need 100 hours of runtime, filmed in Colombia, entirely in Spanish [Source: The Economist, 2024].

After García Márquez's death in 2014, his widow held to these wishes until 2019 when Netflix acquired the rights from his sons, agreeing to produce it in Colombia in Spanish [Source: The New York Times Magazine, March 2025]. 

Rodrigo García explained why the time was finally right: "But in the current golden age of series, with the level of talented writing and directing, the cinematic quality of content, and the acceptance by worldwide audiences of programs in foreign languages, the time could not be better to bring an adaptation to the extraordinary global viewership that Netflix provides" [Source: Rodrigo García, via multiple outlets, 2019]. 

Rodrigo García further elaborated: "Making it in Spanish with many episodes, significant resources in Colombia, and a team of Latin American talent. I'm thrilled that it's finally been accomplished" [Source: YouTube interview, 2024].

Francisco Ramos, Vice President of Spanish Language Originals for Netflix (later VP of Latin American Content), said: "We are incredibly honored to be entrusted with the first filmed adaptation of *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, a timeless and iconic story from Latin America that we are thrilled to share with the world" [Source: Francisco Ramos, Netflix press release, 2019; also quoted in multiple outlets].

Netflix's VP of Content for Latin America, Francisco 'Paco' Ramos, also noted that the success of foreign-language content like *Roma* and *Narcos* convinced the company that audiences are ready for strong international material [Source: The Cinemaholic, 2019; CNBC, 2019]. 

In securing the rights to the novel, Netflix agreed to several conditions set by the García Márquez family: the mythical town of Macondo would be recreated in Colombia, built by Colombian hands, the series would be filmed in Spanish, and with Colombian actors [Source: Deadline, December 2024; Netflix official press release, 2024; Variety, 2025]. 

**2. García Márquez Family/Estate Involvement**

García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García (a screenwriter and filmmaker) and Gonzalo García Barcha, served as executive producers on the series [Source: multiple outlets including Variety, The Hollywood Reporter, Deadline, Netflix, 2019–2024].

Rodrigo García gave the production team his blessing, telling them: "The only thing I'm going to tell you is don't let the weight of my father's book bring you down. Do your thing, follow your heart, and enjoy it" [Source: YouTube interview, 2024].

Rodrigo García also noted of his father: "My father didn't want to have it adapted... he preferred that the book live in the imagination of the reader... But he did sometimes muse that if it could be done in many hours and in Spanish and in Colombia, he would consider it" [Source: Variety, 2025].

Gonzalo García Barcha noted that his father believed only a soap opera could reflect the novel's scope [Source: Ground News aggregate, citing La Vanguardia, 2024].

The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors [Source: Wikipedia, citing production notes; multiple outlets]. The commitment made with the García Márquez family established that the town of Macondo had to be located in Colombia and built by Colombian hands [Source: Netflix official press release, 2024].

The author's son Rodrigo García supported the adaptation because he believed a series format could better capture the novel's immersive quality of "having experienced 100 years of life" [Source: The New York Times, December 2024].

**3. Budget**

The series' actual budget has never been disclosed [Source: Deadline, December 2024]. However, the series has been described as:
- "Netflix's most expensive production in Latin America" [Source: The Arts Fuse, 2025; The Guardian, December 2024]
- "One of the most ambitious projects in Latin America to date" [Source: Deadline, quoting Netflix, October 2024]
- "The biggest TV project ever out of Colombia" [Source: Deadline, December 2024]
- "A monumental undertaking" [Source: Variety review, 2024]

While the budget itself was not disclosed, Netflix did disclose the economic impact: the series contributed over 225 billion Colombian pesos (approximately $51.8 million USD at the time of reporting, or $52–$53+ million depending on the source) to Colombia's economy. This figure measures the impact on Colombian GDP, including the streamer's direct spending on production plus downstream supply chain spending, but excludes the series' budget itself [Source: Deadline, December 2024; Netflix official press release, 2024; Variety, 2025; Colombia Travel, 2024].

The production utilized the CINA incentive—a 35% tax rebate on location shoot expenses for international projects. Colombia also benefits from the Colombia Film Fund (FFC), providing cash rebates covering 40% of audiovisual services and 20% of logistical costs [Source: Variety, 2025].

**4. Production Timeline**

- **March 2019**: Netflix announces acquisition of rights to adapt *One Hundred Years of Solitude* [Source: multiple outlets].
- **2022**: Open casting call held; more than 10,000 candidates applied for 25 main roles. Only 30% were professional actors. 20,000 extras were selected [Source: Wikipedia, 2024].
- **May–December 2023**: Principal photography for Part 1 took place over approximately nine months, followed by a year of post-production [Source: Wikipedia, 2024; YouTube interview, 2024].
- **February 2025**: Production on Part 2 began [Source: Wikipedia, 2024].
- **December 11, 2024**: Part 1 (Season 1, 8 episodes) premiered on Netflix [Source: multiple outlets].
- **August 5, 2026**: Part 2 first seven episodes premiered on Netflix [Source: Netflix Tudum, May 2026; Rio Times, May 2026].
- **August 26, 2026**: The series finale (a standalone feature-length grand finale episode, described by trade publication Variety as a cinematic, nearly two-hour event) is scheduled to be released [Source: Rio Times, May 2026; Netflix Tudum, May 2026].

The series took more than six years to realize from the 2019 announcement to the 2024 premiere [Source: TIME, December 2024].

The series was filmed entirely in Colombia across the departments of La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, and Tolima [Source: Netflix official press release, 2024]. Filming locations included 22 municipalities [Source: Colombia Travel, 2024].

This Variety article (by John Hopewell) details the extensive location scouting and production design for Netflix's acclaimed adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "One Hundred Years of Solitude," produced by Bogotá-based Dynamo ("Narcos"). The series, directed by Alex García and Laura Mora, was filmed across 32 provinces (departamentos) in Colombia, with the fictional town of Macondo built from scratch rather than found as a single existing location.

Key locations include:
- **Alvarado, Tolima**: The primary Macondo backlot was built on the Arizona ranch, centered around a large caucho cartagénero tree. The real-life Western Andes rise behind, with snow-capped Sierra Nevada peaks added via VFX.
- **Manaure, La Guajira**: The rose-tinted salt flats were used for Rebeca's dramatic arrival (Ep. 2-3), capturing the series' visual aesthetic.
- **Valledupar area**: An old ranchería near the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta was used for José Arcadio and Úrsula's native village (Ep. 1), capturing the Caribbean seaboard's light and climate.
- **Río Ancho, near Dibulla**: The river with "smooth white rocks like prehistoric eggs" (from the novel's famous description) was shot 700 miles north of the main Macondo set.
- **Páramo de Chingaza**: The high mountain moors (13,000 ft peaks) used for the expedition scenes in Ep. 1, where José Arcadio's mule slips into the void.
- **Ciénaga Grande swamp**: A mangrove/river/saltwater mix that was cleaned and prepared for the memorable swamp-crossing scenes.
- **Cuevas del Mohan, Tolima**: A 160-foot waterfall cave used for the night birth scene of José Arcadio.

The article notes that García Márquez's widow Mercedes Barcha and sons insisted the series be shot in Colombia by Colombians. Carolina Caicedo (executive producer) emphasized the need for locations near airports and Bogotá for logistical reasons. The series also serves an industrial agenda to showcase Colombia's production capacity, as the country approved 64 international projects over 2023-24 totaling $249.8 million in investment.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Magical realism (also called magic realism or marvellous realism) is a style of fiction and art that presents a realistic view of the world while incorporating magical elements, often blurring the lines between speculation and reality. It is commonly found in novels and dramatic performances, and is distinguished from fantasy by its use of substantial realistic detail to make a point about reality, rather than separating from it. The term originated in 1925 with German art critic Franz Roh (magischer Realismus) to describe a painterly style known as Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity). It was later applied to literature, particularly Latin American literature, by writers such as Gabriel García Márquez, Isabel Allende, Jorge Luis Borges, Alejo Carpentier, and others. Key characteristics include: fantastical elements in a real-world setting, authorial reticence (withholding explanations of magical events), plenitude (abundance of disorienting detail), hybridity (multiple planes of reality), metafiction, heightened awareness of mystery, and political critique. The genre often mixes history and fantasy, and is seen as a subversive form that challenges socially-dominant forces. Major works include García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) and Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949). Notable authors span multiple languages and cultures, including English (Neil Gaiman, Salman Rushdie, Alice Hoffman), Russian (Mikhail Bulgakov), Japanese (Haruki Murakami), Chinese (Mo Yan), Polish (Olga Tokarczuk), and Bengali (Nabarun Bhattacharya) writers.

This is a dissertation by Cody Lang (PhD, York University, August 2020) analyzing magical realism in transnational cinema. The central argument is that magical realism in film is best understood as a transgeneric critical category rather than a conventional film genre. The project extends literary theory on magical realism into film studies, noting the semiotic differences between literature and cinema while identifying shared aesthetic strategies.

Key sections cover: metafiction (overt and covert forms), representation of historicity, representation of marginalized subjectivities (class, gender, race, sexual identity), and utopian discourses in magical realist cinema. It also discusses the relationship between magical realism, modernism, and postmodernism, noting that magical realism spans both periods.

URL: https://journals.library.ualberta.ca/crcl/index.php/crcl/article/download/29857/21596/78446

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article by Cody Lang, published in the Canadian Review of Comparative Literature (2022), examines the treatment of history and historicity in magical realist cinema. The author argues that the representation of history is a defining characteristic of magical realism, distinguishing it from surrealism and fantasy. The article identifies two primary formal topoi (recurring narrative devices) in magical realist films that engage with historicity:

1. **The Anachronous Community**: Magical realist films frequently depict communities that exist "out of sync" with dominant historical development—geographically, socially, or magically isolated. The article analyzes several films through this lens:
   - **Happy as Lazzaro (2018)** by Alice Rohrwacher - Uses time-travel to dramatize Italian history and the transition from feudalism to modernity, with Biblical imagery coding the characters and settings.
   - **Daughters of the Dust (1992)** by Julie Dash - Set in 1902 on Saint Helena Island, South Carolina, examining Gullah culture through the Peazant family. Uses a ghost from the future (the Unborn Child) to represent historicity at the crossroads of past and future, embodying Carpentier's theory of *lo real maravilloso* (marvelous realism).
   - **Underground (1995)** by Emir Kusturica - A monumental work spanning WWII, the Cold War, and the Yugoslav Wars. Depicts Communist rebels trapped underground unaware that WWII has ended, manipulated by an opportunistic leader. Uses slapstick, carnivalesque imagery, and self-reflexive techniques (including Kusturica casting himself) to critique state-organized historical deception.
   - **Pleasantville (1998)** - Uses magical time-travel into a 1950s TV sitcom world to interrogate nostalgic representations of the past, dramatizing the shift from black-and-white to color as a metaphor for confronting historical repression.

2. **The Witness to Historical Trauma**: A marginalized observer figure tethered to significant historical events. The key example analyzed is **Oskar from The Tin Drum (1979)** by Volker Schlöndorff, adapted from Günter Grass's novel. Oskar, who stops growing at age three, witnesses the Nazi occupation of Danzig (Gdańsk) and represents the irrationality of National Socialism, lacking heroic qualities and being ambivalently complicit with the regime.

The article draws on theorists including Fredric Jameson (on historicity and the political unconscious), Georg Lukács (on historical fiction), Linda Hutcheon (on postmodern historiography), and Wendy B. Faris (on magical realism's characteristics). Lang argues that magical realist cinema continues the tradition of historical fiction but uses magical elements to expand the horizon of historical consciousness and confront secular humanist ideologies inherent in realist forms.
</summary>

"History and historicity are two of the most persistent themes in the magical realist mode. Nearly all definitions of literary magical realism evoke history as essential to explanations of the genre.", "Magical realism, more so than other genres, takes this ground as one of its primary raw materials for narrative creation.", "Magical realist films' most common way of representing history is through stories that depict an anachronous collective space that is out of sync with the dominant culture's historical development.", "Kusturica condemns the Yugoslavian state during the Cold War by implicating himself and the Serbian ethno-state within the process of dealing with this historical period.", "The other formal topos in magical realist films that engage with questions of historicity is the 'witness' to historical trauma, a marginalized observer that is deeply tied to historical conflict."

<summary>
# Summary of The Paris Review: "Gabriel García Márquez, The Art of Fiction No. 69"

This webpage from The Paris Review (Issue 82, Winter 1981) contains a lengthy interview with Nobel Prize-winning author Gabriel García Márquez, conducted by The Paris Review. The interview took place over three late-afternoon sessions at his studio in San Angel Inn, Mexico City, with his two sons assisting with translation.

**Key topics covered in the interview:**

1. **On Journalism vs. Interviewing**: García Márquez expresses discomfort with tape recorders during interviews, noting they make him defensive. As a journalist himself, he never used tape recorders for interviews, preferring long conversations followed by writing from memory. He recounts his famous series about a shipwrecked sailor, published under the sailor's name, which wasn't recognized as his work until after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

2. **Journalism as His True Profession**: He states, "I've always been convinced that my true profession is that of a journalist." He now enjoys being able to choose topics that interest him, having achieved financial independence through novels. He cites John Hersey's *Hiroshima* as an exceptional piece of journalism.

3. **Novel vs. Journalism**: He argues there is no fundamental difference between journalism and fiction: "The sources are the same, the material is the same, the resources and the language are the same." The key difference: "In journalism just one fact that is false prejudices the entire work. In contrast, in fiction one single fact that is true gives legitimacy to the entire work."

4. **Writing Process**: He describes writing much more slowly now than in his newspaper days, sometimes producing only a short paragraph of four or five lines in a good day's work.

5. **Early Influences and Beginnings**: He started by drawing cartoons. Reading Kafka's *The Metamorphosis* was a revelation—"the first line almost knocked me off the bed." He later read Joyce's *Ulysses* and learned the technique of interior monologue. The American Lost Generation writers helped him connect literature to life.

6. **The Bogotazo (April 9, 1948)**: The assassination of political leader Gaitan and the ensuing riots in Bogotá were pivotal. He realized his short stories had nothing to do with the reality of his country.

7. **Return to Aracataca (1950-51)**: Visiting his birthplace with his mother to sell his childhood home was transformative. He felt he was "experiencing it as if I were reading it" and realized everything had literary value. This led to his first novel, *Leaf Storm*.

8. **On Reality vs. Imagination**: He insists that "there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality." The Caribbean reality, he says, "resembles the wildest imagination."

9. **Writing for an Audience**: He writes for specific friends, but after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, he no longer knows who among millions of readers he is writing for, which "upsets and inhibits" him.

The page also includes an interview with Yan Lianke (The Art of Fiction No. 269) about Chinese censorship, rural life, and literary freedom, as well as numerous other contents from Issue 82 and subsequent issues.
</summary>

<summary>
**One Hundred Years of Solitude** (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a 1967 novel by Colombian author Gabriel García Márquez. It is a multi-generational family saga of the Buendía family, whose patriarch José Arcadio Buendía founded the fictional town of Macondo. The novel is a landmark work of magical realism and a key representative of the literary Latin American Boom of the 1960s-70s. It has been translated into 46 languages and sold over 50 million copies. In 2024, it was adapted into a Netflix television series.

**Background:** García Márquez was inspired by his maternal grandparents—his grandfather's accounts of the Thousand Days' War and his grandmother's superstitious beliefs. The English translation by Gregory Rabassa was published in 1970.

**Plot:** The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family. José Arcadio Buendía kills Prudencio Aguilar and flees to found Macondo after a dream of a "city of mirrors." The town experiences gypsy visits, civil war (Aureliano Buendía becomes a revolutionary colonel), technological progress, a banana plantation strike and massacre (based on the 1928 Banana Massacre), and eventual decay. The story ends with the final Buendía, Aureliano Babilonia, deciphering a prophecy that the family is doomed to be wiped from the earth as Macondo is destroyed in a windstorm.

**Major Characters:** The family tree spans seven generations including the patriarch José Arcadio Buendía, matriarch Úrsula Iguarán, Colonel Aureliano Buendía (who fathers 17 sons), Amaranta, Remedios the Beauty, the twins José Arcadio Segundo and Aureliano Segundo, and others. Key themes include subjectivity of reality and magical realism, solitude, fluidity of time, incest, and elitism.

**Relation to Colombian history:** The novel incorporates the Thousand Days' War, the arrival of American banana companies, and the Banana Massacre of 1928.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Emir Kusturica - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_Kusturica

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Emir Kusturica (born 24 November 1954 in Sarajevo) is a Serbian film director, screenwriter, actor, producer, and musician. He has been active since the 1970s and is one of the most acclaimed European filmmakers, having won the Palme d'Or at Cannes twice (for *When Father Was Away on Business* in 1985 and *Underground* in 1995), the Best Director prize at Cannes for *Time of the Gypsies* (1989), a Silver Bear at Berlin for *Arizona Dream* (1993), and a Golden Lion at Venice for *Black Cat, White Cat* (1998). He is also a Commander of the French Ordre des Arts et des Lettres and a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour.

Kusturica grew up in a secular Muslim family in Sarajevo and graduated from the FAMU film school in Prague in 1978. His feature debut *Do You Remember Dolly Bell?* (1981) won the Golden Lion for Best First Work at Venice. His 1995 film *Underground* sparked controversy, with some critics accusing it of pro-Serb propaganda. In the late 1990s, he joined (and later fronted) The No Smoking Orchestra. He has also written five books, including the autobiography *Death is an Unverified Rumour* (2010). Since the mid-2000s, his primary residence has been Drvengrad, a traditional village he built for his film *Life Is a Miracle* in Serbia. He also founded the Küstendorf Film and Music Festival and built Andrićgrad. He has been a UNICEF ambassador since 2002. His political views, including support for Slobodan Milošević-era positions and Vladimir Putin, have been controversial.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Emir Kusturica is a Serbian film director, screenwriter, actor, film producer and musician., He has competed at the Cannes Film Festival on five occasions and won the Palme d'Or twice (for When Father Was Away on Business and Underground), as well as the Best Director prize for Time of the Gypsies., Kusturica has also been recognized for his projects in town-building., Kusturica taught Film Directing at Columbia University's Graduate Film Division., Kusturica became a UNICEF National Ambassador for Serbia in 2002.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Bringing 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' to the Screen ... - Vanity Fair ---
URL: https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/story/bringing-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-to-the-screen

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Vanity Fair article (June 2024 issue) by Silvana Paternostro about Netflix's upcoming adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's masterpiece "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The article covers the novel's history, García Márquez's long resistance to film adaptations, and the details of Netflix's ambitious 16-episode Spanish-language series shot in Colombia.

Key points:
- García Márquez (Gabo) always doubted his novel could be adapted for film, saying it would need 100 hours to tell properly and insisting any adaptation must be in Spanish and shot in Colombia.
- After his death in 2014, his sons Rodrigo and Gonzalo García Barcha gave Netflix the rights, overruling his earlier objections. His widow Mercedes died in 2020.
- Netflix's VP of Latin American content Francisco Ramos championed the project, with the family demanding the series be long enough, in Spanish, and filmed in Colombia.
- Macondo was built near Ibagué in the Andes, designed by Eugenio Caballero (Pan's Labyrinth) and Bárbara Enríquez (Roma).
- The directing is split between Argentine Alex García López (Marvel series) and Colombian Laura Mora (The Kings of the World), with vastly different styles.
- The screenplay is by José Rivera (The Motorcycle Diaries), and the adaptation is linear, closely tied to Colombian history between 1850-1950.
- No major stars are used; the cast includes Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, Marleyda Soto as Úrsula Iguarán, and Diego Vásquez as José Arcadio Buendía.
- The article also explores García Márquez's background, the novel's cultural significance in Colombia and Latin America, and the controversy over the posthumous publication of his unfinished novel "Until August."
- Feminist critiques are noted, particularly regarding García Márquez's portrayal of women and underage characters in his works.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Gabo said to us that once he was dead, we could do whatever we wanted," García Barcha says. "It is the living that have to make decisions.", "I don't want Netflix to tell me what Colonel Aureliano Buendía looks like," says Colombian-born Gustavo Arango. "I've always imagined he looks like my grandfather. As every Colombian has.", "The real magic is Gabo's writing," says Jaime Abello of the Gabo Foundation., "García Márquez wrote an epic about the birth and rebirth of civilization, written from the other side of the world. He is Latin America's Homer," says Colombian writer Carolina Sanín., "That I criticize his portrayal of the women does not mean I don't admire the author or that I dismiss the importance of his work," says Nadia Celis.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: A Film Rumination: Underground, Emir Kusturica (1995) | Science Fiction and Other Suspect Ruminations ---
URL: https://sciencefictionruminations.com/2010/06/27/a-film-rumination-underground-emir-kusturica-1995

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review of Emir Kusturica's 1995 film "Underground" (winner of the Palm d'Or at Cannes 1995), rated 9.5/10 and called a "Masterpiece" by the reviewer Joachim Boaz. The film is a sprawling, madcap cinematic experience that intertwines the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states through the story of two friends who build an underground weapons complex during WWII. One friend remains hidden underground while the other rises through Tito's regime, maintaining the fiction that the war is still ongoing.

The review addresses criticism of Kusturica's interpretation of historical events, particularly accusations of glossing over Serbian atrocities. The reviewer defends the film, arguing that a single film cannot encompass all aspects of a country's history, and that Kusturica's focus on a single family necessarily excludes discussion of some atrocities. The reviewer notes that the film's chilling message may be about how many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, actions that should be understood in context. The film is praised for its impeccable acting, magical realism (a technique rarely used in cinema), spectacular cinematography, and exceptional music. The reviewer describes it as both heart-wrenching and astoundingly funny—a cinematic masterpiece.

The comments section includes a lengthy discussion about the political controversy surrounding Kusturica, including accusations of Serb nationalism, the role of French intellectual Alain Finkelkraut, and the complex nature of ethnicity and nationalism in the former Yugoslavia. The author also discusses Kusturica's other films and the film "Four Friends" by Steve Teisch as a possible template.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Seldom, if ever, have I been so enamored with a movie. Emir Kusturica weaves a poignant, comic, vicious, madcap, sprawling, and physics defying cinematic experience deftly intertwined with the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states.", "The monumental task of embodying the history of a country, the feelings of a people, into an extended family over 60 years cannot and should not include everything.", "Many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, but in the context of the extreme isolation of Tito's regime and WWII these actions are definitely not to be forgiven but perhaps, understood in context to a greater degree.", "Emir is the master of using the technique [magical realism], for example, the glorious Underground wedding scene with the bride connected to the wheeled wooden arm.", "The movie is also heart wrenching (perhaps the symbolism is occasionally heavy handed) while being astoundingly funny — a dichotomy paramount for his message."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: On Underground (Emir Kusturica, 1995) | Brick ---
URL: https://brickmag.com/on-underground-directed-by-emir-kusturica-1995

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an essay by David Bezmozgis, published in *Brick* 108 (Winter 2022), reflecting on Emir Kusturica's 1995 film *Underground* and its connection to a friend, Chris, who died by suicide in April 2020. The author revisits the film after 25 years, prompted by Chris's death. The essay summarizes the film's plot: a love triangle between two friends (Marko and Blacky) and actress Natalija during WWII and post-war Yugoslavia. Marko deceives Blacky into living in a cellar for 20 years, believing the war continues, while Marko becomes a hero under Tito. The author reflects on Chris's resemblance to the character Blacky in exuberance and charisma, and learns that Chris had suffered business failure, illness, and psychiatric hospitalization before his death. The essay concludes with the film's final scene where the dead are brought back to life, suggesting a fantasy that art could have saved him.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"If history is either tragedy or farce, Kusturica chooses farce without denying the tragedy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Adapting One Hundred Years of Solitude Sounded Impossible. It Wasn’t. ---
URL: https://www.theatlantic.com/culture/archive/2024/12/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-netflix-review/680972

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from The Atlantic, written by Shirley Li, reviews Netflix's 16-episode adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's novel "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The first half of the series is now streaming. García Márquez, who died in 2014, had long claimed the book was impossible to adapt to film, believing it was "written against the cinema" and insisting it would need to be told in Spanish over 100 hours. Netflix's version, filmed in Colombia and told in Spanish, has the blessing of the author's sons.

The adaptation focuses on the Buendía family and the mythical town of Macondo, tweaking the novel's chronology for a more linear storytelling approach. Li praises the series for successfully conveying the same emotional impact as the book, particularly through its visual representation of magical realism. The camerawork, production design, and score all work to create a dreamlike quality that mirrors the novel's style. While noting that some of García Márquez's prose cannot be fully captured on screen, Li concludes that the series rejects literal translation in favor of an evocative one, creating a "spellbinding effect" of its own.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Netflix's 16-episode take, the first half of which is now streaming, isn't 100 hours long, but it is a superb translation anyway—as haunting and wondrous as García Márquez's readers would hope for it to be., Netflix's Solitude succeeds because it conveys the same sense of revelation the book does., Most impressive is how the series visually captures García Márquez's style of 'magical realism.', Writing is a hypnotic act, García Márquez once said.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: How Laura Mora adapted 'One Hundred Years of Solitude' ... ---
URL: https://monocle.com/culture/one-hundred-years-of-solitude-show

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Monocle (published August 2, 2026) features an interview with Colombian filmmaker Laura Mora about her work adapting Gabriel García Márquez's classic novel *One Hundred Years of Solitude* for Netflix. Mora directed three of eight episodes in season one (released 2024) and serves as showrunner for season two, which drops seven episodes on August 5, 2026, followed by a two-hour finale on August 26, 2026.

Mora emphasizes shifting the adaptation's focus from magical realism to the novel's political and historical dimensions. Key points include:
- She insisted on directing the arrival of the banana company, the American presence, and the 1928 massacre of banana workers by the Colombian military—events that García Márquez helped bring to light.
- The seven-year rain that follows the massacre in the novel symbolizes Colombia's tendency to erase memories of violence.
- She required the cast and crew to take history lessons about the massacre.
- Scenes were shot in real locations (banana company, country club, American residences) at her request.
- Mora notes that Latin American audiences relate to the novel differently than European or Anglo-Saxon audiences, seeing it as more than just fantasy.
- She comments on the timing of season two's release, which coincides with the inauguration of right-wing Colombian president Abelardo de la Espriella, expressing hope that the series will spark political conversations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We are so attached to magic realism that we look away from the political side of the book. I told Netflix that if I was going to be involved, I had to direct the arrival of the banana company, the Americans and the massacre of the workers.", "I wanted to show that the rain that lasts for seven years right after was meant to erase the memory of that violence, as we Colombians have always done.", "We are entering a new right-wing government and we hope that this second part gives some enlightenment to our political future. We are going back to the language of violence with our opponents. And we already know what happens.", "The yellow butterflies come with a character that goes through a very tragic social event. This is not only about a fantastic world. This is a beautiful and poetic way of telling something that is hard and that happens to us here."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: News That Netflix Will Adapt One Hundred Years of ... ---
URL: https://www.latinorebels.com/2019/03/08/100yearsnetflix

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On March 6, 2019 (what would have been Gabriel García Márquez's 92nd birthday), Netflix announced it had acquired the rights to adapt his masterpiece "One Hundred Years of Solitude" into a series. The news received mixed reactions from fans, with many expressing both excitement and concern about how the beloved novel will be translated to screen. The book, first published in 1967 and translated into 46 languages, will be adapted for the screen for the first time. García Márquez had previously opposed adaptations, famously rejecting a $1 million offer from Anthony Quinn in 1982, and later jokingly suggesting to Harvey Weinstein that a film adaptation should release one two-minute chapter per year for 100 years. However, García Márquez's sons, Rodrigo García Barcha and Gonzalo García Barcha, negotiated with Netflix and will serve as executive producers. The series will be produced entirely in Spanish and filmed partially in Colombia. Key concerns from fans include: honoring Gabo's legacy, casting primarily Latin American actors (avoiding stars like Antonio Banderas, Javier Bardem, or Penélope Cruz), and how the series will depict sensitive scenes such as the 1928 United Fruit Company massacre, which is a climactic passage in the novel. The article includes a lengthy excerpt from the book describing the massacre's aftermath from the perspective of José Arcadio Segundo.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"I don't think I want to see #Cienaños on Netflix when it comes out. Have read that book so many times that how I view it my head will always been how I interpret it. But at the same time, what if the series becomes a global phenomenon? What a dilemma." — Julio Ricardo Varela, "Now is a good time for series, and with Netflix's reach —of course— I think the work, the author, Colombia and the world of Macondo will reach a larger audience." — Rodrigo García Barcha (García Márquez's son), "Anthony Quinn, with or without his million dollars, will never be Coronel Aureliano Buendía to me or my readers." — Gabriel García Márquez (1982 column), "I would love to see it. Netflix has to do this well, otherwise, they will be sorry, I think. This is a universally loved book. And no Banderas or Bardem, please. No Penelope Cruz as Remedios La Bella either. Let's get primarily Latin Americans to play these characters." — Pilar Marrero

--- SOURCE 9: One Hundred Years of Solitude (TV series) ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Hundred_Years_of_Solitude_(TV_series)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**One Hundred Years of Solitude (TV Series) – Wikipedia Summary**

*One Hundred Years of Solitude* (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel of the same name. Produced by Netflix and the Colombian production company Dynamo, the series is a Spanish and Wayuu-language drama/magical realism adaptation.

**Key Details:**
- **Seasons/Episodes:** 2 seasons, 15 episodes total (season 1: 8 episodes; season 2: 8 episodes)
- **Release Dates:** Season 1 premiered December 11, 2024. Season 2 Part 1 released August 5, 2026; series finale slated for August 26, 2026.
- **Creators:** Written by José Rivera, Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, Albatrós González, and María Camila Arias. Directed by Alex García López, Laura Mora, and Carlos Moreno.
- **Cast:** Claudio Cataño (Colonel Aureliano Buendía), Diego Vásquez (José Arcadio Buendía), Marleyda Soto (Úrsula Iguarán), Viña Machado (Pilar Ternera), Loren Sofía (Amaranta), Akima (Rebeca), Janer Villarreal (Arcadio), Moreno Borja (Melquíades), Ruggero Pasquarelli (Pietro Crespi), and others.

**Production:**
- Netflix acquired rights in March 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing a feature film was insufficient for proper adaptation.
- Filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, with Colombian actors.
- Open casting call in 2022; more than 10,000 candidates for 25 main roles. Only 30% were professional actors; 20,000 extras were selected.
- Principal photography for Part 1: May–December 2023. Filmed entirely in Colombia (La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, Tolima). The fictional town of Macondo was built near Alvarado, Tolima by 1,100 workers, with four versions constructed to depict the passage of time.
- Production generated 225 billion COP ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy.
- Production on Part 2 began in February 2025.

**Reception:**
- Rotten Tomatoes: 83% positive from 30 critics (avg. 7.9/10). Consensus: "faithfully realizes García Márquez's seminal novel with sumptuous polish."
- Metacritic: 80/100 ("generally favorable").
- Critical praise for faithfulness to source material, performances (especially Soto and Cataño), cinematography, production design, and direction. Some criticism of pacing and literal translation of novelistic content.

**Awards:**
- Won Best Ibero-American Miniseries or TV Series at the 2025 Platino Awards.
- Claudio Cataño won Best Actor and Jairo Camargo won Best Supporting Actor at the Platino Awards.
- Multiple wins at Premios India Catalina 2025 including Best Fiction Series, Best Leading Actor/Actress, Best Supporting Actor/Actress, and Best Fiction Script.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"One Hundred Years of Solitude faithfully realizes Gabriel García Márquez's seminal novel with sumptuous polish, making for an adaptation that is nothing short of magical." — Rotten Tomatoes consensus, "As a filmmaker, as a Colombian, it has been an honor and an enormous challenge to work on a project of the complexity and responsibility of One Hundred Years of Solitude..." — Director Laura Mora, "The series was filmed with the support of García Márquez's family, who requested that it be shot in Colombia, in Spanish, and with Colombian actors." — Production notes, "Considering the difficulty of the assignment, it's remarkable how close Netflix's splendid One Hundred Years of Solitude comes to recreating not just the substance, but also the kinetic spirit of the book." — Judy Berman, Time, "Netflix reported that series' production generated 225 billion COP ($51.8 million USD) for Colombia's economy."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: Cinco años, 18 versiones y una novela que “no se agota en una lectura”: así trabajaron las guionistas de ‘Cien años de soledad’ - Infobae ---
URL: https://www.infobae.com/cultura/2026/08/06/cinco-anos-18-versiones-y-una-novela-que-no-se-agota-en-una-lectura-asi-trabajaron-las-guionistas-de-cien-anos-de-soledad

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Infobae article reports on an interview with Colombian screenwriters Natalia Santa and Camila Brugés, who adapted Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude) for Netflix. The writers spent over five years working on the adaptation, which many considered impossible to translate to screen. The second part of the series was recently released with seven episodes covering the decline of the Buendía lineage and the fall of Macondo, with a feature-length finale scheduled for August 26.

The screenwriters emphasized their commitment to fidelity—a "very faithful adaptation" that translates the novel to audiovisual language rather than reinterpreting it freely. They noted that breaking down the novel revealed its darkness: psychological depth, complex family relationships, and political dimensions. Both writers expressed renewed respect for García Márquez, describing the work as "tejed" (woven) such that each reading reveals new layers and symbols.

Regarding the female perspective, Santa stated the team added nothing to García Márquez but made contemporary decisions about how to represent uncomfortable elements like child marriage and violence. Brugés noted that being women influenced which elements were included or excluded, though the series lacks an "explicitly feminine perspective." The writing process involved 18 versions of each script, and the writers acknowledged that screenwriting is only the first stage of a collective creation that continues through filming and editing.

Following the first season's release in December 2024, Colombian publishers reported a 300% increase in novel sales. Brugés expressed hope that the series could serve as a gateway for viewers who might never read the book.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Nos pidieron una adaptación muy fiel. Entonces ya no es percibir el libro desde tu propia lectura, no es tomar una fracción y transformarla. Es traducir todo a otro lenguaje, intentando mantener la fidelidad y haciendo honor a una obra que ya sabemos lo que representa en Colombia y en Latinoamérica" — Natalia Santa, "Al desglosar la novela te das cuenta de lo oscura que es. No es que uno pensara que Gabo era ligero, pero siento que se me había olvidado lo denso que es, en muchas capas: a nivel psicológico de los personajes, de las relaciones familiares, de lo político" — Camila Brugés, "En la versión 18 de cada guion, ya te quieres ir" — Camila Brugés, "Si asumimos que va a haber mucha gente que nunca va a llegar al libro, quizás podamos ser una puerta" — Camila Brugés
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: “El tema de ‘Cien años de soledad’ es la repetición”. Entrevista a Camila Brugés y Natalia Santa | Letras Libres ---
URL: https://letraslibres.com/entrevistas/paulina-barros-entrevista-bruges-santa-cien-anos-de-soledad-serie

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an article from Letras Libres (dated December 4, 2024) featuring an interview with screenwriters Camila Brugés and Natalia Santa about the Netflix adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's "Cien años de soledad" (One Hundred Years of Solitude). The series, directed by Alex García López and Laura Mora, premiered on December 11, 2024, on Netflix, with two parts of eight episodes each.

Key points from the interview:
- Screenwriter José Rivera first organized the novel's non-linear timeline into a chronological structure, which became the foundation for the adaptation.
- The writers used the novel's own language verbatim through a narrator to preserve García Márquez's poetic voice, as they found it otherwise untranslatable to audiovisual media.
- The "magical realism" is treated not as fantasy but as a reflection of the actual worldview of Colombia's Caribbean region, where myth, death, and spirits coexist with everyday reality.
- The central theme identified is "the impossibility of change" and generational repetition — characters are doomed to repeat the same mistakes (obsessions, violence, misguided progress) across generations.
- Úrsula and Colonel Aureliano Buendía were prioritized as essential characters because they live through much of the story and carry its main themes.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Camila Brugés: "Ese fue uno de los retos más grandes, aceptar que había un punto en el que la voz de García Márquez en esa novela era intraducible a menos de que usáramos sus propias palabras..." , Natalia Santa: "El realismo mágico no es un concepto de Gabriel García Márquez... lo que se ha llamado realismo mágico... es mucho lo que pertenece a la idiosincrasia de esa zona de donde él es..." , Camila Brugés: "Hay varios temas, pero uno que permea todos los temas y todas las capas es la imposibilidad de cambiar. Esta es una historia que en muchos aspectos nos habla de generaciones que se repiten." , "Si no alcanza los vuelos metafóricos y poéticos de la novela es, quizá, porque no es su intención. La televisión pone el acento en brindar entretenimiento..." , "La serie se sostiene por su propio pie."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 12: Cien años de soledad - El desafío de adaptar una obra maestra | PENGUIN PODCAST COLOMBIA ---
URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mdJ3Eot4cGM

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Peninsula Podcast Colombia hosted an episode (released Dec 16, 2024) featuring three screenwriters of the Netflix series "Cien años de soledad" (based on Gabriel García Márquez's Nobel Prize-winning novel), which premiered on December 11, 2024. The screenwriters—Natalia Santa, Camila Brugés, and María Camila Arias—discussed the challenges of adapting the novel, which has sold over 50 million copies, been translated into more than 40 languages, and remains culturally relevant 56 years after publication.

Key points from the conversation:
- The adaptation process involved a linear narrative structure (unlike the novel's non-linear timeline), 16 episodes divided into two seasons, and a Colombian writing team that took over from an initial script by Puerto Rican screenwriter José Rivera.
- María Camila Arias created a foundational analysis document that identified key themes, character arcs, and essential elements for the adaptation.
- The writers emphasized the novel's political and historical dimensions—particularly Colombia's recurring cycle of violence and the banana plantation massacre—as central to the series.
- Significant decisions were made regarding sensitive topics: the marriage of Aureliano to the child Remedios was handled with care, making Aureliano's awareness of the problematic nature of the relationship explicit, and adjusting Pilar Ternera's role to avoid complicity in child marriage.
- Female characters, especially Úrsula and Amaranta, were given greater depth and dimension than in the novel, with the writers exploring their motivations and traumas.
- The adaptation process involved extensive research, collaboration with directors, and an "archaeological" approach—finding clues in the novel to reconstruct scenes and dialogue that García Márquez only suggested.
- The writers aimed to create a series that works both for readers of the novel and newcomers who haven't read the book.
- Favorite characters among the writers: Amaranta, Arcadio, and Fernanda del Carpio—with Amaranta noted as a complex, bitter character whose pain the writers came to understand and empathize with.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Cien años de soledad is the most important work of Colombia, but I think also of the world. 56 years after its publication, it has sold more than 50 million copies and has been translated into more than 40 languages.", "We wanted to give force and space and greater dimension to characters like Úrsula, who became a central character throughout the entire season.", "When you put it on screen—a man marrying a 9-year-old girl—you can't make it look good. We were terrified about how to make Aureliano not come across as a pedophile, because he is a man of his time, inscribed in a culture.", "We didn't want to clean the novel or make it politically correct. We wanted it to be what it was, but to be conscious of what we were saying with this.", "The process of being able to read this novel and discuss it among ourselves endlessly—no one can take that away from us."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 13: Cien años de soledad (serie de televisión) - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cien_a%C3%B1os_de_soledad_(serie_de_televisi%C3%B3n)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
"Cien años de soledad" is a Colombian television series based on Gabriel García Márquez's 1967 novel of the same name. Directed by Alex García López and Laura Mora, produced by Dynamo and distributed by Netflix, the series stars Claudio Cataño, Marco González, Susana Morales, and others. The series premiered on December 11, 2024, with an 8-episode first season; a second season is planned.

**Synopsis:** The story follows cousins José Arcadio Buendía and Úrsula Iguarán who, after marrying against their parents' wishes, leave their village and found the utopian town of Macondo. The series traces multiple generations of the Buendía family, haunted by madness, impossible loves, a bloody war, and a curse of one hundred years of solitude.

**Production:** Netflix acquired rights in 2019. García Márquez had previously refused to sell film rights, believing film couldn't capture the novel. Filmed entirely in Colombia (La Guajira, Magdalena, Cesar, Cundinamarca, Tolima) from May to December 2023, with Macondo constructed near Ibagué. Four versions of the town were built to show the passage of time. Over 10,000 candidates auditioned for 25 main roles; only 30% of the cast are professional actors. The production employed nearly 600 crew members, all Colombian, and generated 225 billion COP ($51.8 million) for Colombia's economy.

**Critical Reception:** The series received strong reviews. On Rotten Tomatoes, 94% of 16 critic reviews are positive (average 8.6/10). Metacritic score is 79/100, indicating "generally favorable" reviews. Critics praised the faithful adaptation, performances (especially Marleyda Soto and Claudio Cataño), cinematography, and production design, though some noted pacing issues and challenges translating magical realism to screen.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 12: Magical realism - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magical_realism

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Magical realism (also called magic realism or marvellous realism) is a style of fiction and art that presents a realistic view of the world while incorporating magical elements, often blurring the lines between speculation and reality. It is commonly found in novels and dramatic performances, and is distinguished from fantasy by its use of substantial realistic detail to make a point about reality, rather than separating from it. The term originated in 1925 with German art critic Franz Roh (magischer Realismus) to describe a painterly style known as Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity). It was later applied to literature, particularly Latin American literature, by writers such as Gabriel García Márquez, Isabel Allende, Jorge Luis Borges, Alejo Carpentier, and others. Key characteristics include: fantastical elements in a real-world setting, authorial reticence (withholding explanations of magical events), plenitude (abundance of disorienting detail), hybridity (multiple planes of reality), metafiction, heightened awareness of mystery, and political critique. The genre often mixes history and fantasy, and is seen as a subversive form that challenges socially-dominant forces. Major works include García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967) and Carpentier's The Kingdom of This World (1949). Notable authors span multiple languages and cultures, including English (Neil Gaiman, Salman Rushdie, Alice Hoffman), Russian (Mikhail Bulgakov), Japanese (Haruki Murakami), Chinese (Mo Yan), Polish (Olga Tokarczuk), and Bengali (Nabarun Bhattacharya) writers.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This academic article by Cody Lang, published in the Canadian Review of Comparative Literature (2022), examines the treatment of history and historicity in magical realist cinema. The author argues that the representation of history is a defining characteristic of magical realism, distinguishing it from surrealism and fantasy. The article identifies two primary formal topoi (recurring narrative devices) in magical realist films that engage with historicity:

1. **The Anachronous Community**: Magical realist films frequently depict communities that exist "out of sync" with dominant historical development—geographically, socially, or magically isolated. The article analyzes several films through this lens:
   - **Happy as Lazzaro (2018)** by Alice Rohrwacher - Uses time-travel to dramatize Italian history and the transition from feudalism to modernity, with Biblical imagery coding the characters and settings.
   - **Daughters of the Dust (1992)** by Julie Dash - Set in 1902 on Saint Helena Island, South Carolina, examining Gullah culture through the Peazant family. Uses a ghost from the future (the Unborn Child) to represent historicity at the crossroads of past and future, embodying Carpentier's theory of *lo real maravilloso* (marvelous realism).
   - **Underground (1995)** by Emir Kusturica - A monumental work spanning WWII, the Cold War, and the Yugoslav Wars. Depicts Communist rebels trapped underground unaware that WWII has ended, manipulated by an opportunistic leader. Uses slapstick, carnivalesque imagery, and self-reflexive techniques (including Kusturica casting himself) to critique state-organized historical deception.
   - **Pleasantville (1998)** - Uses magical time-travel into a 1950s TV sitcom world to interrogate nostalgic representations of the past, dramatizing the shift from black-and-white to color as a metaphor for confronting historical repression.

2. **The Witness to Historical Trauma**: A marginalized observer figure tethered to significant historical events. The key example analyzed is **Oskar from The Tin Drum (1979)** by Volker Schlöndorff, adapted from Günter Grass's novel. Oskar, who stops growing at age three, witnesses the Nazi occupation of Danzig (Gdańsk) and represents the irrationality of National Socialism, lacking heroic qualities and being ambivalently complicit with the regime.

The article draws on theorists including Fredric Jameson (on historicity and the political unconscious), Georg Lukács (on historical fiction), Linda Hutcheon (on postmodern historiography), and Wendy B. Faris (on magical realism's characteristics). Lang argues that magical realist cinema continues the tradition of historical fiction but uses magical elements to expand the horizon of historical consciousness and confront secular humanist ideologies inherent in realist forms.
</summary>

# Summary of The Paris Review: "Gabriel García Márquez, The Art of Fiction No. 69"

This webpage from The Paris Review (Issue 82, Winter 1981) contains a lengthy interview with Nobel Prize-winning author Gabriel García Márquez, conducted by The Paris Review. The interview took place over three late-afternoon sessions at his studio in San Angel Inn, Mexico City, with his two sons assisting with translation.

**Key topics covered in the interview:**

1. **On Journalism vs. Interviewing**: García Márquez expresses discomfort with tape recorders during interviews, noting they make him defensive. As a journalist himself, he never used tape recorders for interviews, preferring long conversations followed by writing from memory. He recounts his famous series about a shipwrecked sailor, published under the sailor's name, which wasn't recognized as his work until after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*.

2. **Journalism as His True Profession**: He states, "I've always been convinced that my true profession is that of a journalist." He now enjoys being able to choose topics that interest him, having achieved financial independence through novels. He cites John Hersey's *Hiroshima* as an exceptional piece of journalism.

3. **Novel vs. Journalism**: He argues there is no fundamental difference between journalism and fiction: "The sources are the same, the material is the same, the resources and the language are the same." The key difference: "In journalism just one fact that is false prejudices the entire work. In contrast, in fiction one single fact that is true gives legitimacy to the entire work."

4. **Writing Process**: He describes writing much more slowly now than in his newspaper days, sometimes producing only a short paragraph of four or five lines in a good day's work.

5. **Early Influences and Beginnings**: He started by drawing cartoons. Reading Kafka's *The Metamorphosis* was a revelation—"the first line almost knocked me off the bed." He later read Joyce's *Ulysses* and learned the technique of interior monologue. The American Lost Generation writers helped him connect literature to life.

6. **The Bogotazo (April 9, 1948)**: The assassination of political leader Gaitan and the ensuing riots in Bogotá were pivotal. He realized his short stories had nothing to do with the reality of his country.

7. **Return to Aracataca (1950-51)**: Visiting his birthplace with his mother to sell his childhood home was transformative. He felt he was "experiencing it as if I were reading it" and realized everything had literary value. This led to his first novel, *Leaf Storm*.

8. **On Reality vs. Imagination**: He insists that "there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality." The Caribbean reality, he says, "resembles the wildest imagination."

9. **Writing for an Audience**: He writes for specific friends, but after *One Hundred Years of Solitude*, he no longer knows who among millions of readers he is writing for, which "upsets and inhibits" him.

The page also includes an interview with Yan Lianke (The Art of Fiction No. 269) about Chinese censorship, rural life, and literary freedom, as well as numerous other contents from Issue 82 and subsequent issues.
</summary>

**One Hundred Years of Solitude** (Spanish: *Cien años de soledad*) is a 1967 novel by Colombian author Gabriel García Márquez. It is a multi-generational family saga of the Buendía family, whose patriarch José Arcadio Buendía founded the fictional town of Macondo. The novel is a landmark work of magical realism and a key representative of the literary Latin American Boom of the 1960s-70s. It has been translated into 46 languages and sold over 50 million copies. In 2024, it was adapted into a Netflix television series.

**Background:** García Márquez was inspired by his maternal grandparents—his grandfather's accounts of the Thousand Days' War and his grandmother's superstitious beliefs. The English translation by Gregory Rabassa was published in 1970.

**Plot:** The novel follows seven generations of the Buendía family. José Arcadio Buendía kills Prudencio Aguilar and flees to found Macondo after a dream of a "city of mirrors." The town experiences gypsy visits, civil war (Aureliano Buendía becomes a revolutionary colonel), technological progress, a banana plantation strike and massacre (based on the 1928 Banana Massacre), and eventual decay. The story ends with the final Buendía, Aureliano Babilonia, deciphering a prophecy that the family is doomed to be wiped from the earth as Macondo is destroyed in a windstorm.

**Major Characters:** The family tree spans seven generations including the patriarch José Arcadio Buendía, matriarch Úrsula Iguarán, Colonel Aureliano Buendía (who fathers 17 sons), Amaranta, Remedios the Beauty, the twins José Arcadio Segundo and Aureliano Segundo, and others. Key themes include subjectivity of reality and magical realism, solitude, fluidity of time, incest, and elitism.

**Relation to Colombian history:** The novel incorporates the Thousand Days' War, the arrival of American banana companies, and the Banana Massacre of 1928.
</summary>

The novel is often cited as one of the supreme achievements in world literature, The magical realist style and thematic substance of the book established it as an important representative novel of the literary Latin American Boom of the 1960s and 1970s, The novel, considered García Márquez's magnum opus, remains widely acclaimed and is recognized as one of the most significant works both in the Hispanic literary canon and in world literature, García Márquez famously praised Rabassa's work, stating that he preferred the English translation to his original Spanish text, The book has been translated into 46 languages and sold more than 50 million copies

--- SOURCE 1: Emir Kusturica - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emir_Kusturica

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Emir Kusturica (born 24 November 1954 in Sarajevo) is a Serbian film director, screenwriter, actor, producer, and musician. He has been active since the 1970s and is one of the most acclaimed European filmmakers, having won the Palme d'Or at Cannes twice (for *When Father Was Away on Business* in 1985 and *Underground* in 1995), the Best Director prize at Cannes for *Time of the Gypsies* (1989), a Silver Bear at Berlin for *Arizona Dream* (1993), and a Golden Lion at Venice for *Black Cat, White Cat* (1998). He is also a Commander of the French Ordre des Arts et des Lettres and a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour.

Kusturica grew up in a secular Muslim family in Sarajevo and graduated from the FAMU film school in Prague in 1978. His feature debut *Do You Remember Dolly Bell?* (1981) won the Golden Lion for Best First Work at Venice. His 1995 film *Underground* sparked controversy, with some critics accusing it of pro-Serb propaganda. In the late 1990s, he joined (and later fronted) The No Smoking Orchestra. He has also written five books, including the autobiography *Death is an Unverified Rumour* (2010). Since the mid-2000s, his primary residence has been Drvengrad, a traditional village he built for his film *Life Is a Miracle* in Serbia. He also founded the Küstendorf Film and Music Festival and built Andrićgrad. He has been a UNICEF ambassador since 2002. His political views, including support for Slobodan Milošević-era positions and Vladimir Putin, have been controversial.
</summary>

URL: https://www.vanityfair.com/hollywood/story/bringing-one-hundred-years-of-solitude-to-the-screen

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Vanity Fair article (June 2024 issue) by Silvana Paternostro about Netflix's upcoming adaptation of Gabriel García Márquez's masterpiece "One Hundred Years of Solitude." The article covers the novel's history, García Márquez's long resistance to film adaptations, and the details of Netflix's ambitious 16-episode Spanish-language series shot in Colombia.

Key points:
- García Márquez (Gabo) always doubted his novel could be adapted for film, saying it would need 100 hours to tell properly and insisting any adaptation must be in Spanish and shot in Colombia.
- After his death in 2014, his sons Rodrigo and Gonzalo García Barcha gave Netflix the rights, overruling his earlier objections. His widow Mercedes died in 2020.
- Netflix's VP of Latin American content Francisco Ramos championed the project, with the family demanding the series be long enough, in Spanish, and filmed in Colombia.
- Macondo was built near Ibagué in the Andes, designed by Eugenio Caballero (Pan's Labyrinth) and Bárbara Enríquez (Roma).
- The directing is split between Argentine Alex García López (Marvel series) and Colombian Laura Mora (The Kings of the World), with vastly different styles.
- The screenplay is by José Rivera (The Motorcycle Diaries), and the adaptation is linear, closely tied to Colombian history between 1850-1950.
- No major stars are used; the cast includes Claudio Cataño as Colonel Aureliano Buendía, Marleyda Soto as Úrsula Iguarán, and Diego Vásquez as José Arcadio Buendía.
- The article also explores García Márquez's background, the novel's cultural significance in Colombia and Latin America, and the controversy over the posthumous publication of his unfinished novel "Until August."
- Feminist critiques are noted, particularly regarding García Márquez's portrayal of women and underage characters in his works.
</summary>

"Gabo said to us that once he was dead, we could do whatever we wanted," García Barcha says. "It is the living that have to make decisions.", "I don't want Netflix to tell me what Colonel Aureliano Buendía looks like," says Colombian-born Gustavo Arango. "I've always imagined he looks like my grandfather. As every Colombian has.", "The real magic is Gabo's writing," says Jaime Abello of the Gabo Foundation., "García Márquez wrote an epic about the birth and rebirth of civilization, written from the other side of the world. He is Latin America's Homer," says Colombian writer Carolina Sanín., "That I criticize his portrayal of the women does not mean I don't admire the author or that I dismiss the importance of his work," says Nadia Celis.

--- SOURCE 3: A Film Rumination: Underground, Emir Kusturica (1995) | Science Fiction and Other Suspect Ruminations ---
URL: https://sciencefictionruminations.com/2010/06/27/a-film-rumination-underground-emir-kusturica-1995

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a review of Emir Kusturica's 1995 film "Underground" (winner of the Palm d'Or at Cannes 1995), rated 9.5/10 and called a "Masterpiece" by the reviewer Joachim Boaz. The film is a sprawling, madcap cinematic experience that intertwines the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states through the story of two friends who build an underground weapons complex during WWII. One friend remains hidden underground while the other rises through Tito's regime, maintaining the fiction that the war is still ongoing.

The review addresses criticism of Kusturica's interpretation of historical events, particularly accusations of glossing over Serbian atrocities. The reviewer defends the film, arguing that a single film cannot encompass all aspects of a country's history, and that Kusturica's focus on a single family necessarily excludes discussion of some atrocities. The reviewer notes that the film's chilling message may be about how many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, actions that should be understood in context. The film is praised for its impeccable acting, magical realism (a technique rarely used in cinema), spectacular cinematography, and exceptional music. The reviewer describes it as both heart-wrenching and astoundingly funny—a cinematic masterpiece.

The comments section includes a lengthy discussion about the political controversy surrounding Kusturica, including accusations of Serb nationalism, the role of French intellectual Alain Finkelkraut, and the complex nature of ethnicity and nationalism in the former Yugoslavia. The author also discusses Kusturica's other films and the film "Four Friends" by Steve Teisch as a possible template.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Seldom, if ever, have I been so enamored with a movie. Emir Kusturica weaves a poignant, comic, vicious, madcap, sprawling, and physics defying cinematic experience deftly intertwined with the history of Yugoslavia and its successor states.", "The monumental task of embodying the history of a country, the feelings of a people, into an extended family over 60 years cannot and should not include everything.", "Many people in Yugoslavia were misguided, but in the context of the extreme isolation of Tito's regime and WWII these actions are definitely not to be forgiven but perhaps, understood in context to a greater degree.", "Emir is the master of using the technique [magical realism], for example, the glorious Underground wedding scene with the bride connected to the wheeled wooden arm.", "The movie is also heart wrenching (perhaps the symbolism is occasionally heavy handed) while being astoundingly funny — a dichotomy paramount for his message."
